pages.markdown_text:
# Documentation

millivolt is one self-hosted service for routing model traffic across OpenAI
Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses and Anthropic Messages, seeing what happened,
and controlling the operator surface. Start with the path
that matches what you need to do.

## First ten minutes

1. [Install and first run](install.md) from Compose or a source checkout.
2. Send one request on a client protocol and find it in the
   [dashboard](dashboard.md).
3. Read [configuration](configuration.md) before changing the example or a
   setting.
4. Read [security](../SECURITY.md) before exposing the listener.
5. Keep [operations](operations.md) nearby for health, storage and the known
   limits.

## If you want to ...

| Task | Start with |
| --- | --- |
| Install and send a first request | [Install and first run](install.md) |
| Configure a setting, request override or provider alias | [Configuration](configuration.md) |
| Look up a setting's default or a CLI flag | [Settings reference](settings.md) |
| Expose the listener behind TLS or a network boundary | [Reverse proxy](reverse-proxy.md), [security](../SECURITY.md) |
| Debug a 429 or a 5xx | [Routes and debugging](routes.md#error-storm-protection), [pause and limits](routes.md#pause-and-limits) |
| Back up or restore | [Settings backup and restore](containers.md#settings-backup-and-restore), [image-only backup](containers.md#image-only-backup-and-restore), [online database backup](operations.md#storage-and-accounting) |
| Upgrade or restart | [Versions and images](containers.md#versions-and-images), [reload, restart and shutdown](containers.md#reload-restart-and-shutdown) |
| Integrate a client or translate between protocols | [Protocol](protocol.md), [adapters](adapters.md) |
| Drive the operator plane from an LLM | [MCP server](mcp.md) |
| Drive it from a terminal | [Operator CLI](cli.md) |
| Contribute a change | [Contributing](../CONTRIBUTING.md), [architecture](architecture.md), [support](../SUPPORT.md) |

The [operations overview](operations.md) owns health, storage and the runtime
cost model. Measurements live in [performance](performance.md); ownership and
invariants live in [architecture](architecture.md). Project pages are
[support](../SUPPORT.md), [releases](https://github.com/LLM-4-People/millivolt/releases),
[license](../LICENSE) and [third-party notices](../THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

## Verification and limitations

The generated [settings reference](settings.md) lists every setting and proxy
flag with its type, default, accepted values and reload behavior.
[proxy.example.yaml](../proxy.example.yaml) is the commented deployment example.
`internal/config` owns defaults, validation and Settings metadata; local
`proxy.yaml` is not a public reference or a test fixture.

Current commands live in [Contributing](../CONTRIBUTING.md#checks). Runtime
limits live in [operations](operations.md#known-limits); measurement caveats
live in [performance](performance.md#limitations). The
[architecture map](architecture.md) connects invariants to their shared
implementation and regression coverage. Past development notes are not an
operating guide or a capacity guarantee.

pages.markdown_text:
# Install and first run

Install millivolt from the published image or a source checkout, set the
operator credential, and send a first request on each client protocol. The
[quickstart](../README.md#quickstart) is the short form of the same procedure;
this page carries the full path.

## Before you start

The container path needs Linux with Docker Engine and the Compose plugin. No Go,
Node or source checkout is needed for it. The source path needs the Go toolchain
required by [go.mod](../go.mod).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> One shared operator credential protects the dashboard and operator plane only.
> Inference is transparent: it forwards your upstream key and does not use the
> operator token. There are no user accounts. Keep the listener on loopback, or
> put the network or ingress boundary in front. With the token unset, the
> dashboard denies every request. Read [Security](../SECURITY.md) before network
> exposure.

## Install with Docker Compose

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LLM-4-People/millivolt/main/compose.yaml -o compose.yaml
export MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN='replace-with-a-long-random-value'
docker compose up -d
```

Open [http://127.0.0.1:8080/](http://127.0.0.1:8080/) and sign in with that
token. If the container exits, run `docker compose logs --tail 50`.

The Compose file publishes on loopback only. It keeps history and settings in
named volumes, runs non-root with a read-only root filesystem, and accepts
`MILLIVOLT_PORT` for an unused host port. For bind mounts, pre-create
directories writable by UID/GID `65532:65532`; see
[persistent state](containers.md#persistent-state-and-configuration). For image
selection, backups, updates, shutdown, or protected ingress, see
[container operation](containers.md#containers) and the
[reverse-proxy guide](reverse-proxy.md).

The published image is `ghcr.io/llm-4-people/millivolt:main` for amd64 and
arm64. Version tags identify releases; pin a digest when exact bytes matter. See
[versions and images](containers.md#versions-and-images).

## Install from a source checkout

Install the Go toolchain required by [go.mod](../go.mod), then:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/LLM-4-People/millivolt.git
cd millivolt
test -e proxy.yaml || cp proxy.example.yaml proxy.yaml
export MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN='replace-with-a-long-random-value'
go run ./cmd/proxy -config proxy.yaml -listen 127.0.0.1:8080
```

For isolated development and checks, see [Contributing](../CONTRIBUTING.md).

## Environment and defaults

The Compose inputs are environment variables; their defaults live in
[compose.yaml](../compose.yaml), not server configuration. Supply them
consistently through the environment or an ignored local `.env` file.

| Variable | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN` | The single operator credential. It is read once at boot from the process environment and never from `proxy.yaml`, so rotating it requires a real process restart. A nonempty value shorter than 16 or longer than 512 bytes fails the boot. Unset or empty leaves the dashboard denied. |
| `MILLIVOLT_IMAGE` | Image reference; defaults to `ghcr.io/llm-4-people/millivolt:main`. |
| `MILLIVOLT_PORT` | Loopback host port; default `8080`. |
| `MILLIVOLT_STOP_GRACE_PERIOD` | Container stop grace; default `30s`. |
| `MILLIVOLT_MEM_LIMIT` | Container memory ceiling; default `1g`. |
| `MILLIVOLT_PIDS_LIMIT` | Process and thread ceiling; default `512`. |

`docker compose config` shows the resolved deployment. A source deployment
configures the same service through `-config PATH` (default local `proxy.yaml`),
`-listen ADDRESS` and `-db-path PATH`; the generated example and the Settings
schema are the field reference. See [configuration](configuration.md).

## Send a first request

Point a client at the proxy and supply the upstream base URL and key on each
request. The proxy registers no providers or keys. `X-Proxy-Format` selects a
different upstream protocol; absent, the request passes through. See
[protocol](protocol.md) and [adapters](adapters.md).

OpenAI Chat Completions:

```sh
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "X-Proxy-Base-URL: $UPSTREAM_BASE_URL" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $UPSTREAM_API_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$UPSTREAM_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"hello\"}]}"
```

OpenAI Responses:

```sh
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/responses \
  -H "X-Proxy-Base-URL: $UPSTREAM_BASE_URL" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $UPSTREAM_API_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$UPSTREAM_MODEL\",\"input\":\"hello\"}"
```

Anthropic Messages, using the native upstream's own auth header, prefix and API
version:

```sh
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/messages \
  -H "X-Proxy-Base-URL: $UPSTREAM_BASE_URL" \
  -H "X-Proxy-Key: $UPSTREAM_API_KEY" \
  -H 'X-Proxy-Auth-Header: x-api-key' \
  -H 'X-Proxy-Auth-Prefix;' \
  -H "anthropic-version: $ANTHROPIC_VERSION" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$UPSTREAM_MODEL\",\"max_tokens\":1024,\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"hello\"}]}"
```

The semicolon in `-H 'X-Proxy-Auth-Prefix;'` is important: curl sends a present
empty header. `-H 'X-Proxy-Auth-Prefix:'` instead omits it, leaving the proxy's
`Bearer ` default. A response means the proxy answered; check the status code
for the upstream outcome. The request appears in the dashboard.

On a shared Compose network, use `http://millivolt:8080/v1` instead of loopback.
`/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses` and `/v1/messages` are all available.
Each can reach Chat, Responses or Anthropic upstreams; only a Chat client can
target the Cursor bridge. Read
[upstream compatibility](adapters.md#client-and-upstream-compatibility) and
[cross-protocol translation](adapters.md#cross-protocol-translation).

## The dashboard

The dashboard is the site root, [http://127.0.0.1:8080/](http://127.0.0.1:8080/).
It asks for the operator token once per browser tab, keeps it in sessionStorage,
attaches it to gated calls only and drops it as soon as the server rejects it.
The same credential gates `/metrics/*`, `/admin/*` and `/mcp`; transparent
inference does not use it. See [operator access](routes.md#operator-access) for
the canonical open-path list.

## What to read next

[Documentation](README.md) routes by task. For the next step, read
[configuration](configuration.md) before changing settings, or
[the dashboard tour](dashboard.md) to find the request you just sent.

pages.title: Dashboard guide
pages.description: The overview shows the complete dashboard. Use this guide to follow its charts, explorer, request drawer, operator console and Settings without hunting...

sections.heading: Error storm banner
sections.text: When enabled in Settings, error storm protection adds a live banner below the header. Click an incident to inspect the number of requests with selected errors, failed upstream attempts, error category, queued requests, next retry time and recovery progress. It names the affected provider or exact provider/model, shows its safe error category, failed upstream-attempt percentage and window, queue count and recovery probe state. Provider incidents require all models active in the same window to have elevated errors. The banner shows that active-model evidence; its attempt percentage differs from the Errors chart's affected-request rate. It clears when protection recovers and can be hidden independently in Settings. See configuration and behavior . The static captures below show no banner because the capture session has no active incident; the banner stays hidden until protection fires.

sections.heading: Timelines
sections.text: The KPI band remains global. Explorer filters scope the timeline and request log together. The timeframe control in the card head changes chart history, not the global KPI band. It offers a zoom ladder from one minute through one year plus All time , and the calendar presets today, yesterday, this week and this month. Its panel draws the stored coverage as a rail and disables any window wider than the stored history, so a selection can never promise more history than exists; All time means exactly the retained history, and a calendar preset clamps its start to the oldest stored request. The selection persists per browser. Legend controls show or hide individual series; hover a bucket for its precise values and time interval. Counts, sums and percentiles come from the server. A window with fewer than four plotted points paints a waiting message instead of the chart: one to three buckets are too few to read a trend, and the totals strip still tells the story until a fourth point arrives. A span with no stored history says so; a span inside history with no requests says that instead. A failed chart request never blanks a good payload: one transient error should not hide the history yo

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Overview is the summary: it carries no plot at all. The tiles are the whole surface and they take the card - every headline metric reads its period value first, then its measured companion fact, then its evolution sparklines: requests / tokens (the request count over the blended token volume), tokens in/out/cached (one in / out / cached triple, with the input share of all tokens and the cache hit share of input underneath - each share line names what it compares), spend with the server's blended per-Mtok price (the same blended-price rule as the KPI band, scoped to the viewed period and cost-reporting requests only), the health pair (errors in the error red / rate-limited requests in the 429 tone, over the request denominator), and the merged timing tile: average latency / average speed over every measured request in the period (server-computed from the same samples the percentiles rank, never an average of bucket percentiles), each metric's low-high sample range underneath. Each tile carries one sparkline; combined tiles draw one self-scaled line per metric half in exactly the half's color. Sparks span only traffic-bearing buckets - the same empty-bucket removal the plots apply -

sections.heading: Traffic
sections.text: Traffic compares request and error counts. Bars represent bucket totals, not smoothed rates. Empty intervals may be omitted in this preset; the chart explains that below its legend.

sections.heading: Errors
sections.text: Errors compares the count of affected requests with an error-rate line on a separate percentage axis. A request that only encountered HTTP 429 is not an error. A recovered failure can still contribute an error signal.

sections.heading: Token usage
sections.text: Tokens compares input, output, reasoning and cached usage. The upstream's reported fields determine which splits are available. The compressed vertical scale keeps large prompt/cache volumes and small outputs readable together. A cache-hit line on a separate percentage axis tracks cached prompt tokens as a share of input per bucket. The totals strip adds each side's share of the blended total, the cache share of input, and the in:out tile: the raw pair (one line, halves in the token bars' colors) with the input share riding underneath - a percentage reads the same in every locale, where a small comma-decimal ratio looked like a count.

sections.heading: Speed and latency
sections.text: Speed + latency compares generation speed (first token to last token) with time to first token on separate axes. TTFT is measured from each request's upstream attempt send, so a retry has its own TTFT. One percentile dropdown controls both series; the legend does not repeat it. Choose p50, p95 or p99. Each statistic needs at least four valid samples; smaller sets and missing measurements remain unavailable. A bucket plots only when both measurements exist at the selected percentile, and those unmeasured buckets compact out of the timeline instead of stranding gap points in dead space - the context row below the plot says when that happened. Period readouts use the period's samples, not an average of bucket percentiles.

sections.heading: Provider-reported cost
sections.text: Cost shows reported spend alongside request counts. Values below $1 use cents, including tooltips and totals. Missing provider cost does not establish a zero bill, and there is no hardcoded per-model price table.

sections.heading: Explorer
sections.text: Changing the dimension in the rail changes the grouping, not the active filters. Selecting a card adds or replaces that dimension's exact filter; selecting it again removes it. Filters from other dimensions remain active. The breadcrumb chips remove individual selections or return to all traffic. The gallery ignores its own dimension's filter so alternatives remain visible; the timeline and request log still use the complete selected scope. Multi-valued dimensions, such as tools and errors, can overlap rather than partition requests. Dimension, in rail order What it groups Providers Server-derived upstream identities after configured aliases. Models Model groups produced by the configured canonicalization rules. Clients Explicit client labels or inferred SDK/User-Agent identities, retention-bounded before the ring and store. Conversations Conversation IDs from explicit sessions, tracked body params ( k: identities) or automatic grouping, with declared ancestry when resolvable. Selecting a conversation selects that leaf, not its descendants. Tools Observed tool names; one request can belong to several tools. Time Request start in the server's local timezone: weekday night 00:00-08:0

sections.heading: Providers
sections.text: Provider cards compare request share, reported cost, tokens, cache use, timing and health. Error and HTTP 429 badges count distinct affected requests and omit zero values independently. A request can contribute to both badges.

sections.heading: Models
sections.text: Model cards group configured model variants for comparison. The shipped rules fold provider decorations (vendor namespaces, tags, quantization, service tiers, release channels and build stamps) into the base model, so one model served by several providers is one card. Model tiers, fine-tunes and parameter counts stay distinct. Selecting a card scopes the timeline and request log together. Model grouping is configuration-owned; stored model spellings remain available for exact export and deletion filters. Adapters can normalize those spellings before storage; see request metadata . Conversation ancestry is explicit, not guessed from timing or names. The authorized snapshot has no parent declarations, so these screenshots do not fabricate an agent tree. See the client protocol for relationship headers and the limits of missing, conflicting or ambiguous declarations.

sections.heading: Request table
sections.text: The request table combines recent finalized records with current in-flight state during ordinary live use. Rows show status, retry information, latency, throughput, token/cache usage, tool calls, duration, queue time and reported cost. Columns size to their content and keep a per-column floor: a value wider than every value seen before grows its column, and a later shorter value never shrinks it back. A live row finalizing from streaming to its recorded status therefore cannot pull the status column back; a final value wider than its in-flight placeholder can still grow its own column once. When the card is narrower than the learned columns, the table scrolls inside its own region. The region is keyboard-scrollable and labelled, the identity cell carries the full client · provider · model value in a hover title, and compact status pills and the actions button abbreviate by design. Its status selector and older-history paging operate on the current scope.

sections.heading: Request details
sections.text: Click a row or its detail button to open the inspector. The header keeps the request identity and the previous/next controls. The summary below it shows the live or final status, method and path, client, provider and model, plus duration, TTFT, tokens, speed, cost and retries when captured. The full field inventory is classified into four sticky groups, each with the number of cards it contains: Request: identity, time bucket, request and response sizes, client/runtime, provider metadata, and captured model and parameters. Content: conversation and parent ids, turn and size composition, prompt and response previews. Usage: input, output, reasoning, answer, cache and generated tokens; timing, throughput, cost, transport decomposition, and tools. Diagnostics: queue and rate limits, absorbed retries, in-band upstream responses, response headers, and the Debug capture when one exists. Only the selected group is shown; its cards behave like the previous single page. Each card header can collapse or expand its section, and both the active group and collapse choices survive live updates until the inspector closes. Copy actions sit on the values that matter (identifiers, conversation ids,

sections.heading: Tokens and performance
sections.text: Open Usage for token splits, cache hit, generated-token composition, timestamps, the adopted attempt's send anchor, throughput, reported cost, finish state and transport timing. Absorbed retry attempts appear under Diagnostics when the selected request has them, each with its status, provider error detail, the attempt's own provider request id, and captured upstream server, model, processing and rate-limit facts. An in-band upstream response that arrived after a committed success is disclosed separately rather than presented as a retry. Clicking an absorbed attempt, a retry sub-row in the request table or an entry in the drawer's retry list opens that attempt's own detail view. These captures deliberately omit request content and Debug payloads; ordinary opt-in captures remain sensitive.

sections.heading: Operator console
sections.text: The header's operator readout is the one control surface. It stays in the header rail at every width, including the phone header; the theme tray and Settings sit behind the actions flyout there. It reads steady when no hold or capture is active, no limit policy is enforcing, no request is parked by the storm/quota gate and no restart is running, then one segment per active hold ( paused 1 ), capture session ( captures 1 ), enforcing limit policy ( limits 2 ) and gated request ( gated 3 ). A stored policy whose schedule window is closed enforces nothing, so it is named separately as off schedule N instead of being counted as a cap; the server owns that verdict and reports it per policy, so the header cannot re-derive a different answer from the stored minutes. The wording names the behaviour, because scheduled N read as "the cap is on a schedule and working" when it meant the opposite. While a rebuild runs, restarting comes first, with · step N when the server reports a real step. The counts are live state: a hold that expires, a stopped capture or a cleared limit leaves on the next state repaint. A hold takes the warning tone because it is the one state that stops live traffic; a r

sections.heading: Rule rows
sections.text: Every rule is one calibration line: a kind tag in its state color, the human scope, the caps or schedule, then a live column for occupancy and actions. The scope sentence is generated from the selector the server enforces, so an empty dimension reads inside the sentence instead of as a separate checklist. Every rule kind offers the dimensions its own matcher honours: a limit and a hold both scope on providers, models, clients, key hashes and conversations, because the scheduler matches both against one request identity, while a capture scopes on clients, providers and models. A limit row names its budgets and schedule plus any remaining request and token budget; who set it rides the row title rather than a third line. A hold row names its remaining time, its queue cap or queue unlimited , and its queued count. A capture row names its retained count, its run time, and its duration or until stopped . A row is the one edit target: activating it opens its composer in edit mode. The action column offers copy, which starts a draft from the same scope and schedule with no budgets, and the terminating action for that kind: remove, resume or stop. A copied limit that still matches its sourc

sections.heading: Composer anatomy
sections.text: Limits, pause and capture share one composer: a titled bench, one scope strip, budget or duration controls, a live preview sentence, and a footer with cancel and the one commit action. The composer opens above the rule list, so its form and its commit are in view the moment the operator asks for one. A phone pins that action row to the pane's bottom edge. The scope is one wrapping strip of dimension chips rather than five stacked rows. An unset dimension is a dim chip you click; a set one carries its values inside the same chip. One picker opens at a time, below the whole strip, with a filter only once the list is long enough to scan, the known values as checkable rows, and a free-value field except for key hashes. Provider, model, client and conversation scopes accept a typed value; the key scope lists only SHA-256 hashes already present in the live record ring. The preview states what the commit will enforce. Limits add concurrency, request and token budgets with their windows, an optional anti-burst ramp, and an optional day-of-week schedule with server-local from and to times. Burst control and schedule are peers on one row, each opening its own body below. A window is a native

sections.heading: Confirmation and the change ledger
sections.text: Removing a limit, resuming every hold, stopping every capture, draining the queue and restarting open the shared confirmation dialog. It states the consequence, focuses cancel first, and names the action on its confirm button. Individual stop, and a resume with nothing queued, commit directly; resuming a hold that has parked requests opens the shared confirmation first, because it releases that backlog to the provider. An edit commits when its composer is applied. All are recorded. The console footer is a bounded session ledger. It shows the newest change and offers Undo while that change has a defined inverse. Undo applies it once and appends an undid: ... receipt; the next change becomes the new undo target. The ledger has one owner: the console footer. Up to eight changes are retained for the page session. Changes without an inverse, such as a download or a restart, are recorded without an undo action. The ledger is browser memory, clears on reload and is not an audit log. A rejected write is named in the open pane, not hidden behind a closed panel.

sections.heading: Export
sections.text: The export section owns record exports. Choose all history or matching records. Matching records offers provider, model, client, conversation and status in the same one-strip selector the composer uses, then errors-only, debug-only, newer-than and older-than, plus an exact error type field. The receipt and its download stay in the same view as the filters that shape them. Provider, model and client merge the server's known vocabularies with whatever the live record ring holds, so a quiet proxy or a fresh restart still offers them; all four accept a typed value as well, so a dimension the server has never seen is not a dead end. Status is the one list-only dimension, because a status code is not a name anyone can type reliably. Both modes preview through the same server count: all history is the same predicate with an empty filter. The receipt always names the number of records the download will carry, the download stays disabled until a nonzero count is ready, and the ledger repeats that number. A mode switch invalidates the count rather than quoting the previous mode's total, and filter mode with nothing selected asks for a filter instead of counting the unfiltered set. Downloads

sections.heading: Request detail
sections.text: A request's detail drawer carries the two console prefills that record can seed: hold this scope and capture this scope . Both close the drawer and open a draft scoped to that request, so holding the client of a slow response does not require reading the value, closing the drawer and retyping it into a picker. They are prefills, not commits: the composer still gates every write, so no confirmation is added. The open is deferred one task, because the press that triggered it would otherwise reach the header's outside-press closer and dismiss the console it had just opened.

sections.heading: System
sections.text: The system section owns restart and the console's link to Settings. It explains the rebuild and handoff, lists the four steps as they actually start ( rebuild from source , finish in-flight streams , flush metrics to disk , start the new process ), and disables restart while a run is active or the build cannot restart in place. A restart asks for confirmation and is recorded in the ledger without an undo action. Queue bounds, retry budgets, storage, retention and dashboard cadence are Settings fields, not console policies; the section links there instead of duplicating them. Static captures of the operator console publish to docs/images/console/ from the same authorized history workflow as the rest of the gallery. The retired menu screenshots were removed with the menus they pictured, and the overview capture was retired with the traffic band it pictured; git history keeps them. The remaining captures are the neutral starting state of the sections they cover: no draft is committed, no rule is selected and no filter is armed. See routes and debugging for exact admission, filtering and failure behavior, containers and data for restart, and operations for persistence, before using the

sections.heading: Theme
sections.text: Theme has two surfaces and eight palettes. Each palette owns a complete surface family (base, panels, rail and borders), its accent family, and its shadow and veil hue, so a switch changes the shell rather than only a few accent edges. Clear is the light family; Black is the near-black family. Instrument (the default), Slate, Midnight, Nord, Forest, Rose, Ember and Contrast are available in both modes. Contrast is the maximum-separation palette: black with signal yellow in Black, white with black in Clear. The theme tray stays open while choosing and shows a two-pane comparator: the committed pair on the left and the candidate on the right. Both panes use the same token-faithful miniature with a three-color series legend; the captions outside the decorative panes name the committed and candidate pairs. The preview line stays muted while it reads "Preview: same" and takes primary ink only for a real candidate. Hovering or focusing a palette or surface updates only the preview pane and captions. Clicking, Enter or Space commits immediately and persists the pair; there is no apply step. Arrow keys, Home and End move focus and the preview cursor without committing, and the focused row

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text: Settings uses the same schema, validation and defaults as configuration files. Search finds fields across categories. Changed values are revision-checked; every row whose field is restart-bound carries its own restart marker instead of only a category banner. Closed vocabularies render as selects from the schema's choices , and duration/byte values are parsed and checked against the schema's numeric band before Apply. A read-only config disables its field controls, not only Apply. The category rail right-aligns its row counts beside the label; on a phone it becomes one horizontally scrollable chip strip so the field pane keeps the height. Switching categories resets the field scroller, and the footer status is a live region with a distinct error tone. Structured fields replace their whole map/list value rather than recursively merging nested entries. The generated configuration example documents every field, including categories not pictured here.

sections.heading: Dashboard cadence
sections.text: Dashboard settings control log-window size and polling/aggregate refresh cadence. Live rows and the in-flight gauge remain distinct from periodic chart and explorer aggregation.

sections.heading: Queue and retry
sections.text: Queue and retry settings bound admission and retry behavior. Their help text distinguishes queue waiting, provider retry hints, retry budgets and capacity. Tune them for the upstream and workload; the picture uses the public example.

sections.heading: Storage
sections.text: Storage settings control the SQLite writer and its bounded queue/batches. Metrics persistence is best-effort under sustained overload; a successful inference response does not prove its record was stored. The dashboard reports process-local storage drops. The category also carries both database deletion controls, which live here and nowhere else: Delete matching removes only the records matching its provider, model, client, status, errors, debug and age filters after a live count preview and a confirmation, and Delete everything permanently deletes all metrics history, the live ring and the entire durable database. Neither action can be undone.

sections.heading: Provider compatibility
sections.text: The example enables Grok, OpenCode Zen and Cursor compatibility profiles without credentials or upstream registrations. Their headers and metadata mappings are editable operator-selected snapshots, not guaranteed current provider contracts. See adapters before relying on them. See Contributing before refreshing the gallery. Never publish private configuration, bodies, credentials or raw history copies.

pages.markdown_text:
# Dashboard guide

The [overview](../README.md#dashboard-overview) shows the complete dashboard.
Use this guide to follow its charts, explorer, request drawer, operator console
and Settings without hunting through the interface.

These are real application captures from explicitly authorized local history.
Recorded timing, token and cost values are retained; identifiers are replaced,
and request content, retained headers, debug captures and operator state are
removed. Settings and the theme tray show the public example, not private
configuration.
No requests, holds, limits or debug sessions were created to make the pictures.
The capture session blocks external requests and disables live SSE, so its
**offline** indicator describes a static screenshot session, not service health.
The images are not latency guarantees, capacity measurements or independent bills.

## Error storm banner

When enabled in Settings, error storm protection adds a live banner below the
header. Click an incident to inspect the number of requests with selected
errors, failed upstream attempts, error category, queued requests, next retry
time and recovery progress. It names the affected provider or exact provider/model, shows its safe
error category, failed upstream-attempt percentage and window, queue count and
recovery probe state. Provider incidents require all models active in the same
window to have elevated errors. The banner shows that active-model evidence;
its attempt percentage differs from the Errors chart's affected-request rate.
It clears when protection recovers and can be hidden independently in Settings.
See [configuration and behavior](routes.md#error-storm-protection).
The static captures below show no banner because the capture session has no
active incident; the banner stays hidden until protection fires.

## Timelines

The KPI band remains global. Explorer filters scope the timeline and request log
together. The timeframe control in the card head changes chart history, not the
global KPI band. It offers a zoom ladder from one minute through one year plus
**All time**, and the calendar presets today, yesterday, this week and this
month. Its panel draws the stored coverage as a rail and disables any window
wider than the stored history, so a selection can never promise more history
than exists; **All time** means exactly the retained history, and a calendar
preset clamps its start to the oldest stored request. The selection persists per
browser.
Legend controls show or hide individual series; hover a bucket for its precise
values and time interval. Counts, sums and percentiles come from the server.
A window with fewer than four plotted points paints a waiting message instead
of the chart: one to three buckets are too few to read a trend, and the totals
strip still tells the story until a fourth point arrives. A span with no stored
history says so; a span inside history with no requests says that instead.

A failed chart request never blanks a good payload: one transient error should
not hide the history you were reading. The context row states which of the two
situations applies. With nothing drawn it reads `chart unavailable - retrying`;
with a last-good payload still on screen it reads the window and `stale,
retrying`, so old buckets are never presented as a current reading. Either way
the next successful request clears it.

The **In-flight** KPI tile separates sending work from parked work. Its summary
names two totals that fit the narrowest tile - active and queued - and the
composition rail under the value splits every live state by color: sending,
pending, operator-paused and throttled. Hover the rail, or focus it with
assistive technology, for the exact per-state counts. Queued covers both the
admission queue (per-key concurrency, pacing, provider caps, operator holds) and
the retry send gate, so a provider's 429 pacing window shows its parked
requests as queued instead of as idle streams. The request table's `throttled`
pill marks the same state per row.

### Overview

**Overview** is the summary: it carries no plot at all. The tiles are the
whole surface and they take the card - every headline metric reads its period
value first, then its measured companion fact, then its evolution sparklines:
requests / tokens (the request count over the blended token volume), tokens
in/out/cached (one in / out / cached triple, with the input share of all
tokens and the cache hit share of input underneath - each share line names
what it compares), spend with the
server's blended per-Mtok price (the same blended-price rule as the KPI band,
scoped to the viewed period and cost-reporting requests only), the health pair
(errors in the error red / rate-limited requests in the 429 tone, over the
request denominator), and
the merged timing tile: average latency / average speed over every measured
request in the period (server-computed from the same samples the percentiles
rank, never an average of bucket percentiles), each metric's low-high sample
range underneath. Each tile carries one sparkline; combined tiles draw one
self-scaled line per metric half in exactly the half's color. Sparks span
only traffic-bearing buckets - the same empty-bucket removal the plots
apply - so window padding never squeezes the data into a corner. The
metrics picker in the card head chooses what shows: one menu of
checkable rows, checked metrics render and unchecked ones leave the band
(it reflows), and the selection persists per browser like every chart
view. Every selected tile always renders in both layouts: the band wraps
into as many whole rows of 170px tracks as the card needs, and the page
scrolls past them in the base layout; the picker's count reports the
selection itself, so it can never disagree with the band. The wide layout is
the 1200x750 one-screen lock: the page locks to the viewport with no
scrolling, the explorer compresses to one gallery row, and the timeline
column floors at 572px so the 5-metric selection wraps into at most two
rows. Every tile keeps one fixed size whatever it carries - spark or not,
one share line or two, and the no-data skeleton swaps in without moving the
card - and the band sits at its natural height at the top of the card.
Only the timeframe control applies. This preset has
no static capture yet; the gallery capture selects the plotted presets only,
so no tiles capture exists.

### Traffic

**Traffic** compares request and error counts. Bars represent bucket totals,
not smoothed rates. Empty intervals may be omitted in this preset; the chart
explains that below its legend.

![Traffic timeline with request and error counts from recorded history](images/charts/traffic.png)

### Errors

**Errors** compares the count of affected requests with an error-rate line on
a separate percentage axis. A request that only encountered HTTP 429 is not
an error. A recovered failure can still contribute an error signal.

![Error timeline with affected-request bars and a separate percentage axis](images/charts/errors.png)

### Token usage

**Tokens** compares input, output, reasoning and cached usage. The upstream's
reported fields determine which splits are available. The compressed vertical
scale keeps large prompt/cache volumes and small outputs readable together.
A cache-hit line on a separate percentage axis tracks cached prompt tokens as
a share of input per bucket. The totals strip adds each side's share of the
blended total, the cache share of input, and the in:out tile: the raw pair
(one line, halves in the token bars' colors) with the input share riding
underneath - a percentage reads the same in every locale, where a small
comma-decimal ratio looked like a count.

![Token timeline with input, output, reasoning and cached usage](images/charts/tokens.png)

### Speed and latency

**Speed + latency** compares generation speed (first token to last token) with
time to first token on separate axes. TTFT is measured from each request's
upstream attempt send, so a retry has its own TTFT. One percentile dropdown
controls both series; the legend does not repeat it. Choose p50, p95 or p99. Each
statistic needs at least four valid samples; smaller sets and missing
measurements remain unavailable. A bucket plots only when both measurements
exist at the selected percentile, and those unmeasured buckets compact out of the
timeline instead of stranding gap points in dead space - the context row below
the plot says when that happened.
Period readouts use the period's samples, not an average of bucket percentiles.

![Speed and latency timeline with independent axes and percentile control](images/charts/speed-latency.png)

### Provider-reported cost

**Cost** shows reported spend alongside request counts. Values below $1 use
cents, including tooltips and totals. Missing provider cost does not establish
a zero bill, and there is no hardcoded per-model price table.

![Cost timeline with spend and request-count axes](images/charts/cost.png)

## Explorer

Changing the dimension in the rail changes the grouping, not the active filters.
Selecting a card adds or replaces that dimension's exact filter; selecting it
again removes it. Filters from other dimensions remain active. The breadcrumb
chips remove individual selections or return to all traffic.

The gallery ignores its own dimension's filter so alternatives remain visible;
the timeline and request log still use the complete selected scope. Multi-valued
dimensions, such as tools and errors, can overlap rather than partition requests.

| Dimension, in rail order | What it groups |
| --- | --- |
| Providers | Server-derived upstream identities after configured aliases. |
| Models | Model groups produced by the configured canonicalization rules. |
| Clients | Explicit client labels or inferred SDK/User-Agent identities, retention-bounded before the ring and store. |
| Conversations | Conversation IDs from explicit sessions, tracked body params (`k:` identities) or automatic grouping, with declared ancestry when resolvable. Selecting a conversation selects that leaf, not its descendants. |
| Tools | Observed tool names; one request can belong to several tools. |
| Time | Request start in the server's local timezone: weekday night 00:00-08:00, work 08:00-16:00, evening 16:00-24:00, or a single weekend group. This is separate from chart history range. |
| Status | Coarse outcome classes and live states. The Requests dropdown instead selects exact HTTP codes or named live states, grouped into live states and HTTP status; it stays a native select so the operating system picker is the touch affordance. |
| Errors | Distinct observed error identities, including absorbed failures; one request can have several. HTTP 429 alone is not an error. |
| Keys | SHA-256 hashes of upstream credentials, never raw keys. Labels show only an eight-hex-character prefix; identical short labels do not establish identical full hashes. |

### Providers

Provider cards compare request share, reported cost, tokens, cache use, timing
and health. Error and HTTP 429 badges count distinct affected requests and omit
zero values independently. A request can contribute to both badges.

![Provider explorer with pseudonymous groups, recorded costs and health signals](images/explorer/providers.png)

### Models

Model cards group configured model variants for comparison. The shipped rules
fold provider decorations (vendor namespaces, tags, quantization, service tiers,
release channels and build stamps) into the base model, so one model served by
several providers is one card. Model tiers, fine-tunes and parameter counts stay
distinct. Selecting a card scopes the timeline and request log together. Model
grouping is configuration-owned; stored model spellings remain available for
exact export and deletion filters.
Adapters can normalize those spellings before storage; see
[request metadata](routes.md#request-rows-and-details).

![Model explorer with pseudonymous model groups and recorded usage metrics](images/explorer/models.png)

Conversation ancestry is explicit, not guessed from timing or names. The
authorized snapshot has no parent declarations, so these screenshots do not
fabricate an agent tree. See the [client protocol](protocol.md) for relationship
headers and the limits of missing, conflicting or ambiguous declarations.

## Request inspection

### Request table

The request table combines recent finalized records with current in-flight
state during ordinary live use. Rows show status, retry information, latency,
throughput, token/cache usage, tool calls, duration, queue time and reported cost.
Columns size to their content and keep a per-column floor: a value wider than
every value seen before grows its column, and a later shorter value never
shrinks it back. A live row finalizing from `streaming` to its recorded status
therefore cannot pull the status column back; a final value wider than its
in-flight placeholder can still grow its own column once. When the card is
narrower than the learned columns, the table scrolls inside its own region.
The region is keyboard-scrollable and labelled, the identity cell carries the full
`client · provider · model` value in a hover title, and compact status pills and
the actions button abbreviate by design. Its status selector and older-history
paging operate on the current scope.

![Request table with recorded statuses, token usage, latency, throughput and cost](images/requests/table.png)

### Request details

Click a row or its detail button to open the inspector. The header keeps the
request identity and the previous/next controls. The summary below it shows the
live or final status, method and path, client, provider and model, plus
duration, TTFT, tokens, speed, cost and retries when captured. The full field
inventory is classified into four sticky groups, each with the number of cards
it contains:

- Request: identity, time bucket, request and response sizes, client/runtime,
  provider metadata, and captured model and parameters.
- Content: conversation and parent ids, turn and size composition, prompt and
  response previews.
- Usage: input, output, reasoning, answer, cache and generated tokens; timing,
  throughput, cost, transport decomposition, and tools.
- Diagnostics: queue and rate limits, absorbed retries, in-band upstream
  responses, response headers, and the Debug capture when one exists.

Only the selected group is shown; its cards behave like the previous single
page. Each card header can collapse or expand its section, and both the active
group and collapse choices survive live updates until the inspector closes.
Copy actions sit on the values that matter (identifiers, conversation ids,
paths, models, headers, error detail and captured bodies), on field-list cards,
and on the header's JSON action for the whole record or the selected attempt.
One polite status line confirms each copy or reports a denied clipboard write.

Long values wrap. Captured prompt, response and Debug bodies open in a bounded
code surface with a line count, wrap toggle, copy action and expand/collapse
control; a long single line scrolls inside that surface instead of widening the
inspector. A final upstream failure appears as a bordered alert above the cards
with its type, code, message and copy action, plus the HTTP status when the
failure was an HTTP response. A rate limit the provider announced in its own
type or code counts in the rate-limit card even when the status was not 429;
a request that ended on one still appears as an alert, and a bare 429 stays
the flow-control handshake it is. On narrow
viewports the inspector fills the width, stacks each key above its value, keeps
touch-sized copy and close targets, and respects the bottom safe area.

Previous/next controls follow the scoped table order. Explicit zero and false
parameter values are retained instead of treated as missing. While a request is
in flight, pause and throttle state appear as explicit rows.

![Request drawer showing pseudonymous identity, the summary readout and recorded request parameters](images/requests/details.png)

### Tokens and performance

Open Usage for token splits, cache hit, generated-token composition,
timestamps, the adopted attempt's send anchor, throughput, reported cost, finish
state and transport timing. Absorbed retry attempts appear under Diagnostics
when the selected request has them, each with its status, provider error detail,
the attempt's own provider request id, and captured upstream server, model,
processing and rate-limit facts. An in-band upstream response that arrived
after a committed success is disclosed separately rather than presented as a
retry. Clicking an absorbed attempt, a retry sub-row in the request table or
an entry in the drawer's retry list opens that attempt's own detail view. These
captures deliberately omit request content and Debug payloads; ordinary opt-in
captures remain sensitive.

![The same request drawer showing token and performance measurements](images/requests/performance.png)

## Operator console

The header's operator readout is the one control surface. It stays in the
header rail at every width, including the phone header; the theme tray and
Settings sit behind the actions flyout there. It reads `steady` when no hold or
capture is active, no limit policy is enforcing, no request is parked by the
storm/quota gate and no restart is running, then one segment per active hold
(`paused 1`), capture session (`captures 1`), enforcing limit policy
(`limits 2`) and gated request (`gated 3`). A stored policy whose schedule
window is closed enforces nothing, so it is named separately as
`off schedule N` instead of being counted as a cap; the server owns that
verdict and reports it per policy, so the header cannot re-derive a different
answer from the stored minutes. The wording names the behaviour, because
`scheduled N` read as "the cap is on a schedule and working" when it meant the
opposite.
While a rebuild runs, `restarting` comes first, with ` · step N` when the server
reports a real step. The counts are live state: a hold that expires, a stopped
capture or a cleared limit leaves on the next state repaint. A hold takes the
warning tone because it is the one state that stops live traffic; a restart
takes it too, with a pulsing dot. If the live stream was open and then drops,
the line keeps its last known words and appends ` · offline`; if the operator
poll instead stops answering, it appends ` · stale`. Both mark the words as last
known rather than current. The header readout is not a live region; it
updates when operator state, connectivity or restart status changes, and the
trigger's accessible label carries the same words plus the action the trigger
performs in its current state. The open console's head line repeats those words
without a second total and is a polite live region.

Activating the readout opens the console. On a wide viewport it is an anchored
popover under the trigger: 520px wide, and only as tall as its content up to a
560px cap, scrolling inside it. At 800px or narrower it becomes a bottom sheet
with a definite height of `min(88dvh, 100dvh - 16px)`, leaving a strip of page
above it for outside-press dismissal. The height is definite rather than a
cap: the body and the pane grow into the remainder, so a tall composer scrolls
inside the pane instead of being clipped by the panel. On a landscape phone
(800px or narrower and 500px or shorter) the header, rail, pane and ledger
tighten and the sheet gives up its top gap, sitting flush with the top edge so
only the 8px bottom dismissal strip remains; a very short viewport turns every
fixed band into space the form loses. The section rail is one
horizontally scrollable strip and fades its trailing edge while more sections
remain; at 560px or narrower, where six chips genuinely cannot share one row,
it becomes a two-row grid. That threshold is the content, not the device class:
a landscape phone is 640-844 wide and keeps the single-row strip. Escape, an
outside press, the close button, or
opening the theme tray or Settings closes it; opening the console closes the
theme tray and Settings first. The session remembers the last section, so
reopening returns where the operator left. Opening the console itself performs
no action.

The rail names six sections: overview, limits, pause, capture, export and
system. Limits, pause and capture carry a count badge: for limits the number of
rules enforcing right now, for pause the active holds, for capture the running
capture sessions. A rule outside its schedule window is installed but enforcing
nothing, so it does not raise the limits badge. The overview is the rule
register: one row per hold, capture and every installed limit, each jumping to
the section that owns it, with an off-schedule limit marked `off schedule`
rather than reading as a live cap, plus the queue drain
control when requests are actually parked. A request parked by the storm/quota
gate is named in its own block instead: that gate runs before admission, so a
drain cannot release it, and the block points at the controls that can. The
counts are not repeated there, because the head line and the section badges
already state them. Limits, pause and capture hold rule rows and one composer;
export holds the download builder, and system holds the restart and Settings
cards.

### Rule rows

Every rule is one calibration line: a kind tag in its state color, the human
scope, the caps or schedule, then a live column for occupancy and actions. The
scope sentence is generated from the selector the server enforces, so an empty
dimension reads inside the sentence instead of as a separate checklist. Every
rule kind offers the dimensions its own matcher honours: a limit and a hold both
scope on providers, models, clients, key hashes and conversations, because the
scheduler matches both against one request identity, while a capture scopes on
clients, providers and models. A limit
row names its budgets and schedule plus any remaining request and token budget;
who set it rides the row title rather than a third line. A hold row names its
remaining time, its queue cap or `queue unlimited`, and its queued count. A
capture row names its retained count, its run time, and its duration or
`until stopped`. A row is the one edit target: activating it opens
its composer in edit mode. The action column offers copy, which starts a draft
from the same scope and schedule with no budgets, and the terminating action for
that kind: remove, resume or stop. A copied limit that still matches its source
selector is refused and named, because a limit's identity is its selector:
applying it would edit the original rather than add a second rule. The edit action is not repeated
there, because the row already performs it. On a narrow phone the row takes
two lines so the scope can be read in full instead of being clipped; the
budget wraps beneath the scope rather than being dropped, because a limit's
scope identifies it while its budget is what it does.

A rule list that outgrows the pane offers a filter once it holds enough rules
to need one, so a console with two rules never spends a row on an empty box.
The filter matches the text each row already renders, which gives limits,
pause and capture one search rule and makes a new row field searchable
without a second list of what to match. A filter that hides everything says
how many rules are in force and offers to clear itself, so an empty result
never reads as an empty policy.

### Composer anatomy

Limits, pause and capture share one composer: a titled bench, one scope strip,
budget or duration controls, a live preview sentence, and a footer with cancel
and the one commit action. The composer opens above the rule list, so its form
and its commit are in view the moment the operator asks for one. A phone pins
that action row to the pane's bottom edge.

The scope is one wrapping strip of dimension chips rather than five stacked
rows. An unset dimension is a dim chip you click; a set one carries its values
inside the same chip. One picker opens at a time, below the whole strip, with a
filter only once the list is long enough to scan, the known values as checkable
rows, and a free-value field except for key hashes. Provider, model, client and
conversation scopes accept a typed value; the key scope lists only SHA-256
hashes already present in the live record ring. The preview states what the
commit will enforce.

Limits add concurrency, request and token budgets with their windows, an
optional anti-burst ramp, and an optional day-of-week schedule with
server-local from and to times. Burst control and schedule are peers on one
row, each opening its own body below. A window is a native select: the list is
long and the track is one number wide, so the current choice is stated in one
line and the rest is the platform's own picker. The ramp is offered only on a single-provider
rule without a schedule. Equal from and to times mean all day, and a window
that starts after its end spans midnight. Pause adds everything, new-clients
and named clients/providers modes, a duration or until-resumed choice, and an
optional queue cap. Its head also carries a one-click bounded hold (`hold all
15m`), which writes the same all-traffic document through the same gate,
ledger and undo path. It is bounded by construction: an indefinite hold is
still available, but only through the composer where the operator chooses it. Capture starts a scoped Debug session and adds client,
provider and model scopes, a duration or until-stopped choice, and the retention
and byte facts for the current configuration.

### Confirmation and the change ledger

Removing a limit, resuming every hold, stopping every capture, draining the
queue and restarting open the shared confirmation dialog. It states the
consequence, focuses cancel first, and names the action on its confirm button.
Individual stop, and a resume with nothing queued, commit directly; resuming a
hold that has parked requests opens the shared confirmation first, because it
releases that backlog to the provider. An edit commits when its composer is
applied. All are recorded.

The console footer is a bounded session ledger. It shows the newest change and
offers Undo while that change has a defined inverse. Undo applies it once and
appends an `undid: ...` receipt; the next change becomes the new undo target.
The ledger has one owner: the console footer. Up to eight changes are retained
for the page session. Changes without an inverse, such as a download
or a restart, are recorded without an undo action. The ledger is browser
memory, clears on reload and is not an audit log. A rejected write is named in
the open pane, not hidden behind a closed panel.

### Export

The export section owns record exports. Choose all history or matching
records. Matching records offers provider, model, client, conversation and
status in the same one-strip selector the composer uses, then errors-only,
debug-only, newer-than and older-than, plus an exact error type field. The
receipt and its download stay in the same view as the filters that shape them.

Provider, model and client merge the server's known vocabularies with whatever
the live record ring holds, so a quiet proxy or a fresh restart still offers
them; all four accept a typed value as well, so a dimension the server has
never seen is not a dead end. Status is the one list-only dimension, because a
status code is not a name anyone can type reliably.

Both modes preview through the same server count: all history is the same
predicate with an empty filter. The receipt always names the number of records
the download will carry, the download stays disabled until a nonzero count is
ready, and the ledger repeats that number. A mode switch invalidates the count
rather than quoting the previous mode's total, and filter mode with nothing
selected asks for a filter instead of counting the unfiltered set.

Downloads are gzip JSON artifacts. Configuration and database backups stay in
Settings, and the console links there.

### Request detail

A request's detail drawer carries the two console prefills that record can
seed: `hold this scope` and `capture this scope`. Both close the drawer and open
a draft scoped to that request, so holding the client of a slow response does
not require reading the value, closing the drawer and retyping it into a picker.
They are prefills, not commits: the composer still gates every write, so no
confirmation is added. The open is deferred one task, because the press that
triggered it would otherwise reach the header's outside-press closer and
dismiss the console it had just opened.

### System

The system section owns restart and the console's link to Settings. It explains
the rebuild and handoff, lists the four steps as they actually start (`rebuild
from source`, `finish in-flight streams`, `flush metrics to disk`, `start the
new process`), and disables restart while a run is active or the build cannot
restart in place. A restart asks for confirmation and is recorded in the ledger
without an undo action. Queue bounds, retry budgets, storage, retention and
dashboard cadence are Settings fields, not console policies; the section links
there instead of duplicating them.

Static captures of the operator console publish to `docs/images/console/` from
the same authorized history workflow as the rest of the gallery. The retired
menu screenshots were removed with the menus they pictured, and the overview
capture was retired with the traffic band it pictured; git history keeps them.
The remaining captures are the neutral starting state of the sections they
cover: no draft is committed, no rule is selected and no filter is armed.

![Limits section with no policy set](images/console/limits.png)

![Pause section before any hold exists](images/console/pause.png)

![Capture section with no session start](images/console/capture.png)

![Export section previewing the whole-history record count](images/console/export.png)

![System section with restart available and the step list](images/console/system.png)

See [routes and debugging](routes.md) for exact admission, filtering and
failure behavior, [containers and data](containers.md) for restart, and
[operations](operations.md) for persistence, before using these controls.

## Theme

Theme has two surfaces and eight palettes. Each palette owns a complete
surface family (base, panels, rail and borders), its accent family, and its
shadow and veil hue, so a switch changes the shell rather than only a few
accent edges. Clear is the light family; Black is the near-black family.
Instrument (the default), Slate, Midnight, Nord, Forest, Rose, Ember and
Contrast are available in both modes. Contrast is the maximum-separation
palette: black with signal yellow in Black, white with black in Clear. The
theme tray stays open while choosing and shows a two-pane comparator: the
committed pair on the left and the candidate on the right. Both panes use the
same token-faithful miniature with a three-color series legend; the captions
outside the decorative panes name the committed and candidate pairs. The
preview line stays muted while it reads "Preview: same" and takes primary ink
only for a real candidate. Hovering or focusing a palette or surface updates
only the preview pane and captions. Clicking, Enter or Space commits
immediately and persists the pair; there is no apply step. Arrow keys, Home and
End move focus and the preview cursor without committing, and the focused row
keeps the group's single tab stop so Tab leaves and returns to it. The current
surface's Clear/Black radios sit under a visible Surface label in the caption
bar. Pointer activation commits without writing the polite candidate status;
only keyboard focus announces a preview. The trigger's arrow keys open the tray
on the saved palette; while open they move the preview cursor. Reset restores
Instrument Black; Close only dismisses the tray.

On touch or coarse pointers the comparator, preview line and hover hint are
hidden, leaving the current caption, the surface control, all eight palette
rows, Reset and Close. A window 800px wide or narrower uses the same compact
picker inside the header actions flyout even with a fine pointer, and the
flyout rather than the tray or palette list is the one vertical scroller. At a
viewport height of 760px or below the comparator, preview line and hint are
hidden. In windows wider than 800px the tray scrolls so every action remains
reachable; narrower windows keep the header flyout as the single scroller. At
360px or below the caption bar stacks into one column with a full-width surface
control, and the palette hints are hidden while names and swatches remain.
Reopening the tray or flyout brings the saved palette row into view instead of
restoring an arbitrary previous scroll offset. The choice is stored in
this browser only and is applied before the first paint, so a reload does not
flash the default. Charts follow the selected palette; status colors follow the
selected surface, and the browser's theme color follows the selected palette's
rail. The setting is presentation only: it does not change proxy behavior,
stored history or the configuration revision.

## Settings

Settings uses the same schema, validation and defaults as configuration files.
Search finds fields across categories. Changed values are revision-checked;
every row whose field is restart-bound carries its own `restart` marker instead
of only a category banner. Closed vocabularies render as selects from the
schema's `choices`, and duration/byte values are parsed and checked against the
schema's numeric band before Apply. A read-only config disables its field
controls, not only Apply. The category rail right-aligns its row counts beside
the label; on a phone it becomes one horizontally scrollable chip strip so the
field pane keeps the height. Switching categories resets the field scroller,
and the footer status is a live region with a distinct error tone. Structured
fields replace their whole map/list value rather than recursively merging
nested entries. The generated [configuration example](../proxy.example.yaml)
documents every field, including categories not pictured here.

### Dashboard cadence

Dashboard settings control log-window size and polling/aggregate refresh
cadence. Live rows and the in-flight gauge remain distinct from periodic chart
and explorer aggregation.

![Settings dialog showing public dashboard configuration fields](images/settings/dashboard.png)

### Queue and retry

Queue and retry settings bound admission and retry behavior. Their help text
distinguishes queue waiting, provider retry hints, retry budgets and capacity.
Tune them for the upstream and workload; the picture uses the public example.

![Queue and retry Settings with their public values and field descriptions](images/settings/queue.png)

### Storage

Storage settings control the SQLite writer and its bounded queue/batches.
Metrics persistence is best-effort under sustained overload; a successful
inference response does not prove its record was stored. The dashboard reports
process-local storage drops. The category also carries both database
deletion controls, which live here and nowhere else: Delete matching removes
only the records matching its provider, model, client, status, errors, debug
and age filters after a live count preview and a confirmation, and Delete
everything permanently deletes all metrics history, the live ring and the
entire durable database. Neither action can be undone.

![Storage Settings with bounded writer, queue, persistence and deletion controls](images/settings/storage.png)

### Provider compatibility

The example enables Grok, OpenCode Zen and Cursor compatibility profiles
without credentials or upstream registrations. Their headers and metadata
mappings are editable operator-selected snapshots, not guaranteed current
provider contracts. See [adapters](adapters.md#bundled-compatibility-profiles)
before relying on them.

![Provider Settings showing the public Cursor compatibility profile](images/settings/providers.png)

See [Contributing](../CONTRIBUTING.md#documentation-screenshots) before refreshing
the gallery. Never publish private configuration, bodies, credentials or raw
history copies.

Larger requests are rejected with HTTP 413 without an upstream send. A decoded output cap above 1,000,000 tokens is rejected with HTTP 400 the same way, before any upstream send and at both trust boundaries - the original body's decode and the re-decode of a translated body - for any spelling ( max_tokens , max_completion_tokens or max_output_tokens ). More than one top-level member that folds to the same cap name is also rejected with HTTP 400 before an upstream send, including case variants and escaped spellings: the relay sends every occurrence, so accepting duplicates would let the validated and recorded value differ from the bytes the upstream reads. Queue capacity and wait limits can reject work locally; the configured queue_retry_after duration (for example 2s , never a bare integer) supplies the caller's retry hint. Operator-hold time is excluded from the ordinary queue-wait limit. A hold's own queue cap still applies. For the HTTP relay, upstream_timeout limits waiting for response headers, not the streaming body. X-Proxy-Timeout-Ms instead gives each upstream send a fresh deadline covering headers and body. Neither is a total end-to-end deadline across queueing, holds, retries and backoff; client cancellation is the way to stop the whole request. The request-body progress bound applies only while the body is being read. sections.text: Enable storm_enabled in Settings to add shared provider/model protection to existing admission and retry pacing. Requests wait in the proxy with the caller connected; this is not a client SDK queue. The proxy keeps the existing bounded request bytes and credentials only for the request lifetime. Queues are in memory, cannot survive a restart, and stop waiting when the caller cancels. Each exact recorded model name within its resolved provider has a rolling storm_window . A model qualifies when its sampled attempts meet storm_min_samples and its selected-failure percentage reaches storm_error_percent . Provider-wide protection requires every active model to qualify, as well as the aggregate sample/rate threshold. Only models receiving requests within that same window are active; an idle model or an unused model in a provider catalog cannot affect that decision. This scope combines credentials and clients. sections.heading: Model discovery
sections.text: GET /v1/models and GET /models are constructed discovery services, not ordinary inference records. The proxy normalizes recognized model lists, translates native formats, completes supported pagination, and optionally enriches missing fields. Unrecognized successful list bodies remain verbatim; primary discovery budget/errors fail explicitly, while optional enrichment can fall back to the complete base list. Discovery can apply limit headers without consuming an inference slot. Its time/byte/page/entry limits are configuration-owned. Primary and enrichment entries share one models_discovery_max_entries budget (default 10,000); enrichment degrades to the base list when the remaining budget cannot hold its metadata source. The rendered list is bounded by models_discovery_max_bytes plus a fixed per-entry normalization allowance (512 bytes for each configured entry) and is encoded without HTML escaping, so literal < , > , and & keep their wire size. A rendered list past that derived bound fails closed before any response bytes are written. sections.heading: Automatic grouping
sections.text: An explicit X-Proxy-Session takes precedence, then a configured tracked body param (see tracked body params ). Without either, the tracker partitions requests by client label and credential hash, then compares total user/assistant/tool turn counts against its open conversations. A nonexpired conversation with the greatest previous count no larger than the new count is the nearest match. A reset or idle gap can start another conversation, and the configured open-session cap evicts the oldest tracked conversation in that partition. This is a heuristic for clients that send conversation history, not a content comparison or a universal agent identity. Parallel tasks with similar turn counts can be ambiguous. Tracker state is process-local, so use explicit session IDs when predictable continuity matters and keep the client/key namespace stable. Automatic grouping never establishes a parent/child relationship.

sections.heading: Tracked body params
sections.text: The request body is client data, and one field can double as the conversation identity. When sub_conversations names the request's classified client, the tracked field the client already sends (exemplar: opencode's promptCacheKey ) supplies that request's identity in the k: namespace: behind an explicit X-Proxy-Session , ahead of automatic grouping. Params match only top-level body fields, checked in order. The first present field decides: a present value that is not a JSON string counts as absent and the next field is checked, while a present string that cannot be decoded or fails the identity rules drops the identity for the request - no later field is consulted. A top-level field that occurs more than once is ambiguous and drops the identity the same way, leaving the request on automatic grouping. The body is relayed unchanged unless the entry sets strip , which removes the entry's configured fields from the top level of the client request body before relay or translation. It applies to any JSON body, including a Responses client body. A request translated to the Anthropic wire gains a top-level prompt_cache_key carrying the tracked value.
