pages.markdown_text:
# MCP server

The proxy's own `/mcp` endpoint exposes millivolt's operator and
observability API to an LLM, using the official
[Model Context Protocol Go SDK](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk).
It is a client of a running proxy: it never starts, stops or restarts the proxy
process. Its operator tools can reconfigure a running proxy, but only through
the same credential and the same routes the dashboard uses.

The endpoint serves 25 tools from one implementation. It is operator-gated
and Bearer-only, enabled by default: `mcp_enabled: false` removes it from the
process (the route stays reserved, answering 404 and never inference; restart
to apply), and the limits are config fields in the `mcp` category. It
forwards the caller's own `Authorization: Bearer` credential on its internal
calls, so the dashboard session cookie is refused there.

The token length band matches the proxy's own boot check (16 to 512
bytes). A credential the proxy would refuse to arm with is not a
credential this server can use.

Redirects are refused outright. No operator route redirects, and `net/http` strips
`Authorization` only when the hostname changes, so a same-host different-port or
subdomain `307`/`308` would replay both the credential and the full request body
to the redirect target.

## URL placement

A URL-capable client (an editor agent, a hosted connector, an MCP-capable CLI)
needs no binary and no environment: it points at the proxy's `/mcp` endpoint
and presents the operator credential in an `Authorization` header, the same
credential the dashboard uses.

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "millivolt": {
      "url": "http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer the same value the proxy was started with"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

A remote client uses the reverse-proxied HTTPS origin from
[the reverse-proxy guide](reverse-proxy.md), with `/mcp` appended:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "millivolt": {
      "url": "https://your-hostname/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer the same value the proxy was started with"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The header is the whole setup: the endpoint reads no environment, starts no
process, and no session cookie or per-request state outlives the request. Every
request is independently authenticated, so a missing or wrong Bearer is denied
before any tool runs, and a request presenting only the dashboard session
cookie is refused with 403, because the caller's own credential is what the
internal calls carry. `/mcp/` look-alikes are reserved: an unregistered path
answers 404 and is never forwarded to inference. The published Compose port is
loopback-only, so it is not a remote origin; remote clients terminate TLS at
the ingress as in the [reverse-proxy guide](reverse-proxy.md).

The transport is stateless and request/response only, and its limits are part
of choosing a client:

- `GET` and `DELETE` answer `405` with `Allow: POST`. There is no standalone
  SSE stream and no session to delete.
- There is no session id: the endpoint never sends `Mcp-Session-Id`, and no
  per-request state outlives the request. No session cookie is minted here
  either, unlike `/admin`, `/session`, `/metrics` and `/dash`, so an MCP client's
  cookie jar gains no dashboard credential; a client must not expect or send a
  session id. The admitted credential does key an in-process cache of the SDK
  server object, so repeated calls do not rebuild all 25 tool registrations;
  admitting a different credential replaces it. The credential is only the
  in-memory cache key: it is never logged or persisted.
- SSE resumption is not offered: no event store exists, so `Last-Event-ID`
  replay is not available.
- The server never sends requests to the client: there is no sampling and no
  elicitation, so a client that waits for a server-initiated request waits
  forever.
- Every request must accept both types, for example
  `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream`. A wildcard that covers both
  (`*/*`, `application/*, text/*`) is accepted too; an `Accept` missing either
  type, or one absent altogether, answers `400`.
- The accepted protocol versions are the bundled SDK's full set, newest first:
  `2026-07-28`, `2025-11-25`, `2025-06-18`, `2025-03-26` and `2024-11-05`.
  This build does not narrow them. A classic `initialize` is answered with the
  requested version when it is one of the legacy versions (`2025-11-25` and
  older, verified live) and with `2025-11-25` for any other requested version;
  `2026-07-28` is served only through the SDK's per-request metadata form:
  the request carries `Mcp-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28`, matching `_meta` keys
  `io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion` and
  `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities`
  (`io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo` is optional), and the `Mcp-Method`
  header. `tools/call` additionally requires an `Mcp-Name` header equal to
  `params.name`; a form missing any required piece answers `400`.
- The SDK's localhost DNS-rebinding check is deliberately off. It rejects a
  loopback connection whose `Host` is not loopback, and the documented
  reverse-proxied placement preserves the external `Host` while dialing the
  proxy over loopback, so leaving it on would reject that placement. The
  endpoint is Bearer-only and the operator gate re-validates the credential on
  every request, which is the stronger check for an authenticated endpoint.

## Tools

`describe` is the one to call first for this instance's live schema; without
it, correct SQL is guesswork. `docs_list` is the one to call first for how
millivolt itself works: it indexes the same Markdown as the published site and
needs no proxy request.

| Tool | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `describe` | Live SQLite schema, the complete `requests`/`request_debug`/`meta` column reference, the exact health predicates, a value vocabulary for every filter dimension, the live known client/provider/model and tool names, the indexes, the complete result-limit set (the query row default and explicit `max_rows` ceiling, query bytes, log page band, default page size, explorer group and chart bucket caps, Prometheus line cap and capture byte budget), and the working SQL idioms for this build. |
| `docs_list` | Every published documentation page in navigation order, with its path, title, description, public URL, Markdown URL and section count. Starts the docs flow; local only. |
| `docs_search` | Ranked section search across titles, headings and body text, with path, anchor, heading context and a snippet. Every query word must match; the result reports its total and truncation. Local only. |
| `docs_read` | One page by path, or one anchored section by heading id. Full-page Markdown is capped at 256 KiB with an explicit marker. This is the canonical explanation of millivolt's routes, configuration, protocol and operator behavior. Local only. |
| `query` | One bounded `SELECT`, clamped on both rows and encoded size, truncating with an explicit marker. The only tool that can express a time range. |
| `values` | The distinct values one dimension has in durable history, most frequent first, so a filter value is discovered rather than guessed. |
| `explore` | Faceted breakdown over all matching history by one dimension, with at most 24 groups. No time window. |
| `chart` | Server-authoritative time series, at most 31 clock-aligned buckets. Cannot group. |
| `records` | One durable newest-first log page, with the paired `before_ms`/`before_id` cursor and the page's `model_canon` map. |
| `snapshot` | The dashboard's live snapshot: sequence, feed, counters, storage signal, recent records. With durable storage enabled, a full snapshot is capped at `2 * dash_log_rows`; with storage off the ring is the only history and the snapshot is not capped. |
| `prometheus` | The text exposition, which covers the ring rather than durable since-inception totals. |
| `audit_status` | Capture sessions, their scope and live capture counts, the scope vocabularies, and the storage prerequisite. |
| `audit_start` | Start or edit one capture session. Requires `confirm: "start capture"` and refuses when durable storage is off. |
| `audit_stop` | Stop one session by id, or every session with `stop_all: "stop every capture session"`. |
| `audit_captures_list` | Page the requests that have a stored capture, through a bounded `SELECT` over `requests WHERE debug = 1` whose `request_debug` sidecar exists and has not expired. Ids are canonical: empty and whitespace-padded record ids are excluded because `audit_capture_get` could not read them back. |
| `audit_capture_get` | Read one capture document by request record id. |
| `operator_state` | Pause, limits, quota/storm and restart status in one call. |
| `set_pause` | Create, edit or resume pause holds. |
| `set_throttle` | Set, merge or clear one provider's caps, including the optional anti-burst pair. |
| `resume_quota` | Close one provider's open retry-mode quota gate. |
| `set_config` | Revision-checked partial configuration patch. |
| `config_get` | The live configuration document: values, running overrides (the keys the process pins outside the file, which `set_config` strips), the canonical usage and model metadata field names, defaults, per-key schema, restart-required set and the revision a patch must echo. Credential-class provider headers and last-reload error text are redacted; use the operator CLI with `--reveal` for the raw bytes. |
| `reload_config` | Re-read the configuration file. |
| `purge_preview` | Count what a filter would delete, without deleting. |
| `purge` | Delete matching history permanently. |

The routes are a closed set owned beside the HTTP client, so no tool can name
an arbitrary path: nothing reaches the proxy's transparent inference
catch-all, and no restore-adjacent route is exposed. The HTTP endpoint
dispatches those same calls in process to the proxy's own gated handler, so
they never leave the process and the gate re-validates the forwarded Bearer.

`set_throttle` takes `provider` and any of `concurrency`,
`requests`/`request_window`, `tokens`/`token_window`, `anti_burst` and
`ramp_duration`; omitted dimensions keep their value. A count needs its own
window only when the policy stores none for that dimension, a count of `0`
clears the dimension with its window, and a window without a count is refused
unless a count is already stored. `clear: true` drops the whole policy and
cannot be combined with a dimension. The proxy owns
the duration grammar and band and refuses an explicit on-ramp without an
active limit. This tool addresses one provider and has no selector or schedule
fields. Scoped selectors and recurring schedules are available through the HTTP
API (`/admin/throttle`) and the dashboard console, not through MCP.

`set_pause` refuses a resume that carries a scope, and refuses `all` combined
with `new`, `clients` or `providers`. `config_get` and the `set_config` echo
redact credential-class provider headers and last-reload error text; the CLI's
`--reveal` flag is the explicit operator opt-in. A redacted document posted
back through `set_config` keeps the loaded secret: the marker is restored at the
write owner, so a read-then-repost round trip cannot erase a credential.

### Filters

`explore`, `chart`, `records` and the explorer facets share one grammar, owned in
one place. Filters are `dim:id`, repeated, split on the FIRST colon, AND-ed
across dimensions and OR-ed within one dimension. `dim` is one of `client`,
`provider`, `model`, `conversation`, `key`, `status`, `time`, `tool`, `error`.
`key` is the SHA-256 hash of the client key.

`status` is a single selector: an exact HTTP status code (`0` to `9999`) or a
live in-flight class (`streaming`, `paused`, `throttled`, `pending`). It is not
the explorer's status-class vocabulary, which travels as `status:2xx`.

Two bounds apply to `f=` itself: at most 64 filters, and each `dim:id` value at
most 2048 bytes. The list is refused whole when either is exceeded; no filter
is silently dropped.

An unknown dimension, malformed filter or unknown status is refused before the
request is sent.

`explore`'s `error_total` uses two units. With `dim: error` it is the union of
distinct affected requests represented by the error cards, including recovered
quality failures whose final status is 200; for every other dimension it is the
canonical error count. A card share is `N / error_total` and cannot exceed 100%.
Do not compare it across the two cases as one metric.

### Pagination

`records` and `audit_captures_list` page newest-first with a paired
`(before_ms, before_id)` cursor. Both fields or neither.

The proxy scans a bounded number of rows per call, so a page can be short or
empty while its `more` flag is still true. `exhausted` is true when a page that
was given a cursor returns that same cursor, and also when `more` is false:
treat it as "stop paging". A first page has no cursor to repeat, so any returned
cursor counts as progress, including `(0, "")`. A non-advancing cursor means the
scan budget cannot reach the next row, and treating it as "keep going" is an
endless loop; an empty page with an advanced cursor is instead the normal shape
of "the budget ran out before a match", so page again.

Deep history needs this rather than `OFFSET`, which degrades on every page.

### Volume

A model cannot read ten thousand rows. Every listing defaults to a small page,
and every tool truncates with an explicit marker (`truncation.marker`) naming
what was withheld and the way to continue for that tool, because only some of
them have a cursor.

What is *not* claimed: the explorer caps groups at 24 and the chart caps buckets
at 31 SERVER-SIDE, so those drops happen inside the proxy and those tools'
`truncation.truncated` is `false` when groups were dropped. A model that trusts
that flag alone will read a short breakdown as a complete one.

### What each tool cannot do

These are the limits that otherwise send a model down the wrong path. They are
also in the tool descriptions, which is where a model reads them.

- `describe` first. Without the live schema, the column meanings, the health
  predicates and the value vocabularies, correct SQL is guesswork.
- **`explore` has no time window.** It always folds all history. It is also
  single-dimension: it cannot cross-tabulate provider by model. For either, use
  `query` with a `WHERE` on `started_at` and a `GROUP BY`.
- **`chart` is the only windowed tool, and it cannot group.** A window broken
  down by a dimension is a `query`.
- **`query` is the only tool that can express a time range.** There is no
  `unixnow()` in this SQLite build, so a relative window is
  `strftime('%s','now')*1000`, for example
  `WHERE started_at >= strftime('%s','now')*1000 - 3600000` for the last hour.
  Ready-to-run analysis SQL for exactly these time-ranged questions is
  collected in the [operator recipes](routes.md#operator-recipes).
- An **unknown filter value is an empty result, not an error.** A misspelled
  client, provider, model, tool, conversation or key produces a confident zero.
  Call `values` before filtering on one of those. Model filters take the
  **canonical** name the proxy folds from `model_rules` (which is what the
  `values` tool returns), never a raw stored spelling.
- **`values(model)` is paged and folded.** The tool reads raw spellings in
  bounded keyset pages, so a vocabulary larger than the proxy's
  `storage_query_max_rows` no longer fails with 413, then folds and merges the
  pages through `model_rules`. Past its documented raw-spelling,
  canonical-name, or total page-query bound it fails explicitly rather than
  returning a partial vocabulary. The ordinary `limit` still reports its own
  explicit truncation marker.
- `time` is a **daypart bucket**, not a duration: `time:24h` matches nothing. The
  buckets are `night`, `work`, `evening` and `weekend`.
- `status` takes the proxy's **status classes**, not HTTP shorthand: `2xx`,
  `cancel` (499), `4xx`, `5xx` and `err` (anything outside those, including
  3xx and below 200). There is no `3xx` class of its own.

## Audit semantics

Audit is the proxy's debug-capture subsystem.

**Capture requires durable storage.** With `db_path` empty, `audit_start` is
refused by the proxy with 503 `durable storage is disabled` and creates no
session; every capture read-back is a 404 because no capture document can
exist. `audit_start` and `audit_captures_list` therefore check the storage
signal first and refuse with that explanation, and `audit_status` reports it.
Starting a session that can never capture would be a silent no-op, which is
worse than a refusal.

**Scope is explicit.** An empty dimension matches anything; non-empty dimensions
are AND-ed and names within one dimension are OR-ed. There is no unrestricted
all-traffic scope, and there is no conversation dimension. Model names use the
proxy's native model normalization, so use the `known_models` values rather than
guessing spellings. A scope overlapping a live session is rejected (`409`)
rather than silently replacing it.

**Edits change only named dimensions.** With a session id, an omitted
`clients`, `providers` or `models` field preserves that dimension and an
explicitly empty array clears it. An omitted `duration` preserves the deadline
and an explicit empty string clears it. A create response also carries
`created_id`, the id its own request installed, so concurrent starts resolve
their own sessions. `set_pause` follows the same presence rules for scope and
duration when `hold_id` targets an edit; without `hold_id`, an omitted create
scope is the documented global hold.

**Starting requires a confirmation.** `audit_start` takes
`confirm: "start capture"` because capture stores full request and response
bodies.

**Stopping does not delete, but a purge does.** Stopping a session, or all of
them, ends future captures only: a stopped session's documents stay readable by
record id until `debug_capture_ttl` expires. There is no capture-specific delete
endpoint, but a `purge` deletes the stored capture document of every request it
matches, in the same transaction as the request row. A filter that reaches a
captured request takes its evidence with it. Only a backup taken beforehand
restores it.

**A scope name must be known when the vocabulary is.** `audit_start` checks
every client, provider and model against the vocabulary `audit_status` reports.
When that vocabulary is non-empty, an unknown name is refused with the known
values offered, because a session scoped to a name that matches nothing would
report `enabled: true` and capture nothing. An empty vocabulary is the
exception: a proxy that has seen nothing knows no names, so refusing every name
would make the tool unusable rather than safer and the check is skipped. A
vocabulary that cannot be read is not a skip: the start is refused, because the
guard cannot be applied at all.

**Read-back is by record id.** `audit_capture_get` takes the REQUEST RECORD id
(`requests.id`), not the session id. There is no listing endpoint, so
`audit_captures_list` discovers those ids by querying `requests WHERE debug = 1`
with an existing, unexpired `request_debug` sidecar and reports that it does so.
The listing also excludes an id that is empty or padded with whitespace: the
capture route trims the id before lookup while the sidecar key is stored
verbatim, so such an id could be advertised but never fetched. Every listed id
is therefore readable. Captured documents are sensitive: credentials are
redacted from headers, but body content is not sanitized.

**Sessions survive a restart.** The proxy restores them from its own state, so a
start list may already contain sessions this server did not create.

## The destructive call

`purge` permanently deletes matching request history. The proxy has NO
server-side confirmation, NO confirm flag and NO two-step protocol. The operator
credential and this tool's own guards are the entire gate.

Three guards apply together, and each alone would be insufficient:

1. **The filter must constrain at least one field.** The bodyless request that
   deletes ALL history is never sent by this tool; an empty filter is refused
   before any request.
2. **The confirmation must be an exact phrase.**
   `confirmation: "permanently delete the matching millivolt history"`. It is
   also a required tool argument, so a call that omits it is rejected by the
   schema before the handler runs.
3. **`preview_token` must be the token `purge_preview` issued for THIS filter.**
   It is an opaque HMAC-bound token over the canonicalized filter, the count it
   authorized and an expiry, so it cannot be forged, cannot be reused for another
   filter, and expires **15 minutes after issue**. A bare count could not do this: it is only a number, so
   two different filters matching the same number of rows authorized each other,
   and a count obtained from anywhere - a `query`, a guess, a preview of a
   different filter - satisfied the comparison. That was a live bypass, not a
   theoretical one.

Always run `purge_preview` first and pass its `preview_token` back verbatim.

### What the guard does not prevent

Stated plainly, because an operator needs to know the size of the remaining
window:

- **The count compares a population, not row identities.** The count is
  re-checked immediately before deleting, and the reviewed count travels with
  the delete, where the proxy counts it again inside the delete transaction and
  refuses with 409 when it moved. Nothing un-previewed is deleted by a refused
  call, but two different populations with the same row count are
  indistinguishable, and a refusal means previewing again.
- **A filter that reaches a captured request deletes its capture document too.**
  The preview and the deletion both say so in their output.

Deleted history cannot be recovered from this API. The deletion preserves newer
completions and in-flight work and does not reset live error-storm protection.

`set_config` is the other consequential call, and it is a revision-checked
partial patch: `values` carries only the keys to change, the whole result is
validated before the file is written, CLI-overridden keys are stripped, and the
response names the keys that need a restart. A supplied list or map replaces
that whole field, so call `config_get` first for structured keys such as
`providers` or `model_rules`, and echo the revision it returns.

A failed reload is reported as a save, not as an error. The proxy writes the file
and only then answers 500 with the reload failure in the body, so that response
is decoded as the committed document it is: `saved` is `true` and `error` carries
the reload message. Reporting it as a tool error would tell a model that a
mutation that succeeded had failed, and its retry would then fail with 409.

`reload_config` re-reads the configuration file. It is the one state-changing
route the dashboard never calls. The operator token itself is process-bound and
is not re-read.

## Errors

Every failure is a tool result the model can read and correct, carrying the
proxy's own `.error` text and the status: `401` (credential wrong or missing),
`403` (the proxy's operator plane is unarmed, or the request carried only the
dashboard session cookie), `404`, `409` (overlap or stale
revision), `413` (a result limit), and `429` with its `Retry-After`. An
unreachable proxy, a timeout, and a body that is not the expected document are
reported the same way. The `.error` field is read regardless of `Content-Type`,
because the operator routes are inconsistent and some answer `text/plain` with
a JSON body.

The returned text is scrubbed of the operator credential first, because a
reflecting endpoint could otherwise put the `Authorization` value into its own
failure message and hand it to the model. The scrub removes the literal token,
any contiguous 8-byte fragment of it (so a credential split across two JSON
string fields leaks no usable piece), percent escapes in any hex case
(including full-byte nested forms), the query `+` form of a space, and
JSON-escaped forms, including backslash-doubled text and surrogate pairs. Each
form is decoded to a fixed point before matching: an encoding is either fully
seen or the excerpt fails closed. Text that still decodes after three escape
applications is not published partly decoded: the whole excerpt is replaced by
`[redacted]` instead. That bound applies regardless of whether the credential
appears in the body: a heavily re-encoded failure with no credential in it
still loses its diagnostics, because a credential could be hidden past the
bound. The scan is bounded to the region that can still reach the excerpt, and
the raw bytes it reads are capped; a body whose whitespace collapse does not
reach the excerpt target inside that cap fails closed to `[redacted]` too, for
the same reason. The excerpt itself is whitespace-collapsed and truncated to
4 KiB before the ` [truncated]` marker is appended, so the model-visible text
runs up to the 12-byte marker past 4 KiB. Redaction runs before the truncation,
so a credential straddling the boundary cannot survive as a fragment.

## Try it against a disposable instance

Run the endpoint locally against a disposable instance with the repository's
lifecycle owner, never the main instance on `:8080`, and drive it with one
stateless POST:

```sh
(
  set -e
  trap 'scripts/dev.sh stop' EXIT
  export MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN='dev-instance-credential'
  scripts/dev.sh
  curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8081/mcp \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN" \
    -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"probe","version":"0"}}}'
)
```

The answer carries the server identity. A full client session is the client
configuration above pointed at `http://127.0.0.1:8081/mcp`; a request without
the Bearer credential answers 401 from the operator gate.

## Security

The endpoint is driven with an operator credential, which is the whole
dashboard plane: pause, limits, configuration, restart, purge. Treat the client
configuration that carries it as sensitive and keep it out of shared
repositories. See [Security](../SECURITY.md).

## Verification

The unit suite uses a fake proxy that pins the exact method, path, query and
`Authorization` header of every tool, maps canned responses onto typed output,
and covers the error shapes, setup validation, truncation markers, the pagination
rule and the purge guards. The paging rule has one owner shared with
`audit_captures_list`, so the two listings cannot disagree. One of its tests
runs outside that harness on purpose:

- the redirect test stands up a second listener as the redirect target and
  asserts it received nothing, so "we refused the redirect" is an observation
  rather than an assertion about an error string.
- the capture listing test executes the generated `SELECT` against a real
  SQLite schema with empty, space-padded, tab-padded and NBSP-padded sidecars,
  and asserts they are excluded while every returned id has an unexpired
  sidecar and is the exact spelling `audit_capture_get` can fetch.

This page is mechanically pinned by `tests/python/mcp_docs.py`: the tool table
must match the `addTool` registrations, every "<n> tools" mention must match
that count, every route the client owns must appear in the
[routes and debugging route table](routes.md#operator-and-data-routes), and this page
may name no operator path the client does not own.

The live integration test starts a private instance through
[scripts/dev.sh](../scripts/dev.sh) on a port and scratch database of its own, so
concurrent runs do not share a port or database, drives the tools through a real MCP session,
and runs a full capture cycle against neutral loopback traffic:

```sh
MILLIVOLT_MCP_INTEGRATION=1 scripts/check.sh go test -count=1 ./internal/mcp/...
```

It runs in CI as part of the isolated browser-fixtures step, which already has a
dev instance and an operator token; it is not part of the core source-and-unit
job, because that job should not have to start a second proxy.

It drives every registered tool against its own disposable instance. The
state-changing tools are `set_pause`, `set_throttle`, `resume_quota`,
`set_config`, `reload_config`, `audit_start`, `audit_stop` and `purge`. The
run exercises `set_pause` (a hold scoped to the fixture client, resumed at
once), `set_throttle` (a limit set and then cleared), `resume_quota`,
`set_config` and `reload_config` against the scratch config copy, a full
capture cycle (`audit_start` and `audit_stop`), and the purge path: the
missing confirmation, the wrong phrase, an unauthorized token and a token
issued for a different filter each refuse with the row count unchanged, and
then an authorized purge deletes the fixture rows. The read-only tools are
`describe`, `docs_list`, `docs_search`, `docs_read`, `query`, `explore`,
`chart`, `records`, `snapshot`, `prometheus`, `audit_status`,
`audit_captures_list`, `audit_capture_get`, `operator_state`, `config_get`,
`values` and `purge_preview`; the run drives each of them. A
successful purge and the config write are safe here because the instance, its
database and its config copy all belong to the test and are discarded.

The same run drives the proxy's own `/mcp` endpoint with a real streamable
HTTP client: `initialize`, `tools/list` (25 tools), and `describe` and
`records` returning the same documents the in-process session returns, plus the
auth boundary (401 without a credential, 401 for a wrong Bearer from the shared
gate, 403 for a cookie-only request or a wrong Bearer beside an admitted
cookie) and the reserved `/mcp/` look-alike answering 404, never inference.

pages.description: mvctl is the human command-line client for millivolt's operator plane. It calls the same documented /admin/* and /metrics/* routes as the dashboard and...

sections.heading: Build and run
sections.text: go run ./cmd/mvctl status --url http://127.0.0.1:8081 go build -o mvctl ./cmd/mvctl ./mvctl --url http://127.0.0.1:8081 status The origin is required: pass --url or set MILLIVOLT_URL . There is no production default, so a command cannot silently address 127.0.0.1:8080 . A trailing slash is normalized away. Only http and https origins are accepted; userinfo, a path, a query and a fragment are rejected.

sections.heading: Authentication
sections.text: mvctl reads the operator credential from MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN , the one variable the proxy's boot gate reads. It never accepts the token on argv, because a command-line value is visible in ps and shell history. The shared client validates the token's length band before sending a request. export MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN='the-value-the-proxy-started-with' mvctl status Every request presents Authorization: Bearer . No cookie jar is kept: a session cookie minted by one call is deliberately not reused, so a rotated token takes effect on the next command. A missing or wrong credential is reported with the operator gate's own status. A non-loopback origin should use https ; the credential is otherwise sent in cleartext.

sections.heading: Output and exit codes
sections.text: Human output is the default. --json (or -j ) prints one JSON document, and command output is stable enough for a pipeline. Diagnostics go to stderr as mvctl: ... . After argument parsing, --json turns a command failure into {"error": "..."} on stdout so a caller can parse one stream. A usage error detected while parsing the arguments still goes to stderr and exits 2, because JSON mode is not established yet; a usage error a command reports after a successful parse follows --json like any other failure. [--yes] revision-checked save mvctl config reload [--yes] re-read the config file config set reads GET /admin/config for the current revision and the schema. Set dimensions intersect and an unset dimension matches any value, exactly as they do for a limit. --duration and --max-queued are optional. pause off deliberately rejects scope flags: the proxy identifies a hold by id , and a scope-looking command that cleared every hold would be unsafe. # Operator CLI (mvctl)

`mvctl` is the human command-line client for millivolt's operator plane. It
calls the same documented `/admin/*` and `/metrics/*` routes as the dashboard
and reads them through the shared MCP operator client, so the origin check,
credential handling, redirect refusal, response bound and credential redaction
have one owner. It adds no server route, no server setting and no second
listener.

`mvctl` is a sibling of `cmd/proxy`, `cmd/stress` and `cmd/release`. It is
source-only: the container image still ships the proxy, and deployment
lifecycle stays with Compose.

## Build and run

```sh
go run ./cmd/mvctl status --url http://127.0.0.1:8081
go build -o mvctl ./cmd/mvctl
./mvctl --url http://127.0.0.1:8081 status
```

The origin is required: pass `--url` or set `MILLIVOLT_URL`. There is no
production default, so a command cannot silently address `127.0.0.1:8080`. A
trailing slash is normalized away. Only `http` and `https` origins are
accepted; userinfo, a path, a query and a fragment are rejected.

## Authentication

`mvctl` reads the operator credential from `MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN`, the one
variable the proxy's boot gate reads. It never accepts the token on argv,
because a command-line value is visible in `ps` and shell history. The shared
client validates the token's length band before sending a request.

```sh
export MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN='the-value-the-proxy-started-with'
mvctl status
```

Every request presents `Authorization: Bearer`. No cookie jar is kept: a
session cookie minted by one call is deliberately not reused, so a rotated
token takes effect on the next command. A missing or wrong credential is
reported with the operator gate's own status. A non-loopback origin should use
`https`; the credential is otherwise sent in cleartext.

## Output and exit codes

Human output is the default. `--json` (or `-j`) prints one JSON document, and
command output is stable enough for a pipeline. Diagnostics go to stderr as
`mvctl: ...`. After argument parsing, `--json` turns a command failure into
`{"error": "..."}` on stdout so a caller can parse one stream. A usage error
detected while parsing the arguments still goes to stderr and exits 2, because
JSON mode is not established yet; a usage error a command reports after a
successful parse follows `--json` like any other failure.

| Exit | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | success, including a preview that made no change |
| 1 | transport, HTTP or proxy-reported failure |
| 2 | usage error, unknown flag or invalid input |
| 130 | interrupted during a request, stream or watch |

`status` and `overview` print an allowlisted state projection with `--json`:
request rows and the full effective config are omitted, so use `requests` and
`config get` for those. Request rows in that projection would carry previews,
response headers and retry metadata that the dedicated commands keep out.

ANSI color is off when stdout is not a terminal. `--color`, `--no-color` and
`NO_COLOR` override the default. Request labels, model ids, error types and
proxy error text are sanitized before a terminal sees them, so a captured value
cannot inject an escape sequence.

## Global flags

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--url URL` | proxy origin; required unless `MILLIVOLT_URL` is set |
| `--timeout DURATION` | bound one request, default the shipped `mcp_timeout`; 0 disables the deadline |
| `--json`, `-j` | emit one JSON document |
| `--yes` | confirm a state-changing command |
| `--color` / `--no-color` | override terminal color detection |
| `--help`, `-h` | command or global help |
| `--version` | print the mvctl version and source revision |

`--` ends flag parsing; when no command has been named yet, the next word may
still name one. Boolean flags accept `--flag`, `--flag=true`, `--flag=1`,
`--flag=yes`, `--flag=on`, and the false spellings `false`, `0`, `no`, `off`.

## Commands

### View

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `mvctl status` | health, origin, dashboard build and headline metrics |
| `mvctl overview` | KPI, storage, pause, throttle and debug state |
| `mvctl requests [N]` | one page of the request log, default the shipped `dash_log_rows`; `N` must be inside that setting's schema band |
| `mvctl query "SELECT ..."` | bounded SQL through `/metrics/query` |
| `mvctl chart` | server-authoritative time series; `--window` is all history or whole minutes, `--filter` scopes it |
| `mvctl prometheus` | the Prometheus text exposition |
| `mvctl watch` | sample live counters and print a sparkline |
| `mvctl health` | check `/healthz` |
| `mvctl url` | print the normalized origin |

`requests` accepts `--before-ms MS` and `--before-id ID` together to fetch the
next page; the id is an opaque keyset position and may be empty, so it is sent
exactly as given. The command prints the next cursor when the page has more
rows. Its
JSON rows intentionally omit captured content previews, response headers and
retry attempts. Use the dashboard capture drawer when full bodies are needed.

`query` accepts `--query-timeout DURATION`; the default is the shipped MCP
query bound, and an explicit value must be greater than zero. The shared HTTP
client carries that shipped bound on its query path too, which is the one
`chart` takes. The statement must be a single `SELECT` without a semicolon,
using the same pre-check as the MCP query tool. The SQL text is sent as one `q`
parameter and is never logged.

`chart` prints the server-authoritative series: bucket geometry, percentile and
stat arrays, blended cost per million tokens and the buckets themselves. Its
fold runs through the client's query path with `--query-timeout` as the one
bound, so `--timeout` (the generic per-request deadline) never cuts it short.
`--window` takes `all` or a whole number of minutes; `--filter` takes
comma-separated `dim:id` pairs using the same dimensions as the log scope
(`client`, `provider`, `model`, `conversation`, `key`, `status`, `time`, `tool`,
`error`). `key` is the SHA-256 hash of the client key. A chart fold covers
finalized requests only, so a live in-flight status class is refused.

`watch` accepts `--samples N`, bounded by the command's settings surface, and
`--interval DURATION` (default the shipped `dash_poll_interval`). Interrupting
any request or stream exits 130.

### Config

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `mvctl config get [KEY]` | show one setting or every saved setting |
| `mvctl config keys [SUBSTRING]` | list schema keys |
| `mvctl config diff` | compare saved file values with built-in defaults |
| `mvctl config set KEY=VALUE ... [--yes]` | revision-checked save |
| `mvctl config reload [--yes]` | re-read the config file |

`config set` reads `GET /admin/config` for the current revision and the schema.
The schema's `kind` decides coercion: `bool`, `int`, `duration`, `bytes` and
`string` take their natural text form; `strings`, `providers`, `aliases`,
`model_rules`, `request_overrides` and `sub_conversations` take a JSON value.
A numeric-looking string stays a string. An empty value is never a boolean. An
unknown key, an empty boolean or an undecodable composite value is a usage
error before any write.

The server writes the file and then answers 500 when the follow-up reload
fails. `mvctl` treats that committed document as a warning, not a failure, and
prints the reload error without inviting a retry that would fail with a stale
revision.

Credential-class provider header values are redacted from `config get`, `config
diff`, the `config set` preview and its post-save document, in human output and
`--json`, using the shared header-name vocabulary. `--reveal` prints them. A historical
`last_reload` error is replaced by the redaction marker because a rejected value
can be quoted there. Token counters, token windows and rate-limit values are
measurements, not credentials, and are never redacted.

### Pause

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `mvctl pause [show]` | list holds and queued requests |
| `mvctl pause on --client X --provider P --yes` | create a scoped hold |
| `mvctl pause on --model M --conversation C --yes` | narrow a hold to a model or conversation |
| `mvctl pause on --new --yes` | hold clients first seen after the hold |
| `mvctl pause on --all --yes` | hold every client and provider |
| `mvctl pause on --id ID [flags] --yes` | edit one hold in place |
| `mvctl pause off --id ID --yes` | remove one hold |
| `mvctl pause off --all --yes` | remove every hold |

`pause on` requires a scope: `--client`, `--provider`, `--model`,
`--key-hash`, `--conversation`, `--new` or `--all`, unless `--id` names an
existing hold to edit. Set dimensions intersect and an unset dimension matches
any value, exactly as they do for a limit. `--duration` and `--max-queued` are
optional. `pause off` deliberately rejects scope flags: the
proxy identifies a hold by `id`, and a scope-looking command that cleared every
hold would be unsafe. Use exactly one of `--id` or `--all`. A resume carries
only the hold id because the proxy has no scope-selective resume.

### Throttle and quota

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `mvctl throttle [show]` | list provider limits |
| `mvctl throttle set --provider P [flags] [--yes]` | merge limit dimensions |
| `mvctl throttle clear --provider P [--yes]` | drop a provider limit |
| `mvctl quota [show]` | show storm and quota state |
| `mvctl quota resume --provider P [--yes]` | close a retry-mode quota gate |

`throttle set` flags are `--concurrency`, `--requests`, `--request-window`,
`--tokens`, `--token-window`, `--anti-burst` and `--ramp-duration`. Windows and
ramps take a duration such as `1m`. A count needs its window unless the policy
already stores one for that dimension, and a count of `0` clears the dimension
with its window; a window without a count is refused unless a count is stored.
At least one dimension is required. The set and clear commands are provider-only. Scoped selectors and recurring
schedules are available through the HTTP API (`/admin/throttle`) and the
dashboard console, not through this CLI.

### Queue and capture

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `mvctl drain --all [--yes]` | release every parked request |
| `mvctl drain --provider P [--yes]` | release one provider's parked requests |
| `mvctl drain --model M [--yes]` | release one model's parked requests |
| `mvctl drain --client C [--yes]` | release one client's parked requests |
| `mvctl debug [show]` | list capture sessions and their bounds |
| `mvctl debug on --client C --yes` | start a scoped capture |
| `mvctl debug off --id ID --yes` | stop one session |
| `mvctl debug off --all --yes` | stop every session |

Exactly one drain scope is required. `debug on` requires a scope unless `--id`
names an existing session to edit, and it has no unrestricted all-traffic form,
matching the MCP tool: a bare enable would capture every request body. Captures
are sensitive even after header redaction, and a capture create needs durable
storage; the proxy answers 503 without it.
`debug off` identifies a session by `id` or `--all`, never by a scope flag,
and the two are mutually exclusive. `debug on` refuses a scope name the proxy
has not seen, because such a session reports enabled but captures nothing.

### History, backup and restart

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `mvctl purge [filters] [--all] [--yes]` | count first, then delete |
| `mvctl backup --out FILE` | download an archive |
| `mvctl restore --file FILE [--yes]` | inspect by default, apply with `--yes` |
| `mvctl restart --yes` | request a graceful restart |

`purge` filters are `--client`, `--provider`, `--model`, `--conversation-id`,
`--error-type`, `--status`, `--before-ms`, `--after-ms`, `--has-error` and
`--debug`. Every value must parse, and a zero or unparsable numeric filter is a
usage error rather than an omitted constraint. `--all` cannot be combined with
a filter. The command always calls `/admin/purge/count` first and prints the
count; only `--yes` calls `/admin/purge`, and an unfiltered purge also needs
`--all`. Before deleting, the command re-counts and refuses when the total
changed since the preview, then sends that count with the delete so the proxy
checks it once more inside the delete transaction. That compares counts, not
row identities, so the guarantee is a refused moved population rather than a
row-identity binding. A missing, fractional, negative or non-finite count is a
failure, never zero. A genuinely bodyless purge is the proxy's
delete-everything form.

`backup --out FILE` is required; there is no default path. `--config` and
`--database` default to true (the command's settings surface) and are always
sent explicitly, so "both off" cannot silently become the server's both-on
default. The download streams to a private temporary file, checks the `MVB1`
magic, syncs the file, renames, and syncs the directory entry only on success.
An existing file is refused unless `--overwrite` is passed. A short HTTP body
is a failed transfer, not a published archive. Backup and restore are bounded
by cancellation, not by `--timeout`.

`restore` defaults to `inspect=1`, which validates the archive without applying
it; `--inspect` forces that mode even with `--yes`. `--yes` applies it. The
preview decodes and preflights the whole archived database member on the server,
so it costs about as much as the apply's decode; `--yes` alone skips the
preview and applies directly. The
member selection (`--config`, `--database`) and the mode (`--config-mode`,
`--database-mode`; `merge` or `replace`) are always sent explicitly, and both
the inspect and apply output name the selected members and modes. The default mode is `replace`, the proxy's documented default, so the
preview names the broader action instead of hiding it. An inspect document's
archived provider headers are redacted; `--reveal` prints them. The apply
response's `restart_required` keys are called out in the output.

## Scope and non-goals

`mvctl` does not install, start, stop or update containers. It does not read or
write `proxy.yaml` directly, does not add a listener, and does not keep a second
copy of the proxy's routes, config schema, credential rules or backup grammar.
Those facts stay with `internal/mcp`, `internal/config` and
`internal/backup`. The command uses only the Go standard library and those
repository packages. Because the shared operator client lives in
`internal/mcp`, the resulting binary links the MCP Go SDK and its OAuth2 and
jsonschema dependencies. The backup grammar and archive magic live in the
dependency-free `internal/backup/params` leaf, so `mvctl` does not link SQLite
or zstd and never opens a database.

# Operations

> [!WARNING]
> Read the [security boundary](../SECURITY.md) before exposing the listener.

The whole embedded dashboard is protected: every dashboard, `/metrics/*`,
`/admin/*` and `/mcp` request requires the `MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN` credential
and is denied while it is not configured. At the application gate, only the
unauthenticated `/healthz` liveness and `/readyz` readiness probes, the
`POST /session` login handshake, origin-root brand/PWA files and transparent
inference stay open; see the canonical [operator access](routes.md#operator-access)
list.

## Overview

This page is the operating overview. It covers health and readiness, durable
storage and accounting, the runtime cost model, and the known limits. Each
task-shaped page carries the detail.

| If you want to | Start with |
| --- | --- |
| Change a setting, an override or a provider alias | [Configuration](configuration.md) |
| Install, back up, upgrade or restart the deployment | [Containers and data](containers.md) |
| Call an operator route, or debug traffic | [Routes and debugging](routes.md) |
| Protect the listener | [Security](../SECURITY.md), [reverse proxy](reverse-proxy.md) |
| Measure the deployment | [Performance and resource usage](performance.md) |

## Health and readiness

Liveness (`/healthz`) answers "the process is up and serving HTTP". Readiness
(`/readyz`) additionally answers "this instance can persist": it fails with
`503` and a reason when the durable writer is wedged. Two arms answer that: the
oldest record on the queue has waited, or no flush has succeeded, for longer
than one flush interval plus a progress window. The window is four flush
intervals clamped to at least 30 seconds and at most two minutes; the record's
own interval is allowed on top, so a record inside its own cadence never
convicts and a long configured interval cannot postpone the verdict by more
than that one cadence. Every clock starts on arrival: the oldest record on the
queue ages the first arm, and while no flush has succeeded since boot the first
accepted record ages the second one, so a writer that never picks records up is
convicted all the same. Readiness also fails when
any durable flush has failed since boot.
Readiness stays red after the first failed flush even once writes recover,
because a lost batch is worth an operator's attention; restart or investigate.
With durable storage disabled both routes answer `200`, since there is no
pipeline to wedge.

The Compose files use `-readycheck` as the service healthcheck, so
`docker compose ps` reports `healthy` only for an instance that can persist.
Point an external load balancer or orchestrator at `/readyz` for the same
signal; both probe routes are unauthenticated and answer the exact body
`{"ok":true}` on success.

Storage state is also scrapeable at `/metrics/prometheus` (behind the operator
credential) as `llm_proxy_storage_enabled`,
`llm_proxy_storage_queue_depth`, `llm_proxy_storage_queue_capacity`,
`llm_proxy_storage_dropped_total{cause}` (`overflow`, `after_close`, `panic`,
`flush_failed`), `llm_proxy_storage_flush_failed_total`,
`llm_proxy_storage_last_flush_timestamp_seconds` and
`llm_proxy_storage_wedged`. The block is rendered on every scrape, outside the
memoized request aggregate, so queue and drop movement shows up immediately.
Alert on `llm_proxy_storage_wedged`, on a rising `flush_failed` counter, and on
`overflow` drops that are not explained by a burst.

## Storage and accounting

SQLite retains finalized records; the ring and pending registry support live
observation. Full bootstrap windows are capped in durable mode and older log
rows page from storage. Without storage, the ring is the available history.

The durable log order owns one secondary index, `idx_requests_log(started_at,
id)`. The log page pushes exact provider, client, key-hash, conversation and
canonical numeric status predicates into SQL and rechecks them on that scan;
model, status-class, tool, error and time-bucket filters stay Go-owned because
they match canonical/derived values, not raw stored text. The export and purge
filter surface is different: it accepts exact provider, model, client,
conversation, error type, status code, `has_error`, `debug`, and time bounds,
with no key-hash selector, and its equality-only preview count or purge scans
the table instead of maintaining per-dimension composite indexes.
`BenchmarkStoreDiskBytes` measures
this on its deterministic synthetic fixture (10,000 and 100,000 seeded
records). The current per-record and total bytes are published in
[storage and retained projection](performance.md#storage-and-retained-projection);
that is a reproducible fixture scope, not a prediction of a deployment's disk
use or a capacity ceiling.

Dropping a superseded request-log index only moves its pages to SQLite's
freelist, so the first startup that finds and removes one also runs a one-time
`VACUUM` after the migration. Fresh and already-migrated databases skip it. A
`VACUUM` needs free temporary space up to roughly twice the database size; if
it fails for space, locking or interruption, startup logs a warning and
continues with every row intact, but the freed pages stay on the freelist.
Reclaim them manually during a maintenance window: stop the proxy, run
`sqlite3 /data/proxy.db 'VACUUM;'` (or any SQLite client) against `db_path`,
and confirm `PRAGMA freelist_count` returns 0. The automatic pass is never
retried on a later boot, so a failed attempt needs this manual step.

Boot migrations also own a small set of one-shot data repairs for shapes older
binaries could write but current writers never produce: an empty-string JSON
document in `attempts` or `tool_names` is rewritten to the canonical `null`,
and a positive `ttft_ms` with `final_attempt_at = 0` (the pre-0.3.34
start-anchored TTFT, recorded with upload, queueing and retry backoff
included) is reset to 0 because the original per-attempt anchor was never
stored and cannot be recovered. Each repair has its own `meta` marker
(`attempts_repaired`, `tool_names_repaired`, `ttft_anchor_repaired`): the
marker is written after a clean probe or after the rewrite, later boots read
one row instead of rescanning the table, and deleting the marker (or restoring
a database that predates it) re-arms the probe. A repair that cannot run fails
boot closed instead of serving history its own consumers would reject. The
first boot after an upgrade that finds rows to rewrite may pause while it
scans and rewrites them, and the totals rebuild follows: the rewrite advances
the projection epoch, which invalidates the persisted totals document. The
rewrite can transiently grow the WAL, so keep free space on the database
volume as for any other large write.

Enqueue is bounded and nonblocking. Overflow or write failures can lose durable
records even when HTTP succeeds. Bootstrap's
`storage:{enabled,dropped,totals_degraded}` reports cumulative process-local
loss and a failed startup history scan. Either appears in the status footer;
degraded since-inception totals count only rows committed since process start.
Increasing queue size absorbs bursts, not arbitrary sustained overload.
Storage overload remains an unresolved capacity boundary, not a lossless mode.
Measure it with the [isolated stress workflow](../CONTRIBUTING.md#performance-evidence):
successful responses, exact durable accounting and process-local drops are
separate acceptance criteria. A short successful burst does not establish
sustainable writer throughput or an absolute request-capacity ceiling.

`storage_query_timeout` bounds interactive dashboard reads (chart, explorer,
log/bootstrap, capture reads) and the ad-hoc query route. A capture read waits
first for the in-flight sidecar save of the same request, bounded by the
drawer client's own request context, and only then starts the read budget, so a
slow save cannot spend the budget the read needs. Startup projection
preload, the boot totals rebuild, an administrative purge, and a backup merge's
totals scan run under a separate internal ten-minute maintenance budget: they
legitimately read or rewrite full history and must not inherit the interactive
bound. The
maintenance budget still honors an earlier caller cancellation or deadline, and
its expiry fails the operation closed (a purge transaction rolls back). It is a
fixed implementation guardrail, not a configuration field.

One shared analytical projection retains compact data and sorted metric orders
proportional to stored history. Initial preload costs startup CPU/RAM; fast
dashboard reuse is not free startup or bounded total-history memory.
Concurrent independent proxy writers sharing a database are not a supported
coherent-KPI deployment.

Expired debug sidecars are hidden from reads immediately by their TTL. Physical
reclamation deletes bounded batches per writer tick and continues on a
near-term tick, so a large expired set drains without holding the sole writer
connection; the sidecar byte cap accounting is updated exactly for the rows
removed.

Scheduler groups and some observed-identity sets also retain historical labels.
Bounded request queues do not bound all process memory; long-running workloads
with many unique identities need their own memory/cardinality measurements.

From a source checkout with Python installed, use the existing online backup
into a new destination:

```sh
python3 scripts/backup_db.py proxy.db /path/to/new-backup.db
```

The helper opens the source read-only and includes committed WAL state. Do not
plain-copy an open database or omit its WAL. Protect backups, debug captures and
exports as sensitive data.
This helper backs up the database, not configuration. Operators can also
download a self-checked config and/or database archive from
[Settings backup and restore](containers.md#settings-backup-and-restore). For image-only
deployments and both persistent volumes, use
[container backup and restore](containers.md#image-only-backup-and-restore).

## Performance and footprint

Separate deployment size, cold startup, idle footprint, request overhead and
loaded throughput. They answer different questions; a small image is not a RAM
limit, and a cached dashboard read is not a cold-start measurement.

The runtime contains a stripped Go binary with embedded UI assets, dependency
notices and the generated configuration, on a minimal non-root base. There is
no frontend build/runtime dependency in deployment. Docker's reported image
size describes an image artifact, not compressed network transfer, persistent
volume growth or the process's resident memory.

On the request path, one bounded body read/metadata decode feeds shared routing
and accounting. Upstream connections are pooled; streamed observation and durable
enqueue avoid a per-request history scan or synchronous SQLite write. On the
dashboard path, the initial HTML embeds bootstrap state and shared analytical
projections/cache slots avoid building a separate history copy for each view.
These implementation choices reduce repeated work, not every cost of a request.

RAM still includes active request/response buffers, connection pools, the live
ring and pending state, and the history/cardinality costs documented under
[storage](#storage-and-accounting). Raising queue/body/pool limits or concurrency
changes that footprint. Retained history and observed identities have no universal
process-memory cap; configuration limits must be evaluated together.

The startup preload decodes every stored row once, so its transient allocations
(SQL strings, attempts and tool-name JSON) exceed the retained projection several
times over. The process returns those burst pages to the OS immediately after the
preload completes; idle RSS after readiness reflects retained state, not the
startup burst. The projection's per-record retained footprint is measured
reproducibly by `BenchmarkProjectionFootprint` (retained and transient bytes per
record over a seeded scratch database) and `BenchmarkProjectionProcessRSS`
(process RSS after readiness), without a live instance; the
[performance workflow](../CONTRIBUTING.md#performance-evidence) owns the commands.

`go_memory_limit` is the operator's steady-state RSS lever: a soft cap on Go
runtime managed memory (heap, stacks, runtime structures) applied once at
startup. With the setting at 0, an operator `GOMEMLIMIT` wins and otherwise a
detected finite cgroup memory ceiling of at least 80MiB (v2 `memory.max` or v1
`memory.limit_in_bytes`) becomes a soft limit at 80% of that ceiling so a
container's own bound actually reaches the Go runtime; smaller ceilings are
ignored and, with no `GOMEMLIMIT`, the runtime stays unbounded. A set value
overrides `GOMEMLIMIT`, not `GOGC`, for the process lifetime. `GOGC` remains
independent. The limit is soft - exceeding it makes the collector
more aggressive (capped near 50% of CPU time) instead of failing requests - and
bounds Go-managed memory only, never SQLite's page cache or OS overhead.

The [performance and resource usage](performance.md) page is the single source
for the current measured tables, hardware, method, reproduce commands and
limitations. This section owns the implementation cost model above and the
`go_memory_limit` behavior. Use the [isolated performance workflow](../CONTRIBUTING.md#performance-evidence)
when adding evidence. Short local-upstream bursts and microbenchmarks are useful
regressions, not sustained production capacity, provider-latency or lossless
storage guarantees.

## Known limits

- Recognized provider fields drive usage/cost; this is not independent billing.
- Non-streaming usage/cost inspection keeps a bounded prefix, so larger valid
  responses can forward completely without complete accounting.
- Optional non-streaming translation reads the complete upstream 200 body and
  the translated document under the configured `translated_response_max_bytes`
  each (default 32 MiB). Exceeding either fails closed with 502
  `response_too_large` before any client bytes; discovery budgets do not
  bound the path.
- General multi-line SSE accounting/native event assembly remains incomplete;
  some split terminal/content shapes can affect classification, not just metrics.
- SQL result limits do not bound every intermediate SQLite allocation.
- Automatically grouped sessions are not proof of agent ancestry. Explicit parent
  declarations and exact-leaf filtering are described in [protocol](protocol.md).
- Existing values lost by older storage formats cannot be reconstructed.
- Extreme numeric data can produce explicit accounting/encoding errors rather
  than invented saturated prices or token counts.
