pages.markdown_text:
# Containers and data

This page covers the image, Compose operation, persistent volumes, backups,
versions and the restart lifecycle. The settings surface is in
[configuration](configuration.md).

> [!WARNING]
> This is an offline backup: stop callers first, allow active work to finish,
> and keep the service stopped while copying. Never copy an open SQLite database
> as plain files. Restore into a new project and fresh volumes, leaving the
> original deployment and backups untouched.

## Containers

The [Dockerfile](../Dockerfile) builds Linux `amd64` and `arm64` targets and runs
as UID/GID `65532:65532`, with no source tree, Go toolchain or shell in the
runtime image. JavaScript/CSS are embedded in the Go binary; Node and Python
are test tools, not runtime dependencies. The binary is stripped of debug and
symbol tables. The final stage copies only that binary, dependency notices,
the generated example and prepared state directories onto the minimal distroless base.
The [Compose quickstart](../README.md#docker-compose) downloads the image-only
[compose.yaml](../compose.yaml). Normal deployment never builds from source.
Local builds use the separate
[development Compose](../CONTRIBUTING.md#container-development).
A registry tag is usable only after its publishing workflow succeeds.

### Compose operation

Keep the same Compose project name to reuse its named volumes. The normal file
names the project `millivolt`; an explicit `-p` overrides it. The deployment
inputs are `MILLIVOLT_IMAGE` (image reference),
`MILLIVOLT_PORT` (loopback host port), `MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN` (the
operator credential, forwarded into the container environment only),
`MILLIVOLT_STOP_GRACE_PERIOD` (container
stop grace), `MILLIVOLT_MEM_LIMIT` (container memory ceiling, default `1g`) and
`MILLIVOLT_PIDS_LIMIT` (process/thread ceiling, default `512`). Their defaults
live in [compose.yaml](../compose.yaml), not server
configuration. Supply them consistently through the environment or an ignored
local `.env` file. `docker compose config` shows the resolved deployment.

The memory ceiling is also the source of the runtime's own soft limit: with
`go_memory_limit` at its `0B` default, a detected finite cgroup ceiling at or
above 80 MiB becomes a soft limit at 80% of itself, so the container bound
reaches the Go runtime instead of leaving it unbounded. Raise the ceiling with
`history_size`, request buffers, concurrency or observed identity cardinality;
a ceiling under 80 MiB is ignored by the runtime and leaves only the hard OOM
kill. `pids_limit` bounds process and thread amplification, not goroutines.
The image carries a Dockerfile `HEALTHCHECK` that probes the unauthenticated
`/healthz` through the binary's `-healthcheck` mode, so `docker compose ps`
reports health without any operator credential. Both Compose files replace that
probe with the [readiness check](operations.md#health-and-readiness), which is
strictly stronger.

```sh
# Start or adopt a newly pulled image while preserving volumes.
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps
docker compose logs --tail 100

# Stop without removing containers or data.
docker compose stop

# Remove this project's containers and network, retaining named volumes.
docker compose down
```

Do not add `--volumes` or `-v` to `down` unless deliberately deleting its
configuration and history. Changing the Compose project name selects different
volumes and can look like missing data. Back up before an upgrade; the existing
image can be replaced, but a database migration is not necessarily reversible.
See Docker's [Compose lifecycle](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/up/)
and [volume removal](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/down/)
documentation for the underlying behavior.

Do not add a build section to the deployment file. The
[development Compose](../CONTRIBUTING.md#container-development) owns
source builds, its private port and its separate project identity.

The Compose service drops Linux capabilities, disallows privilege escalation,
uses a read-only root filesystem and a bounded temporary filesystem. These
controls do not add application authentication or a tenant boundary. Access to
a rootful Docker daemon through the `docker` group is effectively root access;
see Docker's [Linux post-installation guidance](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/linux-postinstall/).

### Persistent state and configuration

| Container path | Persistence and permissions |
| --- | --- |
| `/data` | Writable database directory, including SQLite WAL/SHM sidecars. Mount the directory, not just `proxy.db`. |
| `/config` | Writable private configuration directory. The image bundles `/config/proxy.yaml` from the generated example; if deliberately absent, the application uses neutral built-in defaults. |

Fresh named config volumes receive the image's bundled example, owned by
UID/GID `65532:65532` with mode `0600`. No separate configuration download is
required. Replacing an image does not overwrite an existing saved configuration;
review example-profile changes deliberately when upgrading.

These bundle semantics apply to images built from this revision. Existing release
images are not changed by a main-branch update; consult the documentation at the
selected release tag for older images.

Existing volumes and host bind mounts must be owned by the runtime UID, or the
database file must already be mode `0600`. Read/write permission alone is not
sufficient: startup narrows a broader database mode to `0600` and fails closed
when it cannot, naming the file path, owner and current mode. A foreign-owned
`0600` database is left unchanged; a broader foreign-owned file must be pre-set
to `0600` or chown'd to `65532:65532`.
Bind mounts hide bundled files: supply a config yourself when using one, or
intentionally accept the application's missing-file defaults.
Use private directory permissions and mode `0600` for a supplied config; with
rootless Docker or user namespaces, account for the host UID mapping. Do not
make sensitive directories world-writable to work around ownership failures.

A first launch cannot prepare its own bind-mount host directories. When a
bind-mount target does not exist, Docker creates it as `root:root` mode `0755`,
which the runtime UID cannot write, and startup fails with SQLite's
`unable to open database file` error. The log names the database path, the
directory state and the runtime UID. Pre-create the host `data/` and `config/`
directories owned by `65532:65532` before the first start, or
`chown -R 65532:65532` them after a failed start, then start the container
again. Named volumes avoid this entirely: Docker seeds them from the image
with correct ownership.

Settings saves by creating a temporary file beside the resolved config and
atomically renaming it; a symlinked config path is followed to its final
target, so the link stays in place and the target receives the document. The
restore rollback publishes through the same writer, so a failed restore of a
symlinked config keeps the link too. A
read-only mount, or a bind mount of only the config file, cannot
support that save contract. Mount the whole writable directory, or deliberately
use read-only configuration and update it outside the dashboard. Do not mount
the committed example as a mutable runtime config.

The container listens on `:8080`; restrict publication on the host with
`-p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080`. Binding to loopback *inside* the container prevents
ordinary published-port access. Docker port publication does not add operator
authentication. Do not share one database among independent proxy containers.

Upstream URLs are reached from the proxy container, so `localhost` in
`X-Proxy-Base-URL` means that container, not the Docker host. Use an upstream
hostname reachable on its network, such as another Compose service name.
Host-service access needs an explicitly configured host-gateway mapping or
another reachable host address; it is not included in the supplied deployment.

Arguments after the image replace its complete default command. If overriding
a server flag, also keep `-config /config/proxy.yaml -db-path /data/proxy.db`
unless intentionally selecting other paths or disabling storage. The
`-print-config` and `-print-example-config` commands print their respective
documents without starting a server.

Replace the container to upgrade or adopt startup-bound settings; the dashboard
cannot rebuild an immutable image. Keep the same volumes and back them up before
upgrades. If only a saved config file changed, ordinary `up -d` need not replace
the container. Apply startup-bound changes explicitly:

```sh
docker compose up -d --force-recreate millivolt
```

Container stop sends SIGTERM, which cancels unfinished requests before
draining storage. Allow enough stop grace time for the configured shutdown and
queued writes; forced termination can prevent that drain. No stop/flush can
recover records already dropped under storage overload.

### Image-only backup and restore

The supplied deployment can back up both named volumes without a source checkout,
Python, a shell inside the image or a helper image. This is an **offline** backup:
stop callers first, allow active work to finish, and keep the service stopped
while copying. Run from the deployment directory with the same Compose project
and environment used to start it. If you use `-p`, repeat that selection on every
Compose command. Do not concurrently replace or restart the source container.

The following saves the original Compose file, the pulled image's registry digest,
and both volume archives in a new private directory. It expects the supplied
single-service layout, `/data` and `/config`, with a saved `proxy.yaml` present.
Privately retain any local `.env` or other deployment inputs as well.

```sh
(
  set -eu
  umask 077
  backup_dir="$(mktemp -d ./millivolt-backup.XXXXXXXX)"
  printf 'Backup directory: %s\n' "$backup_dir"
  container_id="$(docker compose ps -q millivolt)"
  test -n "$container_id"
  image_id="$(docker inspect --format '{{.Image}}' "$container_id")"
  docker image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' "$image_id" > "$backup_dir/image.txt"
  cp compose.yaml "$backup_dir/compose.yaml"
  docker compose stop millivolt
  test "$(docker inspect --format '{{.State.Status}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' "$container_id")" = 'exited 0'
  docker compose cp millivolt:/data/. - > "$backup_dir/data.tar"
  docker compose cp millivolt:/config/. - > "$backup_dir/config.tar"
  docker compose start millivolt
)
```

A failed stop or copy exits without automatically restarting the service; inspect
the failure before resuming. Copy the completed backup to protected independent
storage. The data archive includes any WAL/SHM files, not just `proxy.db`. Never
use this file-copy procedure while SQLite is open. An archive cannot recover
records already dropped or writes lost through forced termination.

Restore into a **new project and fresh volumes**, leaving the original deployment
and backups untouched. Enter the completed backup directory and an unused
loopback host port when prompted. The original supplied Compose file is required:
do not substitute resolved `docker compose config` output, custom external-volume
names or bind mounts, which can point the new project at existing data.

```sh
(
  set -eu
  umask 077
  printf 'Backup directory to restore: '
  IFS= read -r backup_dir
  test -s "$backup_dir/data.tar"
  test -s "$backup_dir/config.tar"
  MILLIVOLT_IMAGE="$(head -n 1 "$backup_dir/image.txt")"
  case "$MILLIVOLT_IMAGE" in *@sha256:*) ;; *) exit 1 ;; esac
  printf 'Unused loopback host port: '
  IFS= read -r MILLIVOLT_PORT
  case "$MILLIVOLT_PORT" in ''|*[!0-9]*) exit 1 ;; esac
  test "$MILLIVOLT_PORT" -ge 1
  test "$MILLIVOLT_PORT" -le 65535
  export MILLIVOLT_IMAGE MILLIVOLT_PORT
  restore_dir="$(mktemp -d ./millivolt-restore-XXXXXXXX)"
  restore_project="$(basename "$restore_dir" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')"
  cp "$backup_dir/compose.yaml" "$restore_dir/compose.yaml"
  restore_compose() {
    docker compose --env-file /dev/null -p "$restore_project" -f "$restore_dir/compose.yaml" "$@"
  }
  existing_containers="$(docker ps -aq --filter "label=com.docker.compose.project=$restore_project")"
  test -z "$existing_containers"
  existing_volumes="$(docker volume ls -q --filter "name=^${restore_project}_")"
  test -z "$existing_volumes"
  restore_compose create millivolt
  restore_compose cp --archive - millivolt:/data < "$backup_dir/data.tar"
  restore_compose cp --archive - millivolt:/config < "$backup_dir/config.tar"
  restore_compose up -d millivolt
  restore_compose logs --tail 100 millivolt
  printf 'Restored project: %s\nCompose directory: %s\nHost port: %s\n' "$restore_project" "$restore_dir" "$MILLIVOLT_PORT"
)
```

Keep the tar streams intact and retain `--archive` on restore: the private config
must remain owned by runtime UID/GID `65532:65532` with mode `0600`; the restored
database is subject to the same ownership and mode check at boot.
Check Settings and retained history on the new private port before redirecting
clients. Save the printed project name and deployment inputs for later commands;
the example bypasses automatic `.env` loading during recovery.

Docker documents [tar-stream copying](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/cp/)
and [Compose archive mode](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/cp/).
The repository's isolated container check exercises stopped-volume backup and
restore into fresh volumes, including settings, history and file permissions.
Source deployments can instead use the live SQLite
[online-backup helper](operations.md#storage-and-accounting) or the Settings archive
described next.

### Settings backup and restore

The dashboard Settings Backup category downloads and restores a self-checked
`.mvb` archive. Choose config, database, or both. The archive is a packed
SQLite snapshot (`VACUUM INTO`, so free pages are not copied) and/or the
schema YAML, then zstd-compressed with a content checksum and an outer SHA-256
of the uncompressed payload. Encoding streams each member into the compressor
while hashing and counting it, writes the archive once into a staging file,
and self-checks that file before returning it; an archive that fails decode
or semantic checks is never emitted, so a produced backup is never a silent
corrupt file. The database member is read from the packed snapshot file in
bounded chunks instead of being copied whole into memory, so the download cost
does not grow with a heap copy of the database. A source file that changes
size or cannot be read fails the encode before an archive is emitted.

Restore streams the upload through the `backup_max_bytes` ceiling into one
private staging file and decodes it with the same header, zstd, SHA-256 and
member-framing checks. When a live store can stage it, the database member is
written straight into a private file on the live database's volume instead of
being materialized on the heap; a restore that selects the database member
without a store fails closed before staging, and a member the request did not
select is stream-discarded after its framing checks. Config bytes stay
buffered within the same 16 MiB config-document bound
`Config.Validate` enforces on the canonical rendered YAML, so a config that
validates can never exceed what an archive may retain. A config member that
declares a larger size is rejected before its bytes are copied, and encoding
refuses to emit one, so an older archive whose config member exceeds that bound
fails restore. The bound covers only the config member; the database member
stays streamed under the payload ceiling. It validates that hash, the
zstd frame, member framing and config `Validate()` before applying anything.
A selected database member is decoded into its private staging file first,
then must pass `PRAGMA integrity_check`; only that checked file is published
as the pending snapshot, which restore then preflights for admission before
the config member is written. Decode holds the uncompressed payload to the same `backup_max_bytes` ceiling as
the upload (and to the Schema maximum, whichever is lower), so a small
compressed file cannot expand past what the operator configured; an over-cap
payload answers 413 with the upload's wording and stages no pending snapshot. Download lists how many live settings differ from default and how
many stored requests would be packed. Picking a file first inspects the
archive: created time, size, member sizes, each config key as default vs
modified vs the live file, and the database request span when a live store can
stage the member. Inspect loads the live file through the same strict, bounded
reader used by config reload and restore, not the boot repair path: an unknown
nested field, an extra YAML document, a non-regular file, or a file above the
16 MiB document bound fails the inspect instead of comparing against a repaired
or partial view. Inspect decodes and counts the database member in place and
computes its overlap with the live store without writing another copy. Without a
live store it reports `present:true`, the decoded `bytes`, `inspectable:false`
and the reason, and produces no request span.
Config **replace** loads and validates the backup, writes canonical YAML, and
preserves CLI-overridden `listen` and `db_path`. Config **merge** overlays only
keys that differ from `Default()` onto the live file, so live custom values
stay unless the backup also customized them. An omitted `config_mode` or
`database_mode` defaults to replace; an explicitly empty or whitespace value is
rejected as malformed rather than treated as absent. Either way the restored config
hot-applies through the same owner as a Settings save, is reflected in
`last_reload`, and reports restart-required keys. Database
**replace** streams the decoded file into a pending snapshot next to `db_path`,
syncs it, and atomically renames it into place; Open admits the pending file
only after it checks again, and the restore waits for process restart. A
`db_path` that is a symlink is resolved to its real target first, so staging,
admission, the rollback set and the state marker all belong to the file SQLite
actually opened; the link stays intact and points at the replacement. A
combined merge compares the same resolved identities rather than the two
spellings.
Database **merge** attaches the decoded file read-only and inserts request ids
that are not already in the live store immediately (live rows win on conflict);
the attached snapshot rejects writes, while the live database stays writable
for the merge, and no restart is required. Its request rows, debug sidecars and
since-inception totals commit as one transaction, so a failed totals write
leaves no partial merge behind. Truncated or bit-flipped files are rejected.
The `backup_max_bytes` setting is the encoded-archive and the decoded-payload
ceiling alike; encoding enforces it while the stream is written, so an over-cap
archive is removed instead of partially served, an over-cap upload answers 413
before decoding, and a decoded payload over it answers 413 before staging a
snapshot.

Restore phases are ordered, not atomic. The database member runs first: a
replace stages the decoded file and preflights it with the same schema,
writer-INSERT and request-scan value checks boot runs before touching the live
database, bounded by the same maintenance budget as boot maintenance, and a
merge commits rows into the running store. One restore owns the whole
transaction from the first uploaded byte, so two restores cannot stage and
decode two full members on the database volume at once; an inspect shares that
serialization because it stages the same members. Only then is the
config written and hot-applied. A failed stage, preflight, or merge leaves the
config file and live snapshot unchanged, and a failed config write or reload
rolls the config back and restores a replace's previous pending slot. A
successful live merge has no rollback: if the later config phase fails, the
merged rows stay applied. A crash between the database and config phases is
likewise not atomic; the pending snapshot or completed merge can be durable
while the config file still has its previous bytes. Preserved `.incoming`,
`.incoming.invalid-<token>`, `.incoming.invalid-interrupted-<token>`,
`.previous`, `.snapshot-state`, and `.millivolt-restore-pending-*` files next to
`db_path` are boot-recovery evidence and may need operator inspection after such
a crash; do not remove them while a restore may have been in flight. Quarantine
names carry a unique token and keep their sidecars beside them, so repeated
rejections accumulate instead of overwriting the previous one. The
`.millivolt-restore-pending-*` copy is a hard link to the snapshot that was
queued before the restore; it is created before the successor replaces the slot,
so the pending queue is never empty, and a crash on either side leaves a
recoverable snapshot instead of an orphan that the 24 hour staging sweep
eventually deletes. A volume without hard links (exFAT, vfat, and several FUSE
or SMB mounts) rejects `link(2)`; there the slot is moved aside instead, still
without copying the snapshot bytes, and a crash leaves only the preserved
sibling, which boot re-admits. When the stage fails before the successor
replaces the slot the restore drops the copy again, and when a boot finds a
rejected successor or an empty slot it renames the preserved copy back onto the
slot and admits once, so the queued snapshot is neither hidden nor swept. A combined config and database merge
answers 400 when the restored config's effective `db_path` differs from the
running store's file, because the rows would be written to a database the next
boot does not open; merge the database separately or use database replace.

At boot, a pending snapshot is admitted only after the same schema, trigger,
writer-insert, request-scan value and capture-id preflight `Open` runs. The
trigger fence rejects every unowned trigger in the snapshot, not only those
attached to `requests`: a trigger body is arbitrary SQL, so one attached to
`meta` or `request_debug` can delete or rewrite request rows. The capture-id
fence rejects a `request_debug` id that is NULL, non-text or blank: such a row
can never be fetched by id or reached by the expiry sweep, yet still counts
against the debug byte budget. Restore merge applies the same fence before it
imports any row. Recovery consults
the durable `.snapshot-state` marker rather than inferring a transition from the
files present. A markerless rollback set from a pre-marker release cannot be
classified: when a live main exists, recovery keeps it and removes the
`.previous` debris. Discarding a non-empty `.previous-wal` in that markerless
state logs a startup warning, because its committed frames cannot be
distinguished from debris and may be lost. Marked pending and committed recovery
behavior is unchanged.

Both directions stage database-sized transient files in the live database's own
directory, so capacity follows the data volume rather than a hardened
deployment's small `/tmp` tmpfs. Budget roughly one compressed upload plus one
packed database copy during a restore, and for a replace also the pending copy
at `db_path`. The download's `VACUUM INTO` snapshot directory is removed after
the archive is encoded, including on failure or a client disconnect. A restore
removes its private upload file and decoded database directory after inspect or
apply on every path: a normal response, an invalid or over-cap archive, a
validation or apply failure, or a client disconnect. A config-only upload may
use the process temp directory because it carries no database-sized member. A
packed file already on the staging volume (VACUUM dest, decoded member, pending
`.incoming`) is integrity-checked in place, and inspect, overlap, replace and
merge consume it by path, so none writes a second database-sized copy. A
container's `/tmp` is a small tmpfs by design and never caps backup size.

## Versions and images

[VERSION](../VERSION) is the application release source. The dashboard asset
fingerprint is separate: it detects changed embedded frontend bytes, not a
semantic release or a complete backend change.

`main` is promotion-only. Full source, browser and live MCP integration, and
native container checks run on all `testing` pull requests, code-bearing
`testing` pushes, manually dispatched `testing` gates, and manually pushed `v*`
tags; docs and site-only pushes use `docs.yml`. They also run on Dependabot's `main` security PRs. An ordinary
promotion pull request from `testing` requires its head to be the current
`testing` tip, `main` to be already merged back into `testing`, and a
successful full-gate record for that exact commit: the canonical `check.yml`
push run's own check suite, with `unit`, `browser` and both native container legs. When
a final docs-only commit follows the closest gated `testing` commit, it reuses
that gate if every path since it is docs/site-only; the fallback selects the
closest gated testing commit from canonical `testing` push runs, with no
commit-count bound. The proof polls
pending exact check runs a bounded number of times and fails closed if they are
still pending. For a code-bearing head, let the `testing` `check.yml` push gate
finish before opening or re-running a promotion PR. A docs/site-only head has no
canonical `check.yml` push run of its own, so wait for `docs.yml` or only the
`required` docs validation. It does not rerun the suite. A code-bearing promotion must also have a `VERSION`
newer than every existing release tag. Docs/site-only promotions skip the
version and full-gate proofs, validate docs, workflow policy and the site in
`required` within its ten-minute budget, and do not rebuild images or cut a
release. Merge with a merge
commit. The merged-PR release workflow tags that reviewed merge commit and
publishes the image; a delivered code-bearing main push is an idempotent
fallback. It never pushes `main`. Dependabot security pull requests are the
only other exception and normally do not cut a release by themselves; an
untagged pending `VERSION` can publish. A manually pushed `v*` tag ships exactly
as tagged. If the version tag already points at the released commit but its
GitHub release is missing, the publish job fails closed with a repair
instruction instead of reporting a successful re-run. Repair the existing tag's
release after verifying the image; the job never moves a tag or republishes
images. The full maintainer checklist lives in
[Contributing](../CONTRIBUTING.md#branch-workflow).

`go run ./cmd/proxy -version` (or `/millivolt -version` in the image) prints
JSON with `version`, `revision`, `modified`, and `go_version`. Unavailable VCS
metadata is reported honestly as revision `unknown` or `modified:null`.

The registry target is `ghcr.io/llm-4-people/millivolt`. Check the
[container package](https://github.com/LLM-4-People/millivolt/pkgs/container/millivolt)
and [image workflow](https://github.com/LLM-4-People/millivolt/actions/workflows/check.yml) for what has
actually been published; a version in a checkout does not prove an image exists.
Use a published digest to pin exact bytes. Version tags identify releases but
are not intrinsically immutable; moving branch and stable aliases can change.

The [workflow](../.github/workflows/check.yml) runs source, race and browser
checks, then native container smoke checks on Linux `amd64` and `arm64` for all
`testing` pull requests, code-bearing `testing` pushes, manually dispatched
`testing` gates, and manually pushed `v*` tags, and for Dependabot's `main`
security PRs. The `unit`, `browser` and `container` jobs start together. Docs
and site-only pushes use `docs.yml` instead. A normal
promotion PR proves the current testing tip, merged-back main and the full-gate
record for that commit, or for the closest gated testing commit with only docs
changes after it, and requires a successful
[escalation](../.github/workflows/escalation.yml) run (every Go test under the
race detector plus a five-run clock-sensitive flake sweep) for the reviewed
head; docs-only promotions validate the docs, workflow policy and
site directly. The merged promotion PR carries the reviewed merge commit and
releases it; a delivered code-bearing `main` push only reuses the same reviewed
merge and is idempotent.
Publication is limited to this repository's merged promotion pull requests,
delivered pushes to `main`, matching release tags, and `testing`-branch pushes
(which publish only the moving `testing` tag). The release `publish` job waits
for `required`. The `publish-testing` job waits for `unit`, `browser` and
`container` instead, because a testing push has no promotion proof to wait for. A release
run whose `VERSION` is already tagged, such as a Dependabot security merge,
normally does not publish; if main carries an untagged pending `VERSION`, that
run can publish it. Open or unmerged pull requests do not publish images; a
merged promotion PR does.

| Image tag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `main` | Moving production image for the released current `main` revision; updated by a non-prerelease versioned release cut from a merged promotion PR or a delivered main push. A prerelease does not move it, and a manually pushed release tag does not either. |
| `testing` | Moving development image after a successful testing-branch push; never a release. Its OCI version label reports the embedded `VERSION`, which can lag the latest release. |
| `sha-<full commit>` | Release tag for the exact cut revision built and published; the version bump is part of the reviewed promotion merge, so this is a main commit. Testing pushes do not publish it, while a manually pushed tag publishes it for the tagged revision. |
| Version from `VERSION` | Created by the matching `v`-prefixed release tag on the promotion merge commit, or by a manually pushed tag. |
| `latest` | Moving stable alias updated by every non-prerelease release, including a release cut by a merged promotion PR, a main push or a manually pushed tag. Prereleases and testing pushes do not update it. A tag push moves the version, `sha-` and `latest` tags only; `main` stays where the last main-branch release put it. |

Release builds request an SBOM and max-mode provenance. The image and its
attestations are published before the tag and release are updated; the workflow
never pushes `main`. A failed image build does not leave a public release
pointing at a missing image. Verify
the published manifest and attestations with `docker buildx imagetools inspect`,
verify the repository-associated artifact attestation with
`gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/llm-4-people/millivolt:<version> -R LLM-4-People/millivolt`,
and pin the digest for deployment. A tag name alone is not an integrity check.

Set `MILLIVOLT_IMAGE` to the desired full image reference or published digest
before the Compose pull/up commands. The `0.x` version series is initial
development, not a promise of stable APIs across releases.

GitHub initially publishes GHCR packages privately, even when their repository
is public. A package administrator must make the package public separately and
verify an anonymous pull. Repository linkage grants workflow access, not public
visibility; see GitHub's
[package access documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/packages/learn-github-packages/configuring-a-packages-access-control-and-visibility).

## Reload, restart and shutdown

`SIGHUP`, `POST /admin/reload`, a successful Settings save, and a backup
config restore use the same hot-reload owner. Invalid reloads preserve the
running config. Reloadable transport/scheduler settings affect new work
without closing active transports.

Startup-bound consumers keep their boot settings until restart. Settings reports
`restart_required`; its effective configuration snapshot can contain new values
that those consumers have not adopted yet. The schema/example identify which
fields require restart.

Rebuild & restart requires Go on PATH and the original source tree available at
its compiled-in path. Moved/trimpath builds may report it unavailable. It builds
the working tree exactly as it is: uncommitted, unstaged and untracked files are
compiled, so a restart is not a review gate and a dirty tree ships as-is. The
rebuilt binary is written into the process temp directory, which must be
writable (`TMPDIR`, or `/tmp` when unset); an unusable directory is refused with
that directory named rather than as a build fault. The choreography builds
first, stops acceptance while retaining the listening socket, drains active
handlers, flushes storage, then hands the socket to a ready child. A flush
failure aborts and resumes the old process. A drain timeout still flushes and
hands off: the in-flight requests are cut, but everything finalized before them
is durable before the child opens the database. The flush has its own bound
rather than sharing the drain window. The handoff also takes the config
transaction lock for its whole flush fence, so a start while a reload, Settings
save or backup restore is running is refused with `409` naming the operation
instead of queueing behind it; the fence itself is bounded by
`restart_drain_timeout` plus the flush bound. A restore holds that lock across
its streaming upload, so `POST /admin/reload` and a Settings save answer `409`
while one is in flight rather than waiting for a client-paced upload to finish.
Parked native-adapter runs
are process-local and do not survive a successful restart.

Ordinary SIGINT/SIGTERM shutdown is different: it cancels active stream contexts,
then shuts down HTTP and drains/closes storage. Do not describe it as preserving
unfinished streams. Already-dropped records cannot be recovered by any flush.

Starting another matching proxy executable on an occupied port can trigger
same-binary port reclamation (SIGTERM, then escalation). This is not the graceful
rebuild workflow; choose distinct ports and databases for separate instances.

pages.title: Routes and debugging
pages.description: This page covers the operator and data routes, access control, pause and limits, error storm and quota protection, debug and preview capture, export and...

sections.heading: Operator and data routes
sections.text: The routes below belong to millivolt. They are operator-gated unless the row is marked open; the canonical open-path list is in operator access . Read handlers enforce their supported methods; wrong-method requests must not fall through to inference. The namespace is standardized: /metrics/* and dashboard routes are the protected read plane, and /admin/* is the operator action plane; the credential gates both. Route Action / important contract GET /healthz Unauthenticated liveness probe for Docker HEALTHCHECK and load balancers. Reports process/HTTP liveness only, no storage depth. Trailing-slash look-alikes ( /healthz/... ) are reserved and answer 404, never inference. GET /readyz Unauthenticated readiness probe. 200 when the durable pipeline can persist; 503 with a reason when the writer is wedged or a flush failed since boot. Compose uses it through -readycheck . Trailing-slash look-alikes are reserved and answer 404, never inference. GET /favicon.ico Unauthenticated ICO brand mark. Browsers fetch this without Authorization; it is registered on the mux so it never reaches the inference catch-all. GET /favicon.svg , /apple-touch-icon.png , /icon-*.png Ungated SVG/PNG icons for ta

sections.heading: Operator access
sections.text: MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN is the single operator credential for the whole dashboard. It is read once at boot from the process environment, never from proxy.yaml, so it cannot leak through Settings, -print-config , /admin/config output, snapshots or logs. The gate is deny by default and lives in one chokepoint in front of every route. This is the canonical open-path list; Security and the reverse-proxy guide summarize it instead of maintaining a second list. Open: GET /healthz , GET /readyz , the POST /session login handshake (the one open operator route), origin-root brand/PWA files ( /favicon.ico , icons, /manifest.webmanifest , /sw.js ) and transparent inference. Provider credentials ride the same header name and are never inspected by the gate. Gated: the dashboard HTML and /dash/* assets, every /metrics/* surface and every /admin/* route, including unclassified future admin paths and unsupported methods, plus the /mcp endpoint and its reserved /mcp/* look-alikes. A gated MCP request also needs its credential as a Bearer header: the session cookie alone is refused there ( 403 ), because the caller's credential is forwarded on the endpoint's internal calls. Present the credential

sections.heading: Pause and Limits
sections.text: Pause creates holds; it does not disconnect already-running sends. Matching new sends and retries wait until the hold expires or is resumed. Choose all traffic, any combination of the five scope dimensions, or clients that were unseen when a new-clients hold was created. "New" does not mean new requests or new conversations. A hold scopes on the same five dimensions a limit does: providers, models, clients, upstream key hashes and conversations. Values inside one dimension are alternatives, an unset dimension matches any value, and set dimensions intersect - the same rule limits use, because the scheduler matches both against one request identity. When named clients and new are combined, either client condition may match. A hold has its own duration and queue cap; the cap defaults to max_queue_size when the hold does not set one. Excess waiting work can be refused; an indefinite hold needs an explicit resume. Existing holds can be edited in place or resumed individually, while Resume all clears all holds. Overlapping scopes are rejected instead of silently replacing a different hold. The HTTP shape is closed. A resume carries only paused:false and an optional id ; supplying a scope

sections.heading: Error storm protection
sections.text: Open Settings, select Error storm protection , and turn on Enable protection . It is opt-in in both neutral defaults and the deployment example. Choose the rolling window, minimum samples and failure threshold, then select HTTP failure statuses, transient transport failures and response/stream failures. Provider protection requires all models receiving requests in that same window to meet the thresholds individually. A single affected model is held on its own while other active models remain healthy. If only one model is active, that model can establish a provider-wide incident. Provider and model protection can also be enabled independently. Configure initial/maximum recovery delays, multiplier, jitter, recovery successes, additional retries, queue capacity, per-wait timeout and retained scope capacity in that category. The generated example supplies every type, range and default. Existing Queue & retry limits and provider Limits still apply; neither storm_max_wait nor a per-send deadline is a total request timeout. Use a client timeout appropriate to the desired end-to-end wait. Each clickable banner identifies its current scope and safe failure category (HTTP status, transport e

sections.heading: Quota pause
sections.text: Open Settings, select Quota pause , and choose the reaction to a 429 whose error envelope is a durable account condition - insufficient_quota , insufficient_credits , spend/hard limits, the recognized numeric billing codes (the built-in classification is fixed and quota_error_classes may add spellings; only the reaction is configurable): off (default): the 429 surfaces to the client immediately. Nothing is parked or retried. retry : a provider-wide recovery gate opens on the first such 429 from an OpenAI-wire provider. The triggering request absorbs the 429 and re-sends per the error storm recovery delays; every new request to the provider parks on the gate (bounded by storm_max_queue and storm_max_wait ); the gate closes after quota_pause_recovery_successes consecutive successful probes (the default 1 closes on the first 2xx) and the queue drains. A provider Retry-After on the quota 429 paces the next probe like any other 429. manual : an indefinite provider-scoped pause (an operator hold labeled with the quota class) is created automatically; every request, triggering one included, queues until an operator resumes it on the pause surface. When a pre-existing hold already covers t

sections.heading: Debug and preview capture
sections.text: Debug selects clients, providers and/or models and starts a capture session for a chosen duration or until stopped. At least one dimension is required; selected dimensions intersect, with alternatives inside each dimension. It does not have an unrestricted "all" switch. Sessions can be edited or stopped individually; Stop all ends every active session. A stop carries only enabled:false and an optional session id ; a scope or duration beside a stop is a 400 rather than a silent stop-everything. Conflicting scopes are rejected. Debug model matching uses the native-model normalization in debug.go , separate from display-only model rules. Do not assume that every model spelling is an independent exact scope. The session timer selects future captures. debug_capture_ttl separately controls retained capture lifetime after completion, and debug_capture_max_bytes bounds one capture document: retained headers are charged first and the remainder is split between the request and the client-facing response body. Oversized captures are marked truncated. debug_store_max_bytes (default 512 MiB) caps the whole capture sidecar; once the next write would exceed it, new captures are skipped and TTL ex

sections.heading: Export and deletion
sections.text: The operator console's export section downloads finalized request records as JSON, not the process's stderr log and not a complete administrative audit trail. With durable storage it reads the database; otherwise it uses available ring records. Open export, choose either all history or matching records, and review the previewed count before downloading. Provider, model, client and conversation merge the server's known vocabularies with whatever the live record ring holds, so a quiet proxy can still filter by what has run since it started, and each of them also accepts a typed value. Status is the one list-only dimension, because a status code is not a name anyone can type reliably. A debug-only export can include retained capture sidecars. A debug capture is written beside its record as a debug_capture member, and only when the row still has a stored sidecar. The artifact therefore carries debug bodies only while durable storage is live: a ring-record export, or a sidecar already reclaimed by the capture retention sweep, has the record alone. The bodies remain sensitive either way. The export predicate has no constraint for status_code=0 and debug=0 ; both are off rather than a mat

sections.heading: Settings and Restart
sections.text: Settings only reads configuration when opened. Its search, category rail and structured editors work on a local draft; Apply uses the revision-checked save contract . The console's system section reads restart availability and status when opened. The restart action is disabled while a restart is in progress or rebuilding is unavailable. Progress reports actual build/drain/flush/handoff phases; it is not a simulated timer. After a successful handoff, reconnect/bootstrap refreshes history, aggregates, operator state and config. Changed embedded frontend assets trigger a page reload through that same refresh owner. The lifecycle section distinguishes source rebuilds from container replacement and ordinary shutdown.

sections.heading: Dashboard data and request inspection

Explorer selections and the request status filter scope the timeline and request log; selecting a card adds a filter and entity links pivot within that shared route. Browser back/forward restores hash-based scopes. Chart preset, timeframe, percentile and series visibility persist in browser storage. These saved views are local browser state, not shared server settings. The In-flight tile separates work that is sending from work the scheduler is parking. Its summary names the two totals that fit the narrowest tile - active and queued - and the composition rail under the value splits every live state (sending, pending, operator-paused, throttled) by color; hovering the rail, or focusing it with assistive technology, reads the exact per-state counts. A queued request is one the proxy has not sent upstream yet: it can be waiting in the admission queue (per-key concurrency, pacing, a provider cap or an operator hold) or in the retry send gate behind a 429/5xx pacing window. The request table marks the same state with the throttled pill, and the status selector can filter on it. Explorer dimensions are Providers, Models, Client, Conversations, Tools, Time, Status,

Retry disclosure opens absorbed attempts under the original request, not another inference record. The attempts log keeps the newest max_retries plus storm_max_retries entries (at least one): a durable quota wait re-sends without spending either budget, so the tail is what explains a long parked request. Click the detail arrow or a non-link row cell to open its drawer; previous/next controls navigate requests without changing the scope. Content covers conversation and parent ids, turn and size composition, and prompt/response previews. Usage covers token splits, generated tokens, timing, throughput, cost, transport decomposition and tools. sections.text: Request duration starts after upload and includes metadata work, queue/hold/retry waits and response handling. TTFT is measured from the upstream attempt's own send start to the first token (reasoning or answer), so every retry has its own TTFT. The value excludes proxy scheduler queueing, request parsing and retry backoff, but it does span the upstream transport window from request handoff (dial, TLS, connection-pool wait, header wait). A request that produced no token, one that never sent an upstream attempt of its own (a parked cursor resume), and any non-streamed response have no TTFT: the log shows a placeholder, not 0 ms, and aggregates skip it. Rows written before 0.3.34 stored ttft_ms anchored at request start (upload, queueing and retry backoff included) and were zeroed once by the boot repair, so they report TTFT as absent; their started_at and first_token_at timestamps remain, keeping pre_token_ms and decode windows usable. TPS is the single generation-speed measure: (generation tokens - 1) over the first-token to last-token window. Average TTFT and average TPS are the arithmetic means of those per-request samples. sections.text: The HTML includes the canonical bootstrap state so the first paint need not wait for a second state request. Live SSE carries pending progress and finalization; KPI/operator polling and configured aggregate refresh keep derived surfaces current. Reconnects use sequence/feed identity and fall back to full snapshots when replay cannot be trusted. The footer distinguishes live/offline, active holds/Debug, process-local storage drops, totals degraded by a failed startup history scan, and a degraded operator-state restore. The last one is the difference between "nothing is held" and "a saved hold or limit document could not be read": the served pause and throttle snapshots carry restore_degraded , so a truncated document does not boot as a healthy, unpaused proxy with its saved rules silently gone. The flag stays true for the life of the process; a restart that reads a document which decodes is what clears it. Each key holds one value, so the next accepted operator write replaces the unreadable document rather than preserving it: capture the bytes first if they are needed as evidence.
