pages.markdown_text:
# Reverse proxy and remote access

Use a protected ingress when accessing millivolt beyond a trusted local machine.
The whole dashboard is gated by the shared `MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN`
credential; there is no tenant isolation and no per-user identity. At the
application gate, only the unauthenticated `/healthz` and `/readyz` probes, the
`POST /session` login handshake, origin-root brand/PWA files and transparent
inference stay open, so a load balancer can health-check the service without
holding the credential and a browser can reach the login handshake. The canonical
open-path list is in [operator access](routes.md#operator-access); this
guide only adds the ingress boundary. Read [Security](../SECURITY.md) first.

![Reverse proxy topology: the API client and dashboard browser reach NGINX over TLS, NGINX forwards over loopback to millivolt, and millivolt sends requests to the selected upstream](images/diagrams/reverse-proxy.svg)

The diagram is a text-equivalent summary of the example below: NGINX terminates
TLS and enforces access; millivolt owns routing, the operator session, and the
history; the upstream receives the selected credentials.

## NGINX setup

[deploy/nginx.conf](../deploy/nginx.conf) is the canonical example. It serves
millivolt at the origin root, with NGINX on the same host as the loopback-published
Compose service. Use a maintained NGINX release with the `http2 on` directive
(introduced in 1.25.1), not the deprecated `listen ... http2` syntax.

The sample splits two prefix locations because they do not share an access
model. `location /v1` is the OpenAI-compatible inference base: preserve provider
`Authorization` and routing headers, and allowlist API clients. `location /`
covers everything else, including the dashboard and operator plane (`/dash/`,
`/metrics/`, `/admin/`) plus the application-open `POST /session`, `/healthz`,
`/readyz` and brand/PWA paths: allowlist operators, and keep `Host` plus the session
cookie so Settings origin checks and the live feed work; the comparison is
case-insensitive, so a case-preserving ingress is fine. The `/session`
handshake is open at millivolt so login works, but this location still
allowlists it at the edge. A URL-capable MCP client uses this location with
`/mcp` appended and the operator Bearer header: the application's MCP endpoint
is Bearer-only and refuses the session cookie. Shared streaming proxy settings
live on the `server` so both SSE paths stay unbuffered. Prefix `/v1` wins over
`/` for `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/models`; `GET /models` without that
prefix follows `location /` unless you add an exact `/models` block with the
inference rules.

1. Start the normal [Compose deployment](../README.md#docker-compose), retaining
   its loopback-only host port.
2. Copy the example into your NGINX HTTP configuration. Replace its example
   hostname, certificate paths and the two TEST-NET allowlists. The supplied
   address is a placeholder; unmatched clients are denied. The lists may differ
   when operators and API clients are not the same sources.
   Set `proxy_pass` to the chosen host port if `MILLIVOLT_PORT` is not 8080.
3. Validate with `nginx -t` before reloading your existing NGINX service. Confirm
   a trusted client and a denied client on both `/` and `/v1`.
4. Use `https://your-hostname/` for the dashboard and
   `https://your-hostname/v1` as the client API base. Keep sending the actual
   upstream base/key as described in the [client setup](../README.md#connect-a-client).

The sample is a `server` block, included under NGINX's existing `http` context,
not a replacement for the entire installation configuration. It does not issue
certificates or configure your firewall. Do not expose the original proxy port
alongside the protected HTTPS endpoint.

### Streaming and request handling

The example disables response/request buffering and proxy retries so the edge
does not batch SSE events or independently replay inference. It leaves HTTP
statuses intact, disables edge compression/caching, and ignores special upstream
`X-Accel-*` controls for buffering, redirects, rate limits, caching and charset.
Millivolt uses SSE, not a WebSocket endpoint; no `Upgrade` block is needed.

It preserves the external `Host`, including a nondefault port, so browser-origin
checks on Settings and other mutations keep working. It also overwrites
`X-Forwarded-Proto` with this server's `$scheme`, so a TLS presentation reaches
millivolt as `https` and the session cookie carries `Secure`; a client-supplied
value cannot spoof it. Overwriting is the recommended form. If your ingress
appends its scheme instead (`$http_x_forwarded_proto,$scheme`), the application
still marks the request secure when any token does, so a client-supplied `http`
in first position cannot downgrade the cookie.

The sample also resolves the client address with `real_ip`:

```nginx
set_real_ip_from 127.0.0.1;
real_ip_header X-Forwarded-For;
```

Without it, millivolt sees this hop's address as `RemoteAddr` for every request
and the per-source authentication throttle gets one bucket, so a single wrong
guess locks out every operator. `set_real_ip_from` lists the addresses allowed
to send a replacement address: this host's own loopback. If another load
balancer, tunnel or proxy fronts NGINX, add its address range there and set
`real_ip_recursive on` once every hop in the chain is listed. `real_ip` walks
`X-Forwarded-For` from the right and keeps the last untrusted address, so a
client that prepends a forged entry cannot displace the real one; NGINX's
default `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for` then appends the resolved address on the
way inbound, and the per-source authentication throttle reads that last
element. The record field is separate: `client_ip` records the first
`X-Forwarded-For` element when that header is present and the socket peer
otherwise; the value is diagnostic, never verified, and a directly reachable
caller can set it. The resolved address is a throttle key, not an identity:
keep the location allowlists in force. Those lists evaluate the resolved
address, so a caller that already reaches this host's loopback chooses what
they see: they separate remote networks from each other and from loopback
callers, not loopback callers from each other.

NGINX's body-size gate is
disabled in the sample: millivolt's existing `max_request_bytes` remains the
application limit, rather than an accidentally smaller duplicate at ingress.
Choose edge idle timeouts for your deployment. `proxy_read_timeout` limits the
gap between upstream reads, not the total lifetime of a stream.

These behaviors follow the official [proxy module](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_proxy_module.html),
[HTTP core module](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_core_module.html),
[HTTP/2 module](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_v2_module.html) and
[realip module](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_realip_module.html).

## Credentials and access control

The sample uses a trusted IP/VPN allowlist on each location, preserving
provider `Authorization` on `/v1` and the operator Bearer or session cookie on
`/`. Replace each placeholder with the addresses you intend to trust for that
plane. If another load balancer is in front of NGINX, list its addresses in
`set_real_ip_from` and switch `real_ip_recursive` on, so the trusted chain
matches reality; a hop that appends to `X-Forwarded-For` without being listed
is ignored on the left of the real client. TLS encrypts traffic but does not
authorize callers. A secure presentation also makes millivolt answer
`Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=15552000` (180 days, no
`includeSubDomains`) so a browser pins the scheme; NGINX's own `add_header`
is not needed for it, and adding a second HSTS header at the edge would send
two values.
See NGINX's [access module](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_access_module.html)
and [TLS configuration](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_ssl_module.html).

If you instead add HTTP Basic authentication on `/v1`, `Authorization` contains
the ingress credential and cannot simultaneously contain the provider bearer
key. Supply the provider key through `X-Proxy-Key`, and clear the consumed
ingress header before forwarding with `proxy_set_header Authorization "";`.
The same conflict applies on `/`: a browser behind Basic auth cannot also
present the dashboard's Bearer credential in the same header, so gated actions
fail. Prefer an address/VPN allowlist as in the sample, or an ingress that
adds its own credential through a different mechanism and forwards
`Authorization` untouched. Do not put Basic auth on `/v1` to "protect
inference" while leaving `/` on Bearer: that still overwrites the provider key.
The same separation applies to other ingress-only credentials: do not forward
them to an LLM provider. Clients must support your ingress authentication and
the proxy's custom routing headers.

The session handshake lives at `/session`, outside the admin plane, which
supports one specific pattern: an external authentication layer may front
`/admin/*` alone, because millivolt's own login stays reachable and the
mutation and settings routes become double-gated, the external layer plus
millivolt's credential. Operators fronting `/admin` this way must still pass
the session cookie and `Host` through to the proxy, since the dashboard's
fetch-based mutations rely on both.

## Container networking and other ingress servers

When NGINX itself is a container, `127.0.0.1` points back to NGINX, not millivolt.
Attach it to the same private Docker network and use `http://millivolt:8080` as
its upstream instead. Only the edge needs a publicly reachable port. Do not bind
millivolt to loopback inside its container, which would prevent peer access.
`MILLIVOLT_PORT` changes host publication, not this internal service port.

For another ingress implementation, preserve these same boundaries: protect the
origin, keep inference and the operator plane as separate access rules, forward
the original authority and required custom headers, allow streaming without
response buffering, avoid automatic inference retries, and choose upload/idle
limits deliberately. Subpath hosting is not the supplied deployment: dashboard
assets and routes expect the origin root.

The full run uses the documented levels and durations: 5 seconds for each fast stage, 300 seconds for each sustained level, and 60 seconds for each streaming throughput level. Override the level lists and durations with PERF_FAST_LEVELS , PERF_SUSTAINED_LEVELS , PERF_STREAMING_LEVELS , PERF_FAST_DURATION , PERF_SUSTAINED_DURATION , PERF_STREAMING_DURATION , PERF_STREAMING_HOLD and PERF_STREAMING_CHUNKS . The bundle records what ran; a changed run changes the page. The individual commands below are the same evidence path. Use a fresh DEV_COPY_DB=0 instance for each workload. Never target the main instance on port 8080. The stress harness verifies that the target is the private scripts/dev.sh instance before sending traffic. ( set -e trap 'scripts/dev.sh stop' EXIT export MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN='dev-instance-credential' DEV_COPY_DB=0 scripts/dev.sh go run ./cmd/stress -target http://1

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: The host was shared. Other workloads can change absolute rates and latency. The upstream was a local synthetic server. Provider latency, TLS, retries, payload shape, and real identity cardinality are not represented. These are short closed-loop bursts, not sustained production capacity. No result here is a capacity ceiling or a guarantee. The streaming concurrency table is a short ramp on a 10-frame, roughly 1-second fixture. The streaming throughput table is a 60-second per-level ramp on a 100-frame, roughly 1-second fixture. Both are synthetic-fixture measurements, not universal maxima. The throughput table's 1,024-client level is above the example max_conns_per_host of 512 and measures queueing; it is a fixed level list, not an automatic saturation search. Its token rate is the fixture's usage count, not provider-token throughput. The 300-second sustained sweep uses the fast-response fixture with no intentional stream hold ( -stream-duration 0 ). A level with durable drops is an overload observation, not a maximum streaming rate. The streaming throughput ramp is the only sustained held-stream run; it stops at its fixed levels and does not search beyond the largest listed level.

pages.markdown_text:
# Performance and resource usage

This page is the single source for the published performance and resource
numbers. It records what was measured, how it was measured, and what the result
does not prove. The [performance and footprint](operations.md#performance-and-footprint)
section in operations owns the implementation cost model and `go_memory_limit`
behavior.

These are scoped local measurements of the native proxy process, not deployment
guarantees. The page was regenerated from the result bundle on
2026-11-16 UTC.

## Artifact and idle footprint

| Artifact or state | Bytes | Display | Notes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Static amd64 binary | 21,663,904 | 20.7 MiB | Stripped, no CGO |
| amd64 runtime image | 38,022,232 | 36.3 MiB | Docker-reported content size |
| Compressed image archive | 9,887,262 | 9.4 MiB | `docker save` piped through `gzip -9` |
| Idle process, empty SQLite | 30,204 KiB | 29.5 MiB | After a 15-second quiet interval |
| Idle process CPU | 2 scheduler ticks | 0.067% | 2 ticks over 30 seconds |

The image size includes the distroless base, dependency notices, and the
embedded UI. It is not a compressed download size, a registry digest, or a
persistent-volume estimate. Idle RSS and CPU describe one process on this host.
A short sample cannot prove that a longer idle period uses exactly the same
resources.

## Method

| Item | Setting |
| --- | --- |
| Date | 2026-11-16 |
| Source revision | [`22c0b6b73655`](https://github.com/LLM-4-People/millivolt/commit/22c0b6b73655a349e086c345bc80907efbe16822) |
| Go toolchain | go1.27.4, `CGO_ENABLED=0` |
| Platform | Linux/amd64 under WSL2 |

The public example configuration was used, with private listen and database

| Workers | Proxy CPU | Peak proxy RSS | Upstream peak | Durable rows | Drops |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 1.2% | 31.5 MiB | 1 | Exact, 57 | 0 |
| 8 | 5.5% | 37.1 MiB | 8 | Exact, 448 | 0 |
| 32 | 14.9% | 47.8 MiB | 32 | Exact, 1,824 | 0 |
| 64 | 28.2% | 59.0 MiB | 64 | Exact, 3,648 | 0 |
| 128 | 57.9% | 81.3 MiB | 128 | Exact, 7,296 | 0 |
| 256 | 115.1% | 114.9 MiB | 256 | Exact, 14,592 | 0 |

Throughput peaked at 478.6 requests/s at 1,024 workers. At 1,024 workers the upstream peak stayed at 512, throughput was 478.6 requests/s against 471.5 at 512 workers, and p50 latency rose from 1.06 s to 2.13 s. The extra clients queued behind the configured 512 upstream connections.

Every level completed with exact durable accounting unless its row reports
drops. This run started under the host load the harness recorded, so absolute
rates are comparable only within this page and this host.

## Durable writer and overload

These are isolated Go benchmarks from the test overlay, not HTTP runs. Every
row and drop count is verified against successful requests. The overload
benchmark deliberately fills the bounded queue, so its drop count is a fixture
result, not a recommended operating point.

| Path | Durable rows/s | Allocations |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Direct batch insert at the configured batch capacity | 62,921 | 425,396 B/op, 7,279 allocs/op |
| Queued `Record` plus `Flush` at the queue capacity | 56,055 | 13,594,117 B/op, 232,920 allocs/op |

| Overload fixture | Wire requests/s | Durable rows/s | Dropped rows |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 32 workers | 72,619 | 19,994 | 101,507 |
| 128 workers | 64,161 | 14,605 | 113,242 |

The overload fixture confirms the accounting invariant `durable + dropped =
successful requests`. Increasing queue capacity alone cannot make sustained
overload lossless. A higher HTTP success rate is not a complete-accounting
result unless the durable row count and drop delta agree.

## Storage and retained projection

The storage fixture stores complete records, indexes, projection triggers, and
marshaled response headers in SQLite. Disk bytes include the database, WAL, and
shared-memory sidecar after a final flush.

| Measure | 10,000 records | 100,000 records |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| SQLite bytes total | 6.84 MiB | 49.20 MiB |
| SQLite bytes per record | 717.3 | 515.9 |
| Projection retained, built | 449.6 B/record | 470.8 B/record |
| Projection interned dimensions | 442.0 B/record | 429.1 B/record |
| Projection scanned decode | 580.3 B/record | 576.0 B/record |
| Projection transient allocation | 3,125 B/record | 3,434 B/record |

The projection process benchmark is a relative measure inside the test binary,
not the deployed proxy's RSS. At 100,000 records it
measured 94.6 MiB process RSS and a
66.0 MiB projection delta; at
10,000 records it measured
40.6 MiB process RSS and a
12.0 MiB delta. The test binary and its
linked packages are part of the absolute figure.

A fast-response run reached a 119.0 MiB
peak with 66,813 durable rows while no
dashboard projection was preloaded. Use the projection delta above for the
retained analytical cost, not the loaded-process peak as a substitute.

## Query and metadata paths

The query benchmarks seed a 100,000-row
scratch database and decode a 200-row
page. These are single-iteration measurements on a shared host, so small
differences are not meaningful.

| Query | Before cursor | With cursor | Allocations before cursor |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Provider equality | 4.24 ms | 3.85 ms | 1.38 MB, 5,455 allocs |
| Model equality | 2.81 ms | 2.93 ms | 1.38 MB, 5,445 allocs |
| Client equality | 36.52 ms | 18.73 ms | 1.38 MB, 5,442 allocs |
| Key-hash equality | 33.68 ms | 18.28 ms | 23.5 KB, 265 allocs |
| Conversation equality | 40.16 ms | 21.73 ms | 23.2 KB, 264 allocs |
| Status equality | 38.98 ms | 20.99 ms | 698.1 KB, 2,942 allocs |

The request metadata path performs one bounded metadata decode; the allocation
column is measured per call.

| Metadata body | Time per request | Throughput | Allocations |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 KiB | 428 ns | 2,580.8 MB/s | 16 B, 1 alloc |
| 100 KiB | 4,808 ns | 21,314.0 MB/s | 16 B, 1 alloc |
| 1 MiB | 75,397 ns | 13,908.4 MB/s | 16 B, 1 alloc |

## Reproduce

`scripts/perf.sh` owns the repeatable local run: `bench`, `stress`, `streaming`,
`sustained`, `image`, or `all`. `scripts/perf.sh docs` runs the full set,
writes `perf/results.json`, and regenerates this page. It refuses a dirty tree
unless `PERF_ALLOW_DIRTY=1` is set, because published numbers must name a
commit.

The full run uses the documented levels and durations:
5 seconds for each
fast stage, 300
seconds for each sustained level, and
60 seconds for
each streaming throughput level. Override the level lists and durations with
`PERF_FAST_LEVELS`, `PERF_SUSTAINED_LEVELS`, `PERF_STREAMING_LEVELS`,
`PERF_FAST_DURATION`, `PERF_SUSTAINED_DURATION`, `PERF_STREAMING_DURATION`,
`PERF_STREAMING_HOLD` and `PERF_STREAMING_CHUNKS`. The bundle records what ran;
a changed run changes the page.

The individual commands below are the same evidence path. Use a fresh
`DEV_COPY_DB=0` instance for each workload. Never target the main instance on
port 8080. The stress harness verifies that the target is the private
`scripts/dev.sh` instance before sending traffic.

```sh
(
  set -e
  trap 'scripts/dev.sh stop' EXIT
  export MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN='dev-instance-credential'
  DEV_COPY_DB=0 scripts/dev.sh
  go run ./cmd/stress -target http://127.0.0.1:8081 \
    -concurrency 1,8,32,128 -duration 5s -stream-duration 0
)
```

The isolated benchmarks use the test overlay:

```sh
scripts/check.sh go test -run='^$' -bench='BenchmarkProjectionFootprint|BenchmarkStoreDiskBytes' \
  -benchtime=1x -count=1 ./internal/web
scripts/check.sh go test -run='^$' -bench='BenchmarkProjectionProcessRSS' \
  -benchtime=1x -count=1 ./internal/web
scripts/check.sh go test -run='^$' -bench='BenchmarkStorageWriter' \
  -benchtime=2s -benchmem -count=1 ./internal/storage
scripts/check.sh go test -run='^$' -bench='BenchmarkQueryBeforeEquality' \
  -benchtime=1x -benchmem -count=1 ./internal/storage
scripts/check.sh go test -run='^$' -bench='Benchmark(RequestMetadata|ProxyDurableContention)' \
  -benchtime=2s -benchmem -count=1 ./internal/proxy
```

The image measurements use a disposable local image:

```sh
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t millivolt-perf .
docker image inspect millivolt-perf --format '{{.Size}}'
docker save millivolt-perf | gzip -9 | wc -c
```

## Limitations

- The host was shared. Other workloads can change absolute rates and latency.
- The upstream was a local synthetic server. Provider latency, TLS, retries,
  payload shape, and real identity cardinality are not represented.
- These are short closed-loop bursts, not sustained production capacity. No
  result here is a capacity ceiling or a guarantee.
- The streaming concurrency table is a short ramp on a 10-frame, roughly
  1-second fixture. The streaming throughput table is a
  60-second
  per-level ramp on a
  100-frame, roughly 1-second
  fixture. Both are synthetic-fixture measurements, not universal maxima. The
  throughput table's
  1,024-client level is above the
  example `max_conns_per_host` of 512 and measures queueing; it is a
  fixed level list, not an automatic saturation search. Its token rate is the
  fixture's usage count, not provider-token throughput.
- The 300-second sustained sweep uses the fast-response fixture with no
  intentional stream hold (`-stream-duration 0`). A level with durable drops is
  an overload observation, not a maximum streaming rate. The streaming
  throughput ramp is the only sustained held-stream run; it stops at its fixed
  levels and does not search beyond the largest listed level.
- Performance checks are manual (`scripts/perf.sh docs`), not CI. Each level is
  one run per invocation on one host; there is no repetition or variance study.
- Durable accounting is best-effort. The fast stages happened to remain exact;
  the overload benchmark intentionally does not.
- Container-wide CPU/RSS, cold-start time, browser rendering, arm64 image size,
  disk throughput, and a full dashboard preload over a large authorized history
  were not measured for this page.
- The image archive is a local artifact, not a published registry digest.
- Do not compare these numbers directly across differing hosts, workloads, or
  revisions.

pages.markdown_text:
# Security

## Deployment boundary

millivolt is a trusted-operator tool, not a multi-user security boundary. It
has no authorization roles or tenant isolation. The whole dashboard is gated
by the shared `MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN` environment credential and denied
while it is unset (see [operator access](docs/routes.md#operator-access)):
there is one operator identity, no per-user accounts and no audit trail of
who acted. Only the `GET /healthz` liveness and `GET /readyz` readiness probes,
the `POST /session` login handshake, origin-root brand/PWA assets and transparent
inference stay open at the application gate; the canonical open-path list is
[operator access](docs/routes.md#operator-access). The upstream API key is
forwarded for inference; it does not secure the dashboard or administration.

The supplied listen address binds all interfaces. Prefer an explicit loopback
listen for local use. Before network exposure, restrict access with network
controls and an appropriately authenticated ingress. Protect the entire operator
surface, including dashboard/bootstrap/live records, SQL, Debug, exports,
Settings, Pause, Limits, purge and restart. Inference clients can also change
provider-wide limits through request headers.

For Docker, publish on host loopback, for example `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080`.
A non-root container and a public image do not authenticate callers or make a
publicly reachable operator listener safe. Protect persistent config/data
volumes as sensitive state, including backups and debug captures.

Browser same-origin mutation checks and framing denial are defense in depth
behind the operator credential, not a substitute for it. The live metrics feed
does not opt into cross-origin
browser sharing; the dashboard uses a same-origin EventSource authenticated
by the HttpOnly session cookie. This does not
prevent direct non-browser reads or secure a publicly reachable listener.
Explicit non-browser calls remain supported; gated endpoints need the
`Authorization: Bearer` credential or a session cookie minted through
`POST /session`. The `/mcp` endpoint is the exception: it requires the
operator credential as a Bearer header and refuses a session cookie alone with
`403`, because the caller's credential is forwarded on its internal calls.

## Upstream destinations and credentials

`X-Proxy-Base-URL` selects an HTTP(S) destination. An unrestricted caller can
therefore make the proxy contact destinations reachable from its host.
`allowed_base_urls` constrains accepted upstream targets: an entry admits the
same scheme, host and port (with the scheme's default port filled in) and that
entry's path and its children. A port-less entry therefore admits the default
port only, not every port on that host. Use trusted destinations and
appropriate egress controls. This is not a DNS/IP isolation sandbox.
The proxy does not follow upstream redirects.

Ordinary metrics group credentials by SHA256 rather than retaining the raw key.
Known secret and configured authentication headers are redacted in retained
metadata/captures without changing forwarded headers. This does not sanitize
arbitrary text: request/response bodies, URLs, error messages, model names or
user-supplied labels can contain sensitive data. Preview capture and Debug
capture are opt-in, but enabling them can persist that data.

## Client identity is a claim, not an authentication

`X-Proxy-Client` (and the classified client derived from SDK and user-agent
headers when it is absent) is chosen by the caller. Nothing verifies it: a
request that sends another client's label is treated as that client by every
feature that scopes on client - `request_overrides` (so it inherits that
client's header and token-ceiling rules), `sub_conversations` (so it gets that
client's field mapping and strip list), Debug capture sessions, pause holds
including the "new clients" comparison, and the Cursor parked-run scope. The
recorded client, and therefore dashboard grouping and the `client` filter, also
follow the claim.

The recorded client address is likewise a hint. `client_ip` records the first
`X-Forwarded-For` element when that header is present and the socket peer
otherwise; the value is diagnostic, never verified, and a directly reachable
caller can set it. Do not treat `client_ip` as a verified source for
rate limiting, allowlisting or attribution outside the proxy. The operator
gate's brute-force limiter is a separate key: it reads the address the
immediate hop appended (the last `X-Forwarded-For` element) and falls back to
the socket address, so it distinguishes clients behind a correct ingress but a
directly reachable caller can still pick its own bundle.

The example ingress trusts exactly one loopback hop (`set_real_ip_from
127.0.0.1`, [deploy/nginx.conf](deploy/nginx.conf)) and its `allow` lists
evaluate that rewritten address. A caller that can already reach the loopback
listener therefore chooses the address the lists see: they separate remote
networks from each other and from local callers, not local callers from each
other. Treat a location allowlist as reachability control for a network, not as
identity.

Treat client scoping as a way to separate your own tools and traffic, not as a
security boundary between mutually untrusted parties. A proxy reachable by
someone who should not act as another client needs that separation enforced
outside these labels: distinct `allowed_base_urls`, distinct upstream
credentials per caller, or a separate proxy instance. Credential-class header
names are refused in `request_overrides` and redacted in retained data, so a
claimed label cannot by itself move an upstream secret; the exposure it does
create is the policy attached to the label, not the credential behind it.

Token-refresh handback responses contain credentials in the error body for the client to adopt.
Do not publish them, browser exports, databases, backups, local config,
login-script output or screenshots containing private history.

Provider favicons can make browser requests to Google's favicon service, exposing
the provider hostname and the browser's network address to that service.
`referrerpolicy="no-referrer"` omits the dashboard referrer, not the requested
hostname. Hostname syntax checks do not establish that every qualified provider
label is public. The documentation capture workflow blocks all external browser
requests; that isolation is not the ordinary dashboard's network policy.

## Administrative data and resource limits

SQL is restricted to read-only queries with execution/output limits, not a
sandbox for adversarial resource consumption. Debug has bounded capture sizes
and retention, but captured bodies remain sensitive. Exports and backups can
outlive those retention settings.

Metrics storage is asynchronous and best-effort. Queue overflow/write failures
can lose records; this is not a tamper-proof, complete compliance audit log.
Do not rely on the dashboard as the sole security or billing record. See
[operations and limitations](docs/operations.md#storage-and-accounting).

## Code scanning

GitHub code scanning (CodeQL) reports on pull requests and the default branch.
Alerts are triaged against the [deployment boundary](#deployment-boundary), not
dismissed for convenience. True positives are fixed and covered by regression
tests; accepted false positives record their rationale in the alert instead of
being hidden by a broad path exclusion. The current categories and their
trust-boundary evidence:

- Operator-only read-only SQL (`internal/storage/query_admin.go`). The query
  console sits behind the operator gate, accepts one SELECT, and enforces
  execution time, row, column and result-byte limits. The operator is already
  trusted with the database, so this is not an unauthenticated SQL surface.
- JSON, SSE and gzip response writers. The operator surfaces behind the gate
  encode the proxy's own output, and framing and compression state are bounded
  by the response-size guard. Two writers are intentionally reachable without
  the operator gate: the `/healthz` and `/readyz` probe JSON and the transparent
  inference SSE relay, which streams the upstream response to a client that
  supplied its own provider credentials. Neither exposes operator data (the
  readiness reason names queue depth and flush failures only), so this category
  is not an authentication bypass.
- Bounded allocations (`cmd/proxy/mcp.go`, `internal/sse/frames.go`). The MCP
  recorder cap is the fixed `mcp.MaxResponseBytes` read budget (64 MiB) plus one
  byte, not a configurable limit. The SSE frame's requested size is the
  marshaled payload length plus the fixed framing overhead; `slices.Concat` may
  round the capacity up to the allocator's size class. The payload is bounded by
  the relay's scanner and encoder frame caps and the response-size guard. Input
  is rejected at those bounds before the sized allocation, so neither is an
  attacker-controlled unbounded size.

The operator-cookie and integer-conversion findings were true positives and are
fixed: the operator session cookie now sets `Secure` when the request arrived
over TLS or through an https-forwarding ingress; the jsonnum, config, and
throttle paths now parse or bound at the target width, with regression tests.
The allocation findings are closed by construction, using overflow-safe capacity
owners. The operator SQL console is an accepted boundary, and the transparent
response-writer wrappers are false positives from interface fan-out; their
alerts are dismissed with a recorded reason. Dismissing or resolving a
code-scanning alert is a maintainer action in the GitHub security UI; this note
records triage rationale and does not dismiss any alert automatically.

## Scope

In scope: the proxy, dashboard, MCP server, container image, and repository
automation. Out of scope: findings that require a compromised host, an operator
who already holds the credential, a misconfigured ingress, or a third-party
provider. A report that depends on the documented trusted-operator boundary must
show how that boundary is crossed.

## Safe harbor

The maintainers will not pursue or support legal action for good-faith research
that stays within this scope, avoids privacy violations, service disruption, and
data destruction, and allows reasonable time to fix the issue before disclosure.

## Reporting a vulnerability

Do not publish credentials, private request content, or actionable exploit
details in a public issue.

Use the repository's enabled
[private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/LLM-4-People/millivolt/security/advisories/new)
channel.

Include the affected revision, deployment assumptions, impact, and a minimal
reproduction using neutral local fixtures. Test only systems you own or are
explicitly authorized to assess.

## Supported versions

Security fixes target the latest published release. The `0.x` series is in
active development; older releases are not backported.

| Version | Supported |
| --- | --- |
| Latest published 0.x release | Yes |
| Older releases | No |

## Disclosure process

Reports are acknowledged on a best-effort basis; no response-time SLA is
promised. Maintainers will validate the report, prepare a fix, publish a GitHub
security advisory, and credit the reporter unless they prefer otherwise. Please
allow time for a coordinated fix before public disclosure.

Dependency review and a scheduled Go vulnerability scan run in CI. A clean scan
is not a security guarantee, and neither replaces a private report.

GitHub documents [private vulnerability reporting](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/report-and-fix-vulnerabilities/configure-vulnerability-reporting/configure-for-a-repository).

# Architecture and ownership

millivolt is one Go HTTP service with an embedded, no-build dashboard.
The client-facing protocol and upstream relay/translation are separate
boundaries; the [compatibility matrix](adapters.md#client-and-upstream-compatibility)
defines their supported combinations.
[Contributing](../CONTRIBUTING.md) covers change and verification rules;
[protocol](protocol.md) and the [operations overview](operations.md) describe public behavior.

## Source map

| Owner | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| [cmd/proxy](../cmd/proxy/main.go) | Config/CLI, dependency wiring, routes, process lifecycle. Restart, log, backup and operator-gate handlers have separate existing files. |
| [internal/config](../internal/config/config.go) | Config/defaults/validation, split by subject into `config_types.go`, `config_defaults.go`, `config_clone.go`, `config_load.go`, `config_validate.go` and `config_validate_overrides.go`; schema, YAML generation, revision-checked Settings, model-rule execution, and the credential-class header vocabulary and redactor in `credentials.go`. |
| [internal/settingsdoc](../internal/settingsdoc/settingsdoc.go) | Renders the generated [settings reference](settings.md) from `Schema()`, the defaults passed through the YAML writer and the proxy flag registration; [cmd/docgen](../cmd/docgen/main.go) exposes it as `-write` and `-check`, and the config suite fails when the page drifts. |
| [internal/backup](../internal/backup/archive.go) | Streamed self-checked operator archive format (VACUUM INTO snapshot + zstd + SHA-256), with byte- and file-backed database members. One decoder core serves byte and file callers; restore stages its upload and decoded database as private files instead of heap copies. `params/params.go` owns the backup/restore query keys, boolean spelling, restore modes and archive magic shared by the HTTP handlers and `mvctl`; the leaf imports no encoder, SQLite or zstd. |
| [internal/proxy](../internal/proxy/proxy.go) | Routing, admission integration, retry/relay, request metadata, scoped request overrides, native-run ownership, operator state/capture; inbound/outbound protocol selection and canonical paths in [protocol.go](../internal/proxy/protocol.go); the quota-pause reaction owner [quotapause.go](../internal/proxy/quotapause.go) (settleQuotaFailure/addQuotaHold) and GET/POST /admin/quota. |
| [internal/scheduler](../internal/scheduler/scheduler.go) | Provider/key admission, retry pacing, scoped holds, and limit policies selected by provider, model, client, key hash and conversation with optional recurring schedules; the provider-wide durable quota/billing recovery gate (quota facet, probe-paced recovery). |
| [internal/metrics](../internal/metrics/metrics.go) | Records, numeric/usage/outcome semantics, pending/ring lifecycle, observers and Prometheus. |
| [internal/sse](../internal/sse/analyzer.go) | Streaming content/usage/TTFT inspection for Chat, Responses and Anthropic SSE ([analyzer_anthropic.go](../internal/sse/analyzer_anthropic.go)), split into decode, feed, usage, terminal, error, fill and report modules; client-facing OpenAI SSE frames and completion envelopes. |
| [internal/format](../internal/format) | Explicit wire codecs (Chat, Responses, Anthropic) over the canonical [IR](../internal/format/ir/ir.go), Connect/protobuf framing, and the same-protocol translation facade. |
| [internal/storage](../internal/storage/store_open.go) | Asynchronous SQLite writing, schema/read fidelity, totals, purge fence, packed snapshots and bounded queries. |
| [internal/web](../internal/web/aggregate.go) | Embedded shell/assets, bootstrap, canonical history projection and chart/explorer/log aggregates; `aggregate.go` owns the core row model and each surface has its own `aggregate_*.go` module. |
| [cmd/mvctl](../cmd/mvctl/main.go) | the human operator client: command dispatch, per-command flags, human and JSON rendering, and destructive-action guards. It reuses `internal/mcp` for the operator HTTP client, `internal/config` for setting kinds and bands, and `internal/backup` for archive and query grammar. |
| [internal/mcp](../internal/mcp) | The MCP tool server for the operator plane: one HTTP client owner (credential, request building, error extraction), one scope-filter owner, one tool registry served by the proxy's streamable HTTP `/mcp` endpoint, the destructive-call guards, and the streamable HTTP handler the proxy mounts at `/mcp`. It owns no analytical projection of its own. |

## Logging

[internal/logging](../internal/logging/logging.go) is the one owner of process
log lines. It wraps the standard logger's sink and gives a request-scoped line
the record id minted at the read boundary, so the line joins its stored row,
capture and neighbouring lines. Process and operator-state lines pass no id.
`log.Fatal` exits and the earliest flag errors that precede the process logger
stay direct.

## Release identity and promotion

[version.go](../version.go) owns VERSION validation and SemVer precedence. The
[workflow](../.github/workflows/check.yml) owns the promotion gate and release
publication: `unit`, `browser` and `container` run the full gate on all
`testing` pull requests, code-bearing `testing` pushes, and manually pushed `v*`
tags, plus Dependabot's `main` PRs; docs and site-only pushes use `docs.yml`.
The three gate jobs start independently and `required` aggregates them. `required`
reuses that gate for ordinary promotions by requiring the head to be the current
`testing` tip, `main` to be already merged back into it, a successful full-gate
record for that exact commit or for the closest gated `testing` commit when
every path since it is docs/site-only, and a VERSION newer than every tag for
non-Dependabot code-bearing promotions. A non-Dependabot promotion also requires
a successful [escalation](../.github/workflows/escalation.yml) run (forced
full-race sweep plus the repeated clock-sensitive flake sweep) for the reviewed
head; the proof fails closed while that run is missing, pending, failed, from
another workflow, branch or commit. Pending exact check runs get a short bounded wait and
the proof fails closed if they are still pending; let the `testing` push gate
finish before opening or re-running a promotion PR. Docs/site-only promotions
skip the VERSION and full-gate proofs and validate docs, workflow policy and the
site in `required`. The `required` job has a ten-minute budget for that path.
`publish` tags the reviewed promotion merge, publishes the image and creates the
release without pushing `main`; a manually pushed `v*` tag ships exactly as
tagged. `publish-testing` instead waits for `unit`, `browser` and `container`
directly, because a testing push has no promotion proof to wait for. The
`main-testing-first` ruleset adds the pull-request and merge-commit requirements
with no bypass actors.
[Contributing](../CONTRIBUTING.md#branch-workflow) owns the maintainer
checklist; [operations](containers.md#versions-and-images) owns the published
tag contract.

## Request and scheduling path

`readRequest` retains bounded original bytes and calls the single metadata
decoder. Ordinary content is measured without retaining decoded prompt/schema
trees; opt-in previews stay bounded. Exceptional decoder compatibility belongs
at that owner, not a second routing parser. Before the typed decode,
`parseLLMRequest` bounds decoded JSON-string expansion: valid UTF-8 and JSON
escapes decode to no more bytes than their spelling, so only raw invalid UTF-8
can consume the small allowance (the standard decoder writes a three-byte
U+FFFD per invalid byte). A larger expansion is rejected before materializing;
malformed JSON keeps its passthrough contract, and small invalid sequences still
pass through. `parseLLMRequestFast` is a narrow lexical pre-pass for a minimal
top-level object: `model`, `stream`, `messages` with printable-ASCII role and
content strings, and `system`. It extracts the same routing and composition
fields without the typed decode and delegates every other shape, including all
parameter collections, escapes, duplicates, content part arrays, and preview
capture, to the existing decoder and its bounds. Differential tests pin
byte-for-byte record and rejection equivalence. `SkipJSONString` finds each
candidate quote with one `IndexByte` and reads its escape parity from the
backslash run before it, so escaped content is one forward pass instead of a
restart per escape. The metadata preflight counts message elements, content
parts and tool calls in one walk instead of three. Current scanner and
metadata-shape costs are published under
[implementation benchmarks](performance.md#implementation-benchmarks)
(`BenchmarkSkipJSONString`, `BenchmarkRequestMetadataShapes`).
The streaming analyzer scans each frame once for its classifier keys and
classifies lexically wherever it can. Chat tool-call frames are scanned once
for the element index, id and `function.name`, with the typed decode kept only
as the fallback for a shape the lexical grammar rejects. Current frame and
dedupe costs are published under
[implementation benchmarks](performance.md#implementation-benchmarks)
(`BenchmarkAnalyzerFeed/tool_call`, `BenchmarkAnalyzerToolNameDedupe`). A
differential corpus and a fuzz target compare both paths over every analyzer
field they touch. The Anthropic translator
independently requires valid UTF-8 input,
so it cannot materialize the replacement expansion either. The Start stamp
follows body upload and precedes metadata/translation CPU. Upstream
whole-document buffers share
one process-wide `max_inflight_response_bytes` reservation: translated
non-streaming responses, the non-streaming 200 quality spool, and
model-discovery pages. Admission reserves the declared Content-Length when it
fits the bounded read cap, otherwise that cap, and refuses with a retryable
`503` and `Retry-After` before reading the upstream body.

`resolveRequestOverrides` in
[request_overrides.go](../internal/proxy/request_overrides.go) merges the matching
`request_overrides` rules once per request, after routing metadata is known,
and its merge has exactly two application stages: the final header stage of
`buildUpstreamRequest`, and the cursor identity headers at the native send. Its
body stamp is fail closed (an undecodable or oversize result relays the
original bytes with one log line, prefixed by the request id minted at the read
boundary so the line joins the stored row), and a nil resolution - the feature
off or nothing matched - leaves the request path byte-identical. The sub-conversation
strip is the single body-rewrite engine's second consumer: it fires
independently of override resolution, after the tracked value is extracted
from the buffered body and before translation, with
[conversation.go](../internal/proxy/conversation.go) owning the extraction and
the `k:` identity. A provider's ensured tool names are the same engine's
third consumer: they are restricted to the OpenAI wire, because the injected
stub tools are chat/completions-shaped and must never reach a
translated-anthropic or cursor body, and they fire with any override and
strip actions through one document decode.

Immutable config/client snapshots hot-swap for new work; old transports finish
active requests. Admission is provider+key scoped, with persistent limit
policies layered at the same grant owner. A policy intersects its non-empty
selector dimensions and an empty dimension matches any value, so a provider-only
rule is the provider-wide cap while a narrower rule reuses the same machinery.
Every matching policy charges its own lease, and a scheduled policy outside its
window neither charges nor queues. Acquisition
release settles exactly once. The provider gate and token-bucket epoch captured
at admission keep clearing/replacing a cap from charging another generation's
reservation. A provider-to-groups index in `Scheduler` keeps each group's slot
in a fair-waiting set: a group joins when its queued head was refused by the
shared provider gate (concurrency or the request/token bucket), not when it is
parked on its own pacing window, hold, anti-burst ramp or per-key cap. A release
settles the gate, then drains that set once in rotating one-grant-per-group
passes, starting after the last group served, so one key cannot take the whole
provider allowance while peers wait; the drain stops as soon as a grant refills
a saturated provider concurrency cap. The lock-free fair count is the fast path's precise
witness: an unrelated key admits immediately while peers wait on their own
predicates, and a group that stops on one of those predicates leaves the set. An
anti-burst epoch starts a group at allowance 1 and raises it by
`floor((concurrency-1) * elapsed / ramp_duration)`, clamped to the target; a
fully idle period of at least the ramp duration resets the epoch on the next
grant, a shorter gap continues it, and changing the flag, duration or target
resets every epoch.

[tokenrefresh.go](../internal/proxy/tokenrefresh.go) separates provider exchanges
from response policy. Exchange adapters return credential data only; the shared
`resolveKey` ends successful inference refreshes with handback before admission,
live publication or recording. `resolveKeyTransparent` owns the model-discovery
exception. The token-refresh tests cover both mechanisms, adoption/retry, absent
replacement tokens, applicability/failure gates and bounded exchange responses.

Retries, provider hints, hold waits and per-send deadlines have distinct owners.
Capture context error before canceling it for cleanup. Never retry a canceled
caller or replay meaningful emitted stream content. Quality failure handling is
explicitly exceptional; see [adapters](adapters.md) and the relay tests.

Queue visibility has one owner across both park points: the bounded admission
FIFO and `WaitSend`'s send gate. Every parked request publishes the live queued
edge (`Throttled`) for the whole wait and clears it on the grant. `Stats`
reports send-gate waiters separately (`SendWaiters`) and the operator snapshots
add them to the global and per-provider queue totals, so a 429 pacing window
reads as queued work rather than idle streams; a retrying owner waiting out its
own Retry-After hint is queued for the same reason. Send-gate waits stay
separate from the admission queue bound so `max_queue_size` keeps its own
meaning.

[scheduler/storm.go](../internal/scheduler/storm.go) owns bounded rolling
attempt counters, active-model evidence, cross-key provider/model gates and
exclusive recovery permits. Provider activation requires all models with
activity inside the same window to independently qualify. Old permits cannot
recover newer incidents. Initial admission waits for readiness without reserving
a probe; only the actual send boundary claims a probe after key admission.
Storm policy changes reset observations and wake waiters without mutating
retained history. Each
request carries an observation for its provider and model, moving distinct
failed-request membership between fixed buckets across retries without retaining
a request-ID map. No storm observation scans metrics history or waits for SQLite.

[proxy/storm.go](../internal/proxy/storm.go) maps config once into scheduler
options and bridges existing relay/native send outcomes. A 2xx permit settles
after relay or before an existing quality re-ask or thinking rescue re-send,
preventing double samples and stream replay. Safe protocol-level reason labels
carry no provider error bodies.
The banner uses the canonical bootstrap builder and browser apply/render gates,
with no client-side event arithmetic. Storm scheduler/proxy/config regressions
and the shared UI/browser suite cover these boundaries.

Important coverage includes request metadata/parser fuzz tests,
`BenchmarkRequestMetadata`, `BenchmarkProxyRequest`,
`TestConcurrentStreamingAccounting`, transport lifecycle tests and scheduler
efficiency/race tests. Proxy requests must not perform history scans or wait for
SQLite accounting.

## Finalized records, pending lifecycle and replay

`PublishLive(begin/update)` snapshots pending state without adding durable rows.
The proxy registers its deferred `Record` before publishing `begin`, so a
subscriber that fails while handling the begin event cannot leave a permanent
in-flight row. `Buffer.Record` atomically finalizes the row, retires pending
state, updates its gauge/revision and emits end. Exactly one finalized record per request is the
accounting unit; proxy-owned IDs cannot collide with reused client request IDs.
A debug capture registers its pending sidecar marker in `debugRuntime` before
that publish and encodes/saves after it, so the sidecar write delays neither
the live end nor durable accounting. A drawer fetch for the id waits on the
marker, then reads the authoritative store; a resolved marker without a row
keeps the normal 404.

`Buffer.Record`, `PublishLive` and `Backfill` share the one record-retention
pass ([internal/metrics/retain.go](../internal/metrics/retain.go)) at that
boundary. It bounds client-controlled paths/methods and provider-controlled
model/request/finish/error text, tool names and attempt metadata; normal values
stay byte-identical. The bounds and the UTF-8 cut marker are documented in the
[protocol](protocol.md).

Existing lock order keeps sequence assignment and finalized publication ordered.
A feed epoch changes on restart/deletion; queued fanout retains its mutation
epoch. Subscribers attach before snapshot capture and overflow retires that
subscriber so reconnect can replay, rather than silently dropping permanent rows.
When more than one dashboard subscriber is attached, `Record` and `PublishLive`
attach one lazy observed-JSON cache to that published event
([internal/metrics/event_cache.go](../internal/metrics/event_cache.go)). The
first consuming stream encodes the observer result and every subscriber of that
same event reuses the retained bytes; an encode error is retained too, so all of
them close and resync. Zero or one subscriber keeps the direct `json.Marshal`
path with no cache allocation, and no cache outlives its event or crosses a
feed epoch.

`SnapshotRequest` is the shared atomic cursor/feed gate for bootstrap and SSE.
A foreign/stale cursor requires a full snapshot; deltas are never truncated.
Snapshots include current pending rows and their revision. Full durable-mode
snapshots cap the recent window, with archives fetched separately.

The browser's one upsert owner deduplicates finalized replays. Pending upserts
cannot overwrite finalized rows or a newer pending revision of the same ID.
The authoritative gauge revision is independent: an older event may still add
a missing different row without rolling back the gauge. Full bootstrap closes
the stream before capture; only the winning refresh reopens it. Stale same-feed
full SSE snapshots recapture through that barrier by sequence/pending revision.

Tests live under [tests/](../tests/README.md), with Go package mirrors in
`tests/_go/`. Use the overlay-aware `scripts/check.sh go test` entry point.
See buffer snapshot/stream tests and the harness sections under
`tests/ui_harness/sections/` for the lifecycle and bootstrap races.
Do not collapse these row, gauge, epoch and request-ownership gates into a
