Then wait for required . The proof polls pending exact runs a

sections.heading: Development dependencies
sections.text: Linux is supported. Version sources are: Go: go.mod . Node: .node-version . Python: .python-version . jq : the workflow contract suite executes the promotion gate's shell predicates, so the core checks need the jq binary on PATH . Browser tooling: requirements-dev.txt . Documentation site: requirements-docs.txt . The proxy embeds its vanilla JavaScript/CSS and needs no frontend build or Node runtime in deployment. Node/jsdom, Python/Playwright, Python-Markdown and PyYAML are development and documentation tools. npm ci --ignore-scripts python3 -m venv .venv . .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --require-hashes -r requirements-dev.txt python -m playwright install chromium On fresh Linux installations, Chromium may also need system libraries; use python -m playwright install --with-deps chromium with appropriate installation permissions. Go race checks require CGO_ENABLED=1 and a working C compiler; the regular proxy build does not require a native SQLite driver.

sections.heading: Checks
sections.text: scripts/check.sh The shared script owns the core verification commands, including offline documentation-link, publication-ignore and typography regressions (Git is required), the generated-site contract, and the workflow/automation policy. That policy suite runs the workflow files of the ref under test, and a pull_request run evaluates its own head revision rather than the base branch's: a workflow change is judged as this pull request ships it, which is what lets a workflow edit pass before merge. Review the workflow diff itself, since the run that validates it was configured by the same commit; only the post-merge main state proves what landed. npm test runs the jsdom suites and the request-log merge regression probe separately. All tests and disposable harnesses live in tests/ , with suffix-free physical filenames. Go's temporary overlay adds its required virtual _test.go names; Python unit modules live in tests/python/ . Use scripts/check.sh go test for targeted Go checks and scripts/check.sh go vet or scripts/check.sh go mod tidy to include test code and dependencies. Raw go test ./... does not discover the relocated tests and can report success without running them. Re-run ch

sections.heading: Documentation site
sections.text: The public site is generated from the existing Markdown, not maintained as a second documentation tree. site-src/ owns the layout, styles, and brand assets; scripts/build_site.py renders the pages, rewrites repository links, and emits the search index, sitemap, and 404 page. The generated site/ directory is ignored and never committed. python3 -m pip install --require-hashes -r requirements-docs.txt python3 -B -O -m tests.python.site python3 scripts/build_site.py --output site Both requirements files are hash-pinned and every install command passes --require-hashes , so resolution is reproducible and a substituted file fails the install. After changing a pin, regenerate the hash block for that version from the PyPI JSON document ( https://pypi.org/pypi/<project>/<version>/json , digests.sha256 of every non-yanked file, one --hash=sha256: line each), keep the pins sorted as they are, and run the install above once to prove the file. For a local preview, serve site/ from a separate terminal with python3 -m http.server --directory site 8082 ; do not point it at the proxy or use the main :8080 instance. The docs.yml workflow builds the site for documentation changes, and pages.yml depl

sections.heading: Push gate
sections.text: Never push main directly: open a promotion pull request and merge it with a merge commit. Do not push testing until the exact commit you will push has passed the same CI gate jobs. A request to push is not a waiver. Package-scoped go test and npm test during development are not sufficient. CI's source-and-unit step is the default core suite: scripts/check.sh A run may not start while a code-scanning finding is unresolved. scripts/security_gate.py reads code-scanning/alerts?state=open from the repository API in the unit job and again in publish before the version tag is created. Fix the finding, or record a dismissal with a reason that explains why the code is correct; a dismissed alert is not open, and the security page keeps that reason beside the location. An API the gate cannot read fails closed rather than passing. CI sets GOTOOLCHAIN=local , so the host Go must match the go version in go.mod . On a host with an older base Go, install Go 1.27.2 or select the matching toolchain before running the gate; GOTOOLCHAIN=local alone cannot upgrade an older installation. Full-gate CI events also run the isolated browser fixtures (desktop and mobile) in the browser job. Use scripts/dev.s

sections.heading: Isolated development
sections.text: Never use an existing main instance on port 8080 for tests. Use the lifecycle script, with cleanup even if verification fails: ( set -e trap 'scripts/dev.sh stop' EXIT export MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN='dev-instance-credential' scripts/dev.sh scripts/check.sh browser --target http://127.0.0.1:8081 ) The dev instance shares your shell environment, so a local MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN arms its operator gate; browser and stress harnesses need the same value for gated fixture cleanup. An instance started without it serves reads only and denies every mutation. scripts/dev.sh status reports the private instance. The script builds first, then replaces only its tracked dev process; a failed build leaves it running. The tracked identity is the pid file, and status / stop fall back to the listener on the instance's port when the file names a dead pid: a rebuild child rewrites the file only once it is fully booted, so a child that dies before readiness would otherwise strand the instance. The fallback still requires the process to carry this instance's exact -pid-file flag. Starting/restarting development resets its disposable database and private config, seeded from the public example by defaul

sections.heading: Live Chrome DevTools verification
sections.text: Frontend changes are additionally verified in a visible Chrome window through Chrome DevTools - headful, never headless. Sign in with the dev operator token, drive the real fixture traffic and the actual controls, and check console output, element geometry, the accessibility tree and screen flow in the rendered page. Narrow fixture data passes the harnesses but can hide distribution problems (wide values, wrapping, density); the live session is where those surface. Keep the dev instance and the window open while you look; stop the instance with scripts/dev.sh stop when done. Fixture traffic for these sessions has its own lifecycle owner, never a paid provider and never the main instance on :8080 : scripts/dev-traffic.sh # bursts of neutral loopback traffic at the dev instance scripts/dev-traffic.sh status scripts/dev-traffic.sh stop Bursts land about a minute apart so one-minute chart buckets gain a bucket per burst; each run includes recovered 429s (rate-limited, not errors) and one final 400 so both health surfaces carry data.

sections.heading: Container development
sections.text: Normal compose.yaml only runs a published image. For a local source build, use compose.dev.yaml from the checkout root. It is a complete Compose file, not an overlay: project and service are both millivolt-dev , and the container takes the project-scoped name Compose derives from them. docker compose -f compose.dev.yaml up -d --build docker compose -f compose.dev.yaml logs --tail 50 docker compose -f compose.dev.yaml down The development project keeps its containers and named volumes separate from a normal deployment, including when COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME is set outside the checkout. Its MILLIVOLT_DEV_PORT and MILLIVOLT_DEV_IMAGE inputs are defined only there, and it shares the deployment Compose's MILLIVOLT_MEM_LIMIT and MILLIVOLT_PIDS_LIMIT bounds. Choose an unused development port if scripts/dev.sh is already running. Rerun the same up --build command after source changes. The resulting runtime image has no compiler or source tree, so dashboard rebuild is unavailable. down preserves its named volumes unless you explicitly request deletion. This source-image workflow does not replace scripts/dev.sh : the host browser and stress fixtures require that script's private process/databas

sections.heading: Documentation screenshots
sections.text: The published gallery uses recorded metrics from an explicitly authorized, redacted local-history snapshot, not fabricated timing or cost values. Never point capture tools at a main instance or serve a raw history copy for screenshots. The source is the checkout's local proxy.db , opened read-only through the existing online-backup helper. This workflow needs explicit authorization for that history. From a checkout with browser dependencies installed and that authorized source: ( set -e export DEV_PORT=18081 DEV_HOST=127.0.0.1 export DEV_DB=/tmp/millivolt/millivolt-dev-docs.db export DEV_CONFIG=proxy.example.yaml DEV_COPY_DB=redacted trap 'scripts/dev.sh stop' EXIT scripts/dev.sh up python3 -B -O -m tests.explorer_check \ --target "http://${DEV_HOST}:${DEV_PORT}" --docs-history docs/images ) Choose an unused permitted dev port. Before startup, dev.sh derives a new metrics-only database: identifiers are replaced, content/headers/debug data are removed, and recorded timing, token and cost values are retained. The raw online snapshot is temporary and never served. Treat even the derived database as sensitive; retained usage and timestamps can reveal activity patterns. Capture last. Th

sections.heading: Performance evidence
sections.text: The published tables, method and limitations live in performance and resource usage . That page is the single source for measured numbers; do not copy them into other documentation and do not edit the page by hand. It is rendered from perf/results.json , and tests/python/site.py fails when the two disagree. scripts/perf.sh owns a repeatable local measurement run without touching the main instance. It starts fresh private instances on a disposable port and stops them through scripts/dev.sh : scripts/perf.sh docs # every published measurement, bundle and page scripts/perf.sh bench # isolated Go benchmarks scripts/perf.sh stress # private fast and streaming ramps scripts/perf.sh streaming # sustained end-to-end SSE throughput ramp scripts/perf.sh sustained # fixed-duration fast-response capacity levels scripts/perf.sh image # disposable image content and compressed size scripts/perf.sh all # image, bench, then stress docs refuses a dirty tree, runs the complete documented set, writes perf/results.json , and regenerates docs/performance.md . Commit the bundle and the page together. Never hand-edit either one; a missing stage, failed response or unbalanced durable result aborts the run

sections.heading: Versioning and publication
sections.text: VERSION is the only semantic version source; do not duplicate it in package manifests, build arguments or image metadata. Normal and prerelease SemVer are supported without build metadata. A release tag must be exactly v followed by that file's version. The release CLI validates the same contract: millivolt_version="$(tr -d '\r\n' < VERSION)" go run ./cmd/release -revision "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" -tag "v$millivolt_version" Publication is automatic. A code-bearing versioned promotion releases when the promotion PR merges, after the full gate has passed for the promoted commit, or after the closest gated testing commit plus a docs-only delta. A non-Dependabot promotion also requires a successful escalation run for the reviewed head; the promotion PR starts it automatically, and required waits for it under a bounded, fail-closed proof. The merged-PR event carries the exact merge commit; a delivered main push is an idempotent fallback, so a dropped push event cannot leave the release untagged. A Dependabot security PR targets main and runs the full gate itself rather than reusing a testing result. The release publish job waits for required . The publish-testing job waits for unit , bro

sections.heading: If a release fails
sections.text: Before the tag is pushed, no public release exists. Fix the failure and rerun the main workflow or promote a new version. After the tag is pushed, keep the tag in place. If the GitHub release is missing, create it from that tag or publish a new patch version. An automatic tag push does not start a second workflow run. Do not move or delete a published version tag. For local container verification, build with Docker, resolve the image's immutable ID, then use the same fixture as CI: docker build -t millivolt:check . millivolt_image_id="$(docker image inspect --format '{{.Id}}' millivolt:check)" scripts/check.sh container --image "$millivolt_image_id" The shared container mode validates Compose defaults and owns only its disposable, network-isolated Docker fixture, selected by immutable image ID. It checks startup, HTTP, Settings and durable state across stop/start, then backs up the stopped volumes and restores into another fresh container. Recovery must retain settings, history and private file ownership/modes. It never publishes a host port or reuses an operator volume. It complements, rather than replaces, the host lifecycle in scripts/dev.sh .

sections.heading: Change checklist
sections.text: Use sentence case or lowercase in prose, headings and labels. Avoid em dashes; preserve exact protocol names, identifiers, user data and license wording. Add a targeted regression for a reproduced defect; preserve existing coverage. Keep defaults, units, schemas and state transitions at their canonical owner. Measure allocations/latency when changing the hot path or analytical folds. Check saved views, mobile layout and accessibility for visible changes. Update the relevant existing documentation, not duplicate specifications. Exclude local configs, databases, tokens, captures and generated test artifacts. Preserve dependency licenses. Report vulnerabilities using SECURITY.md , not a public issue containing sensitive reproduction data. Dependabot checks Go, npm, Python, Docker and GitHub Actions dependencies weekly with grouped minor and patch updates. Review dependency changes and re-run checks; runtime version files still require deliberate updates and verification. The Docker golang base is deliberately left manual because its tag must move with go.mod; distroless updates remain automated. Security updates target main as described in the branch workflow. Dependency review runs o

pages.markdown_text:
# Contributing

Start with the [architecture map](docs/architecture.md). Keep changes focused on
existing shared owners, include regressions, and use neutral fixtures rather
than real providers. Setup, safety and verification rules live in this guide.

Use the [issue tracker](https://github.com/LLM-4-People/millivolt/issues) for
non-sensitive bugs and proposals, and
[pull requests](https://github.com/LLM-4-People/millivolt/pulls) for changes.
Security reports belong in the private channel in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

## Support and first change

[SUPPORT.md](SUPPORT.md) routes usage questions, reproducible defects, concrete
proposals, and security reports. For a first change, fork the repository, branch
from `origin/testing`, update the existing shared owner, and add a targeted
regression. Run `scripts/check.sh` and report what ran. Open the pull request
against `testing`, not `main`.

Use the `good first issue` label only for documentation, tests, or tooling with
a clear scope and expected result. Do not label credential handling,
authentication, storage, protocol-core, or release work. Ask in the issue before
starting.

## Branch workflow

New features branch from and land on `testing` first, with their documentation
and relevant checks in the same change. Fetch the current remote branch before
starting follow-up work. Use feature branches targeting `testing` for review,
or push a completed, checked feature directly there when that is authorized.

`main` is promotion-only. Do not develop on it, push it directly, or bypass its
rules. The `main-testing-first` ruleset requires a pull request and the
`required` check, allows merge commits only, and has no bypass actors. The
`long-lived-branch-integrity` ruleset also blocks deletion and non-fast-forward
updates. Administrators have no bypass either. When release automation needs new
behavior, change the workflow in a pull request; never add a bypass actor or use
an administrator override. Inspect the active ruleset with:

```sh
ruleset_id="$(gh api repos/LLM-4-People/millivolt/rulesets \
  --jq '.[] | select(.name == "main-testing-first") | .id')"
gh api "repos/LLM-4-People/millivolt/rulesets/$ruleset_id" \
  --jq '{name,enforcement,bypass_actors,current_user_can_bypass}'
```

It must report `enforcement: active`, an empty `bypass_actors`, and
`current_user_can_bypass: never`.

### Commit as you go

Commit each completed fix locally as soon as its targeted check passes. This
includes every individual finding from a review, audit, or multi-agent round:
do not hold those edits in the working tree until the end, and do not squash
several findings into one final commit. If a fix depends on an earlier
uncommitted change, commit that coherent change first, then commit the
dependent fix. Keep unrelated user changes out of the commit. A push still
waits for the full push gate on the exact commit being pushed.

A commit subject also feeds the generated release notes: every subject whose
type is not one of `build`, `brand`, `checks`, `chore`, `ci`, `deps`, `doc`,
`docs`, `merge`, `refactor`, `release`, `style`, `test`, `tests`, `tooling` or
`version` becomes a Highlight on the release that first contains it, and
internal types are folded under "Other changes". Write the subject for an
operator reading the release page.

Completed feature pushes to `testing` publish only the moving development image.
All pull requests to `testing`, all code-bearing pushes to `testing`, manually
dispatched `testing` gates, and manually pushed `v*` tags run the full gate;
docs and site-only pushes to `testing` run the smaller documentation gate in
`docs.yml`. An ordinary promotion
pull request to `main` runs only `check.yml`'s lightweight `required` promotion
gate: it verifies the head is the current `testing` tip, `main` is already
merged back into `testing`, and the full gate already succeeded for that
commit: the canonical `check.yml` push run's own check suite, with `unit`,
`browser` and both native container legs. A final docs-only commit after the
closest gated `testing` commit reuses that gate when every path since it is
docs/site-only. Every non-Dependabot promotion also starts
[`escalation.yml`](.github/workflows/escalation.yml) on its head and must
carry a successful `race` job for that exact commit; the proof waits under a
bounded budget and fails closed. The fallback selects the closest gated testing
commit from canonical `testing` push runs, with no commit-count bound. For a
code-bearing head, let the `testing` `check.yml` push gate finish before opening
or re-running a promotion PR; pending exact check runs get a short bounded wait
and the proof fails closed while they remain pending. A docs/site-only head has
no canonical `check.yml` push run of its own, so wait for `docs.yml` or only the
`required` docs validation. A Dependabot security pull request targets `main`
directly and therefore still runs the full gate.

### Promote testing to main

1. Fetch and align the branches. `testing` must contain the feature work and
   `main` must be an ancestor:
   ```sh
   git fetch origin
   git switch testing
   git merge --ff-only origin/testing
   ```
   If `main` is not an ancestor of `testing`, merge `origin/main` into
   `testing` first and resolve conflicts before continuing.
2. For a code-bearing promotion, bump `VERSION` on `testing` to a version
   newer than every existing `v*` tag. Normal SemVer precedence applies; a
   prerelease is lower than the same stable version. Commit the bump
   separately:
   ```sh
   printf '<next-version>\n' > VERSION
   git add VERSION
   git commit -m "bump version to <next-version>"
   git push origin testing
   ```
   A docs/site-only promotion may skip this step. `required` detects that every
   changed path is covered by the docs/site filter (for example Markdown,
   `docs/`, `site-src/`, the docs and Pages workflows, and `LICENSE`), and the
   merged main push stays docs-only.
3. Open a pull request from `testing` to `main`. For a code-bearing head, wait
   for the `testing` `check.yml` push gate to finish first; a docs/site-only
   head has no canonical `check.yml` push run of its own, so wait for `docs.yml`
   or only the `required` docs validation. Then wait for `required`. The proof
   polls pending exact runs a bounded number of times and fails closed while
   they remain pending, so opening or re-running the PR early only produces a
   red check. `required` does not rerun the full `testing` gate. For
   every non-Dependabot
   promotion it verifies that the head is the current `testing` tip and that
   `main` is already merged back into `testing`; code-bearing promotions must
   also have a successful full-gate record for that exact commit, or for the
   closest gated `testing` commit when every path since it is docs/site-only,
   and `VERSION` newer than every release tag. A non-Dependabot promotion also
   needs the escalation workflow's `race` job to succeed for this head; it
   starts with the PR, and `required` waits for it under a bounded budget.
   If it fails with "Promote the current testing tip", push the final commit to
   `testing` and reopen or update the PR. If it fails with "Merge main back
   into testing", merge `origin/main` into `testing` first. If it fails with
   "changes non-docs paths after the gated commit", push the final code commit
   and let its full gate finish. If it fails with "VERSION must be newer", bump
   `VERSION` above every tag and push the commit. If GitHub does not create the
   `testing` push run, dispatch the full gate on the current tip and wait for it
   to succeed; the proof accepts that run as an equivalent testing gate:
   ```sh
   gh workflow run check.yml --ref testing
   ```
4. Merge with a merge commit:
   ```sh
   gh pr merge <number> --merge
   ```
   Squash and rebase are disabled on `main`; they would replace the reviewed
   testing history instead of preserving it.
5. The merged-PR release run starts as soon as the promotion merge lands; wait
   for its publish job (and the Pages run, when applicable) to finish, then
   merge `main` back into `testing` so the next promotion is up to date:
   ```sh
   git fetch origin main
   git switch testing
   git merge --ff-only origin/main
   git push origin testing
   ```
   If `testing` moved after the promotion merge, merge `origin/main` normally
   and resolve conflicts before the next promotion.

For a code-bearing promotion, the merged-PR release run creates the annotated
release tag on the reviewed merge commit and publishes the image. It never
pushes `main`. A delivered `main` push is an idempotent fallback; a manually
pushed `v*` tag remains the explicit recovery path. Do not push a `v*` tag as
part of feature work; the manual tag path is only for an explicitly verified
release and must match `VERSION`.

Dependabot version updates target `testing`. Dependabot security updates target
the default branch and are the only exception to the testing-ancestry check;
they also skip the version check. They still run the full gate and the
`required` check. A security-only merge normally publishes no image and creates
no tag because `VERSION` is already tagged; if `VERSION` is still untagged, that
merge can publish the pending version. Merge `main` back into `testing` and
include the fix in the next versioned promotion.

Docs and site-only pushes to `testing` skip image work. A docs/site-only
promotion to `main` skips the `VERSION` and full-gate proofs, validates the
Markdown, generated site, workflow policy and docs contracts in `required`, and
the merged-PR release path records the change as docs-only, so it does not
rebuild images or cut a release. A Pages-relevant change deploys the site from
the `main` push, or from the Pages `workflow_dispatch` fallback when that push
workflow is not delivered.

`AGENTS.md` is intentionally local and ignored by the publication guard. Keep its
working instructions aligned with this shared guide; do not force-add private
instruction files to publish workflow policy.

## Development dependencies

Linux is supported. Version sources are:

- Go: [go.mod](go.mod).
- Node: [.node-version](.node-version).
- Python: [.python-version](.python-version).
- `jq`: the workflow contract suite executes the promotion gate's shell
  predicates, so the core checks need the `jq` binary on `PATH`.
- Browser tooling: [requirements-dev.txt](requirements-dev.txt).
- Documentation site: [requirements-docs.txt](requirements-docs.txt).

The proxy embeds its vanilla JavaScript/CSS and needs no frontend build or Node
runtime in deployment. Node/jsdom, Python/Playwright, Python-Markdown and PyYAML
are development and documentation tools.

```sh
npm ci --ignore-scripts
python3 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --require-hashes -r requirements-dev.txt
python -m playwright install chromium
```

On fresh Linux installations, Chromium may also need system libraries; use
`python -m playwright install --with-deps chromium` with appropriate installation
permissions. Go race checks require `CGO_ENABLED=1` and a working C compiler;
the regular proxy build does not require a native SQLite driver.

## Checks

```sh
scripts/check.sh
```

The shared script owns the core verification commands, including offline
documentation-link, publication-ignore and typography regressions (Git is required),
the generated-site contract, and the workflow/automation policy. That policy
suite runs the workflow files of the ref under test, and a `pull_request` run
evaluates its own head revision rather than the base branch's: a workflow change
is judged as this pull request ships it, which is what lets a workflow edit pass
before merge. Review the workflow diff itself, since the run that validates it
was configured by the same commit; only the post-merge `main` state proves what
landed. `npm test` runs
the jsdom suites and the request-log merge regression probe separately. All tests and disposable harnesses
live in [tests/](tests/README.md), with suffix-free physical filenames. Go's
temporary overlay adds its required virtual `_test.go` names; Python unit
modules live in `tests/python/`. Use `scripts/check.sh go test` for targeted Go
checks and `scripts/check.sh go vet` or `scripts/check.sh go mod tidy` to include
test code and dependencies. Raw `go test ./...` does not discover the relocated
tests and can report success without running them. Re-run checks after your
last edit. Concurrency changes need race coverage. JavaScript unit checks do
not establish real canvas rendering, layout, focus or viewport behavior.

### Documentation site

The public site is generated from the existing Markdown, not maintained as a
second documentation tree. `site-src/` owns the layout, styles, and brand
assets; `scripts/build_site.py` renders the pages, rewrites repository links,
and emits the search index, sitemap, and 404 page. The generated `site/`
directory is ignored and never committed.

```sh
python3 -m pip install --require-hashes -r requirements-docs.txt
python3 -B -O -m tests.python.site
python3 scripts/build_site.py --output site
```

Both requirements files are hash-pinned and every install command passes
`--require-hashes`, so resolution is reproducible and a substituted file fails
the install. After changing a pin, regenerate the hash block for that version
from the PyPI JSON document (`https://pypi.org/pypi/<project>/<version>/json`,
`digests.sha256` of every non-yanked file, one `--hash=sha256:` line each), keep
the pins sorted as they are, and run the install above once to prove the file.

For a local preview, serve `site/` from a separate terminal with
`python3 -m http.server --directory site 8082`; do not point it at the proxy or
use the main `:8080` instance. The `docs.yml` workflow builds the site for
documentation changes, and `pages.yml` deploys from `main` through the official
GitHub Pages Actions flow. Repository-level Pages enablement and the
`github-pages` environment are one-time administrator settings.

The three files every page loads before content renders (`tokens.css`,
`site.css`, `site.js`) are published at content-hashed names such as
`site.11c6502e41.css`. GitHub Pages sets its own `Cache-Control`, so the URL is
the only cache key this repository controls: a page cached from the previous
deployment names the previous hash, and it must find those bytes. The build
therefore republishes the last `SHELL_RETENTION` generations of each file,
regenerated from the revisions that produced them, which is why the Pages
workflow checks out full history. A checkout without history still builds the
current page correctly but cannot retain earlier generations. Do not add a
hand-written reference to the unhashed names; `tests/python/site.py` rejects
one.

The site is published at `https://millivolt.llm4people.dev/`. That origin has two
owners, and neither is a file in this repository: the Pages custom domain in the
repository settings, which is what GitHub serves and certifies, and the DNS
record, which is a `CNAME` from `millivolt` to `llm-4-people.github.io` with the
proxy disabled. `scripts/build_site.py` warns when a build for `SITE_URL` names
a different host than `DEFAULT_BASE_URL`, because that is what a half-finished
migration looks like. GitHub ignores a `CNAME` file in an Actions deployment, so
this repository does not ship one.

### Push gate

Never push `main` directly: open a promotion pull request and merge it with a
merge commit. Do not push `testing` until the exact commit you will push has
passed the same CI gate jobs. A request to push is not a waiver.
Package-scoped `go test` and `npm test` during development are not sufficient.
CI's source-and-unit step is the default core suite:

```sh
scripts/check.sh
```

A run may not start while a code-scanning finding is unresolved.
`scripts/security_gate.py` reads `code-scanning/alerts?state=open` from the
repository API in the `unit` job and again in `publish` before the version tag
is created. Fix the finding, or record a dismissal with a reason that explains
why the code is correct; a dismissed alert is not open, and the security page
keeps that reason beside the location. An API the gate cannot read fails
closed rather than passing.

CI sets `GOTOOLCHAIN=local`, so the host Go must match the `go` version in
`go.mod`. On a host with an older base Go, install Go 1.27.2 or select the
matching toolchain before running the gate; `GOTOOLCHAIN=local` alone cannot
upgrade an older installation.

Full-gate CI events also run the isolated browser fixtures (desktop and mobile)
in the `browser` job. Use `scripts/dev.sh` plus `scripts/check.sh browser` as
below, with `MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN` set. Re-run both after the last commit. A
red GitHub check after a push means the gate was skipped, stale, or unmonitored:
fix, re-run, and push only a passing tree, then watch the new run to completion.

That same `browser` job also runs the live MCP integration test, which
`scripts/check.sh browser` alone does not run. It is mandatory on the same
commit:

```sh
MILLIVOLT_MCP_INTEGRATION=1 scripts/check.sh go test -count=1 ./internal/mcp/...
```

The test starts a private dev instance through `scripts/dev.sh` on its own
loopback port and scratch database, drives every registered tool, and stops the
instance again, so it does not touch the instance the browser check uses.

Before every push, check open pull requests and report any that are awaiting
the user's review or approval. Do not approve or merge them without explicit
authorization. Use:

```sh
gh pr list --state open --json number,title,author,isDraft,reviewDecision,mergeable,statusCheckRollup,url
```

After pushing, monitor the GitHub Actions run for the pushed commit until every
required job completes successfully. The local gate cannot see the browser,
MCP integration, container, code-scanning, or dependency-review jobs. Find the run with
`gh run list --branch <branch> --limit 1`, then wait for it with
`gh run watch <run-id> --exit-status`. A queued or in-progress run is not green.
If any job fails, treat the push as incomplete: fix the root cause, rerun this
gate, and push the fix. Do not leave `testing` or `main` red or start unrelated
work on top of a failing run.

For changes to configuration, update the Config/default/validation/schema owners
and regenerate the example as described in [configuration](docs/configuration.md).
Do not edit `proxy.yaml`: it may be a running operator's configuration.

## Isolated development

Never use an existing main instance on port 8080 for tests. Use the lifecycle
script, with cleanup even if verification fails:

```sh
(
  set -e
  trap 'scripts/dev.sh stop' EXIT
  export MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN='dev-instance-credential'
  scripts/dev.sh
  scripts/check.sh browser --target http://127.0.0.1:8081
)
```

The dev instance shares your shell environment, so a local
`MILLIVOLT_OPERATOR_TOKEN` arms its operator gate; browser and stress harnesses
need the same value for gated fixture cleanup. An instance started without it
serves reads only and denies every mutation.

`scripts/dev.sh status` reports the private instance. The script builds first,
then replaces only its tracked dev process; a failed build leaves it running.
The tracked identity is the pid file, and `status`/`stop` fall back to the
listener on the instance's port when the file names a dead pid: a rebuild child
rewrites the file only once it is fully booted, so a child that dies before
readiness would otherwise strand the instance. The fallback still requires the
process to carry this instance's exact `-pid-file` flag.
Starting/restarting development resets its disposable database and private config,
seeded from the public example by default. `DEV_CONFIG=proxy.yaml` explicitly
opts into copying an operator config; it is never selected implicitly.
UI-triggered rebuilds keep that private config and update the tracked PID.

Overrides are deliberately restricted: `DEV_PORT` is a non-production port,
`DEV_HOST` is loopback, and `DEV_DB` is a permitted scratch filename or `none`.
`DEV_COPY_DB=1` seeds a consistent online backup of local history: use it only
when that history is authorized for the task, and treat the scratch copy as
sensitive. `DEV_COPY_DB=redacted` instead derives the separately validated
documentation copy described below; `0` keeps fresh fixture state. Do not use
broad process kills or start an ad-hoc second main instance.

The browser fixtures share private-target/config/database and redirect guards.
They disable SSE and test bootstrap/poll rendering, not uninterrupted live-feed
delivery. They remove only their synthetic client records. Their assertions must
remain enabled under Python `-O`; the guard suite verifies this.

### Live Chrome DevTools verification

Frontend changes are additionally verified in a visible Chrome window through
Chrome DevTools - headful, never headless. Sign in with the dev operator token,
drive the real fixture traffic and the actual controls, and check console
output, element geometry, the accessibility tree and screen flow in the
rendered page. Narrow fixture data passes the harnesses but can hide
distribution problems (wide values, wrapping, density); the live session is
where those surface. Keep the dev instance and the window open while you look;
stop the instance with `scripts/dev.sh stop` when done.

Fixture traffic for these sessions has its own lifecycle owner, never a paid
provider and never the main instance on `:8080`:

```sh
scripts/dev-traffic.sh         # bursts of neutral loopback traffic at the dev instance
scripts/dev-traffic.sh status
scripts/dev-traffic.sh stop
```

Bursts land about a minute apart so one-minute chart buckets gain a bucket
per burst; each run includes recovered 429s (rate-limited, not errors) and one
final 400 so both health surfaces carry data.

## Container development

Normal [compose.yaml](compose.yaml) only runs a published image. For a local
source build, use [compose.dev.yaml](compose.dev.yaml) from the checkout root.
It is a complete Compose file, not an overlay: project and service are both
`millivolt-dev`, and the container takes the project-scoped name Compose
derives from them.

```sh
docker compose -f compose.dev.yaml up -d --build
docker compose -f compose.dev.yaml logs --tail 50
docker compose -f compose.dev.yaml down
```

The development project keeps its containers and named volumes separate from a
normal deployment, including when `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` is set outside the
checkout. Its `MILLIVOLT_DEV_PORT` and `MILLIVOLT_DEV_IMAGE` inputs are defined
only there, and it shares the deployment Compose's `MILLIVOLT_MEM_LIMIT` and
`MILLIVOLT_PIDS_LIMIT` bounds. Choose an unused development port if `scripts/dev.sh` is already
running.

Rerun the same `up --build` command after source changes. The resulting runtime
image has no compiler or source tree, so dashboard rebuild is unavailable.
`down` preserves its named volumes unless you explicitly request deletion.
This source-image workflow does not replace `scripts/dev.sh`: the host browser
and stress fixtures require that script's private process/database identity.

## Documentation screenshots

The published gallery uses recorded metrics from an explicitly authorized,
redacted local-history snapshot, not fabricated timing or cost values. Never
point capture tools at a main instance or serve a raw history copy for screenshots.
The source is the checkout's local `proxy.db`, opened read-only through the existing
online-backup helper. This workflow needs explicit authorization for that history.

From a checkout with browser dependencies installed and that authorized source:

```sh
(
  set -e
  export DEV_PORT=18081 DEV_HOST=127.0.0.1
  export DEV_DB=/tmp/millivolt/millivolt-dev-docs.db
  export DEV_CONFIG=proxy.example.yaml DEV_COPY_DB=redacted
  trap 'scripts/dev.sh stop' EXIT
  scripts/dev.sh up
  python3 -B -O -m tests.explorer_check \
    --target "http://${DEV_HOST}:${DEV_PORT}" --docs-history docs/images
)
```

Choose an unused permitted dev port. Before startup, `dev.sh` derives a new
metrics-only database: identifiers are replaced, content/headers/debug data are
removed, and recorded timing, token and cost values are retained. The raw online
snapshot is temporary and never served. Treat even the derived database as
sensitive; retained usage and timestamps can reveal activity patterns.

Capture last. The gallery is a picture of the shipped dashboard, so a markup,
CSS or layout change dates every image that shows the affected surface. Recapture
in the same branch once the last layout edit is in, never before it, and
recapture again if a later edit moves what an image shows. A recapture diff is
the review set: inspect each changed file, and expect geometry changes (for
example the request table's 8px cell padding and retry sub-rows) to come with
them.

The capture mode revalidates every row and its provenance, plus exact public
configuration bytes, before and after browser capture. It permits only read-only
same-origin requests: no inference, POST, purge or Settings save. Images are
staged before publication, and the exit trap stops the private process. Review
every gallery image before committing. SSE is deliberately disabled, so the images'
offline indicator describes a static capture session, not current service health.
Captures keep the same category folders under `docs/images/`: `overview`,
`charts`, `explorer`, `requests`, `console` and `settings`. Update the existing
capture owner and Markdown links together when adding a view; the site check
fails on any file under `docs/images/` without a Markdown consumer, so a
recapture that drops a view cannot leave an orphan behind.

The independent `--docs-images` option remains a strict synthetic regression.
Run it only with `DEV_COPY_DB=0` and direct those two images to a scratch directory,
not `docs/images`. It creates and cleans up its own six-request fixture and
rejects copied history. Neither capture mode is a performance or compatibility
benchmark; do not weaken one mode's admission checks to accommodate the other.

## Performance evidence

The published tables, method and limitations live in
[performance and resource usage](docs/performance.md). That page is the single
source for measured numbers; do not copy them into other documentation and do
not edit the page by hand. It is rendered from `perf/results.json`, and
`tests/python/site.py` fails when the two disagree.

`scripts/perf.sh` owns a repeatable local measurement run without touching the
main instance. It starts fresh private instances on a disposable port and stops
them through `scripts/dev.sh`:

```sh
scripts/perf.sh docs      # every published measurement, bundle and page
scripts/perf.sh bench     # isolated Go benchmarks
scripts/perf.sh stress    # private fast and streaming ramps
scripts/perf.sh streaming # sustained end-to-end SSE throughput ramp
scripts/perf.sh sustained # fixed-duration fast-response capacity levels
scripts/perf.sh image     # disposable image content and compressed size
scripts/perf.sh all       # image, bench, then stress
```

`docs` refuses a dirty tree, runs the complete documented set, writes
`perf/results.json`, and regenerates `docs/performance.md`. Commit the bundle
and the page together. Never hand-edit either one; a missing stage, failed
response or unbalanced durable result aborts the run instead of publishing a
partial page.

The bundle is also the source of the facts the page describes: the commit, date
and platform, each stage's response shape (frame count, usage and unit cost),
the configured durations, and the harness declarations for captures, previews
and the observer. `cmd/stress` records the fixture shape in its workload line
and the collector validates it per stage, so a table and the sentence beside it
cannot describe different runs. The landing headline reads the same bundle;
`tests/python/performance.py` renders two bundles that differ only in those
fields and fails if any published sentence keeps its old text.

For request, SSE-event, response-byte and output-token rates, use the
`streaming` mode. It derives those rates from responses the client accepted
byte-for-byte, and it is still a synthetic-fixture measurement, not a universal
capacity claim.

For an individual stress run with the private dev instance already running:

```sh
go run ./cmd/stress -target http://127.0.0.1:8081 -concurrency 1,8,32,128 -duration 5s
```

The harness does not manage or reconfigure the proxy. It uses a local synthetic
upstream and checks exact bytes, durable rows/tokens/cost and the same-process
storage-drop delta. A drop is a failed stage even if every HTTP request
succeeded, unless the run asks for an overload observation with
`-allow-drops`; that mode still requires `durable + dropped = successful
requests` and still aborts on a response failure. Read
`go run ./cmd/stress -h` for workload/safety controls.
The ramp retains its cumulative fixture history across measured stages, then
removes only its unique client records after measurements finish. Cleanup has
its own bounded wait even after cancellation and revalidates private process,
config and database ownership before every deletion. A cleanup failure is
reported, never silently treated as success.

Report workload, duration, concurrency, configuration, contention and whether
storage/observers were active. Separate request throughput from durable
throughput. Closed-loop bursts, microbenchmarks and local upstreams do not
establish sustained production capacity. The current storage contract and
capacity caveats live in [operations](docs/operations.md#storage-and-accounting).
Use the existing `BenchmarkStorageWriter` and `BenchmarkProxyDurableContention`
for isolated writer/contention comparisons; neither replaces a real HTTP run.
For the analytical projection's memory, use the self-seeded
`BenchmarkProjectionFootprint` (retained and transient bytes per stored record)
and `BenchmarkProjectionProcessRSS` (process RSS after readiness) from the test
overlay; they need no running instance:

```sh
scripts/check.sh go test -run='^$' -bench='BenchmarkProjection' -count=1 ./internal/web
```

## Versioning and publication

[VERSION](VERSION) is the only semantic version source; do not duplicate it in
package manifests, build arguments or image metadata. Normal and prerelease
SemVer are supported without build metadata. A release tag must be exactly
`v` followed by that file's version. The release CLI validates the same contract:

```sh
millivolt_version="$(tr -d '\r\n' < VERSION)"
go run ./cmd/release -revision "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" -tag "v$millivolt_version"
```

Publication is automatic. A code-bearing versioned promotion releases when the
promotion PR merges, after the full gate has passed for the promoted commit, or
after the closest gated `testing` commit plus a docs-only delta. A non-Dependabot
promotion also requires a successful
[escalation](.github/workflows/escalation.yml) run for the reviewed head; the
promotion PR starts it automatically, and `required` waits for it under a
bounded, fail-closed proof. The merged-PR
event carries the exact merge commit; a delivered `main` push is an idempotent
fallback, so a dropped push event cannot leave the release untagged. A
Dependabot security PR targets `main` and runs the full gate itself rather than
reusing a `testing` result. The release `publish` job waits for `required`.
The `publish-testing` job waits for `unit`, `browser` and `container` instead,
because a testing push has no promotion proof to wait for:

1. A code-bearing promotion PR owns the version bump. `required` compares
   VERSION against every existing `v*` tag with SemVer precedence and rejects a
   non-Dependabot main PR unless VERSION is newer. Docs/site-only promotions
   skip that comparison, validate docs, workflow policy and the site in
   `required`, and stay release-free. If VERSION is already tagged, no
   release is cut: this is the Dependabot security-merge case, and the next
   versioned promotion releases the change.
2. The workflow creates the annotated `v<version>` tag on the reviewed
   promotion merge commit and builds and publishes the multi-arch image with
   `main`, `sha-*`, `version` and (for non-prereleases) `latest` tags, including
   an SBOM and max-mode provenance. The `sha-*` tag and OCI revision label name
   the promotion merge commit that was built.
3. Only after the image exists does it push the tag and create the GitHub
   release. It never pushes `main`. Release notes filter merge commits, dedupe
   subjects, use the lowercase image path, include the digest, and link the
   compare range. A failed image build leaves no public release pointing at a
   missing image. `main` and `latest` exclude prereleases; the `testing` alias
   never moves them.

Docs and site-only pushes to `testing` skip image work. They validate Markdown,
the generated site, workflow policy and docs contracts. A docs/site-only main
promotion also skips the VERSION and full-gate proofs but runs the same
Markdown, generated-site, workflow-policy and repository checks in `required`;
a Pages-relevant merged main push stays docs-only, so Pages deploys without
rebuilding images or cutting a release; the merged-PR release path classifies
the change and skips publication. A code-bearing promotion must carry a VERSION
newer than every existing tag and cuts a release. A manually pushed `v*` tag
still ships exactly as tagged through the same
pipeline, with the image published before the release is created. A manual tag
must match VERSION. Code-bearing pushes to `testing` publish the moving
`ghcr.io/llm-4-people/millivolt:testing` image after the same checks and
container builds, without cutting a release or any version tag. Its OCI version
label reports the embedded VERSION, which can lag the latest release.
Manual validation of a candidate remains available:

```sh
scripts/check.sh release -revision "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" -tag "v$millivolt_version"
```

Run the shared checks before relying on a release. Confirm the hosted container
build and smoke tests succeed, then check the package visibility and anonymous
pull. Do not report a release/image as available merely because validation or a
local build passed. Image usage and persistence limits live in
[operations](docs/containers.md#versions-and-images). The gate clears inherited
Git routing/configuration variables before checking
source identity, so another worktree or external ignore policy cannot satisfy
the release checks accidentally.

Only push the intended release tag after that check succeeds. Main changes go
through the protected pull request path. The workflow publishes images
automatically and creates the release with notes generated from the commit log.
Native container checks run before the multi-platform publish job. After the
promotion run, verify the published tag and image:
```sh
gh release view "v$millivolt_version"
docker buildx imagetools inspect "ghcr.io/llm-4-people/millivolt:$millivolt_version"
```

### If a release fails

- Before the tag is pushed, no public release exists. Fix the failure and rerun
  the main workflow or promote a new version.
- After the tag is pushed, keep the tag in place. If the GitHub release is
  missing, create it from that tag or publish a new patch version. An automatic
  tag push does not start a second workflow run.
- Do not move or delete a published version tag.

For local container verification, build with Docker, resolve the image's
immutable ID, then use the same fixture as CI:

```sh
docker build -t millivolt:check .
millivolt_image_id="$(docker image inspect --format '{{.Id}}' millivolt:check)"
scripts/check.sh container --image "$millivolt_image_id"
```

The shared container mode validates Compose defaults and owns only its
disposable, network-isolated Docker fixture, selected by immutable image ID.
It checks startup, HTTP, Settings and durable state across stop/start, then backs
up the stopped volumes and restores into another fresh container. Recovery must
retain settings, history and private file ownership/modes. It never publishes
a host port or reuses an operator volume. It complements, rather
than replaces, the host lifecycle in `scripts/dev.sh`.

## Change checklist

Use sentence case or lowercase in prose, headings and labels. Avoid em dashes;
preserve exact protocol names, identifiers, user data and license wording.

- Add a targeted regression for a reproduced defect; preserve existing coverage.
- Keep defaults, units, schemas and state transitions at their canonical owner.
- Measure allocations/latency when changing the hot path or analytical folds.
- Check saved views, mobile layout and accessibility for visible changes.
- Update the relevant existing documentation, not duplicate specifications.
- Exclude local configs, databases, tokens, captures and generated test artifacts.
- Preserve dependency licenses. Report vulnerabilities using [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md),
  not a public issue containing sensitive reproduction data.

Dependabot checks Go, npm, Python, Docker and GitHub Actions dependencies weekly
with grouped minor and patch updates. Review dependency changes and re-run
checks; runtime version files still require deliberate updates and verification.
The Docker `golang` base is deliberately left manual because its tag must move
with go.mod; distroless updates remain automated. Security updates target
`main` as described in the branch workflow. Dependency review runs on pull
requests, and a scheduled `govulncheck` workflow covers the Go module graph.
The scanner is pinned as a tool dependency in `tools.go`, so it resolves from
this module and `go.sum` covers it instead of a version being fetched fresh on
each run. These scans complement tests; a clean scan is not a security guarantee.

pages.markdown_text:
# Support

millivolt is pre-1.0 and maintained on a best-effort basis. There is no
response-time SLA.

## Read first

- [Documentation index](docs/README.md)
- [Quickstart](README.md#quickstart)
- [Operations](docs/operations.md)
- [Reverse proxy](docs/reverse-proxy.md)
- [Security](SECURITY.md)

## Where to ask

- **Usage, configuration, or deployment question:** open a
  [usage question](https://github.com/LLM-4-People/millivolt/issues/new?template=question.yml).
- **Reproducible defect:** open a
  [bug report](https://github.com/LLM-4-People/millivolt/issues/new?template=bug_report.yml).
- **Concrete proposal:** open a
  [feature request](https://github.com/LLM-4-People/millivolt/issues/new?template=feature_request.yml).
- **Security vulnerability:** use the
  [private advisory channel](https://github.com/LLM-4-People/millivolt/security/advisories/new).
  Do not open a public issue.

Search existing issues before opening a new one. Include the millivolt version
or revision and a sanitized configuration shape. Remove credentials, private
prompts, databases, and host-specific paths.

pages.markdown_text:
# Third-party notices

millivolt's [MIT license](LICENSE) covers the project's own work, not a
relicensing of dependencies.

## Embedded dashboard library

[uPlot 1.6.32](https://github.com/leeoniya/uPlot/tree/1.6.32) is vendored as
`internal/web/static/vendor/uplot.js` and `uplot.css`. Copyright (c) 2022 Leon
Sorokin. Its complete [MIT notice](internal/web/static/vendor/uplot.LICENSE)
is kept beside the assets and included in the embedded filesystem.
Preserve that notice when redistributing the library or built dashboard.

The notice was checked against the
[upstream versioned license](https://github.com/leeoniya/uPlot/blob/1.6.32/LICENSE).
Update the version, assets and notice together when changing this dependency.

## Embedded typefaces

The dashboard and the documentation site ship four WOFF2 faces in
`internal/web/static/fonts`: Instrument Sans (roman and italic), Instrument
Serif, and JetBrains Mono. They are Copyright 2022 The Instrument Sans Project
Authors, Copyright 2022 The Instrument Serif Project Authors, and Copyright 2020
The JetBrains Mono Project Authors. All three families are licensed under the
[SIL Open Font License 1.1](internal/web/static/fonts/LICENSE); the complete
notice and copyright lines are kept beside the files and included in the
embedded filesystem. The dashboard, the docs site and the generated brand
plates all consume these exact faces, so no third-party font request is made at
runtime. Preserve the notice when redistributing the fonts or a built
dashboard.

## Module and development dependencies

[go.mod](go.mod) and [go.sum](go.sum) identify Go dependencies; their upstream
module distributions carry their own licenses. [package-lock.json](package-lock.json)
pins development-only jsdom dependencies. [requirements-dev.txt](requirements-dev.txt)
pins Python browser tooling; Playwright selects its corresponding Chromium build.
[requirements-docs.txt](requirements-docs.txt) pins the Python-Markdown renderer
(BSD-3-Clause) used to build the static documentation site; PyYAML (MIT) is a
development dependency used by the workflow policy checks. Node, Python and
these build/test dependencies are not required to run the proxy.

## Container distribution

The [Dockerfile](Dockerfile) runs [the notice collector](scripts/licenses/main.go)
against the exact target binary's Go dependency graph. It preserves module,
package-ancestor and Go toolchain license, copyright, notice and patent files,
plus the embedded uPlot notice, under `/usr/share/licenses/millivolt`.
The deterministic `manifest.json` records versions, relative paths and SHA-256
content hashes. Missing notices and module replacements fail the build for
review; this collector does not classify licenses or grant additional rights.

The pinned distroless runtime retains its own files and dependency notices.
Its [upstream project](https://github.com/GoogleContainerTools/distroless)
documents the base-image contents. Node, Python and development dependencies
are not copied into the runtime image.

When distributing a binary by another route, generate and include the same
bundle with `go run ./scripts/licenses -target linux/amd64 -out NEW_DIRECTORY`
(or `linux/arm64`) and review the actual distribution. This source notice alone
is not a complete binary-release license bundle.
